sourceA.title: A proposal with two incomplete sources
sourceA.text:
Our course project asked us to recommend a use for a vacant town-centre building. We received an estate survey and interviews with residents, but neither source contained a ready-made answer. The survey described size, heating costs and the condition of the roof. The interviews discussed needs, including affordable meeting space and activities for young people.
One group immediately favoured a youth arts centre because the interviews sounded persuasive. Another preferred offices because the estate figures appeared more objective. Our tutor asked both groups what their chosen source could not establish. Residents could describe a need without proving that the building could meet it safely. A cost survey could describe a property without deciding which public purpose deserved priority.
We combined the sources into a table of supported points, uncertainties and decisions requiring further advice. The arts proposal needed information about supervision and sound insulation. The office plan depended on demand that nobody had yet measured. We then developed a limited trial using the safest rooms for scheduled activities while specialists examined the remaining questions.
During the presentation, a partner introduced a new condition: funding would cover only one year of staffing. We had to revise the proposal instead of delivering our prepared ending unchanged. Our written follow-up explained which activities could continue through volunteers and which required trained paid staff.
The assessment recorded reading, writing and interaction separately. It also noted that we had already practised the broad theme, so a later task used a different building and different needs. The purpose was not to award a level for finishing a project. It was to collect clearer evidence of what we could understand, explain and adapt when the information did not match a memorised answer.

sourceB.title: The proposed late-opening library
sourceB.text:
A university considered keeping one library open overnight during examination weeks. A student survey showed strong support, especially among people living in crowded accommodation. A security report explained that the existing staffing plan covered the building only until midnight. Several campaigners treated the report as opposition to students, while some staff treated survey support as proof that all students would attend.
The working group separated the questions. The survey identified a need and a preference; it did not establish expected numbers at each hour. The report identified a constraint; it did not rule out every possible adjustment. The group interviewed students about likely attendance and asked security staff to estimate the requirements of a restricted area rather than the entire building.
A two-week trial kept one accessible floor open with a booking limit, clear support arrangements and a staffed entrance. Usage records showed that demand was highest before two in the morning and much lower afterwards. Feedback also revealed that some students wanted a quiet place but had assumed the trial guaranteed subject tutoring, which it did not.
The final recommendation extended late opening to two rather than continuing all night. It included clearer descriptions and an option to review the pattern during a future examination period. Some students remained disappointed, but the group could explain how the decision followed from both need and practical evidence.
The process did not remove disagreement. It made the disagreement more precise. People could challenge an attendance estimate or staffing condition without claiming that the other side cared nothing about safety or study. That distinction made a limited, revisable agreement possible.

listening.teaching: For an integrated task, I ask learners to keep three columns: what the sources establish, what they suggest and what remains unknown. This prevents an attractive recommendation from appearing before the evidence has been examined. It also helps with writing. A report can identify a real need while explaining that one proposed method still requires testing. During discussion, a partner may introduce a new constraint. Learners should not treat this as an interruption to the answer they memorised. It is part of the communication problem. They need to ask a useful question, consider the consequence and explain a revision. We collect several pieces of evidence rather than award a broad ability level from one polished presentation. An unfamiliar task after a delay is especially useful, though it still samples only part of a person’s ability. Our report therefore describes the conditions, observed strengths and remaining needs. Its value depends on being accurate enough to guide future practice, not on producing the most flattering possible label.
listening.test: I helped select a location for an adult skills course. The cheapest room was attractive on paper, but interviews with potential learners revealed that its last bus left before the class would finish. Another venue cost more and had better transport, though its computer access was limited. We combined the cost information with the interview findings instead of treating one source as the complete answer. Our recommendation used the better-connected venue for discussion sessions and a separate computer room on two planned evenings. Before confirming it, we checked whether moving between venues created new access problems. The final plan was a compromise, and we recorded what needed review after the first month. I learned that combining sources is not merely writing two summaries next to each other. It means explaining how different kinds of information affect the same decision and being clear when a convenient solution creates a new difficulty for someone else. The next review will ask learners about the whole journey between sessions, not merely the quality of each room.

sourceA.title: An evening service with conditions — extended case review
sourceA.text:
A fictional town library is considering two additional evening openings each week. Its manager wants a proposal that distinguishes a useful idea from an affordable commitment. Staff have collected comments, but a popular suggestion is not automatically a workable timetable. The following briefing explains how the team should discuss its evidence and responsibilities. The service is intended for residents who cannot visit during normal working hours, including carers and people on rotating shifts.

The pilot could begin on one evening rather than two, allowing the rota to be checked under ordinary conditions. Comments from visitors should be considered alongside attendance records. Otherwise, a busy first night might be mistaken for evidence that the same level of demand will continue throughout the year.

We must allocate funds before advertising additional opening hours. The survey provides an indication of demand, not a complete forecast. The manager should make a firm commitment only after checking staffing. We need to take account of staff working consecutive evenings. Extended hours could meet the needs of people on rotating shifts. A limited trial would provide evidence without creating an indefinite obligation.

We should draw a distinction between attendance and satisfaction. The council must bear the cost of additional security staff. Early results may shed light on which evening is busiest. A written rota would reduce uncertainty about individual responsibilities. We cannot rule out lower attendance during winter storms. The final report should set out the conditions for continuing.

The library subsequently costed a six-week pilot. Opening on Wednesday required two desk staff and one security officer, with an estimated additional cost of 180 pounds per evening. The council offered 900 pounds, leaving a shortfall of 180 pounds across the full trial. One councillor suggested using volunteers to close the gap. Staff explained that volunteers could help visitors but could not replace the required security officer. The manager therefore proposed five evenings instead of six unless further funding was confirmed. She also added a register of people who arrived shortly before closing, because attendance alone would miss whether the later hours actually helped the intended users.

sourceB.title: A promise about accessible theatre seats
sourceB.text:
The Marlow Theatre advertised twelve accessible seats for each performance in its new studio. The phrase seemed precise, yet a local access group asked what the number meant. Six spaces accommodated wheelchair users, while six conventional seats had removable armrests. The two arrangements met different needs and could not always be exchanged without changing the surrounding layout. Describing all twelve simply as accessible concealed distinctions that mattered when somebody booked.

The theatre's booking manager initially worried that a longer description would confuse customers. The access group argued that customers were already doing the work of discovering the conditions through repeated telephone calls. They proposed a short online table describing each arrangement, the companion seating available and the route to the studio. A telephone option would remain for people who preferred individual discussion. The theatre agreed to test the table for four performances before changing its publicity permanently.

During the trial, staff recorded thirty-one enquiries. Nine concerned companion seating, eight concerned the step-free route and fourteen concerned whether a particular seat arrangement would suit the visitor. The figures did not show how many potential customers had decided not to enquire. Nevertheless, they identified information that could be made clearer. Two customers also reported that the label accessible had led them to assume that every seat could accommodate a wheelchair.

The revised publicity now states the number of wheelchair spaces separately from the number of seats with removable armrests. It promises accurate information and a discussion of individual requirements, rather than guaranteeing that every arrangement will suit every visitor. The theatre has not increased the studio's capacity. Its improvement lies in making the commitment more intelligible and limiting avoidable uncertainty before booking. The access group supports the revision but wants staff training checked again after the summer, when temporary employees join. A clear description can be undermined if people giving advice interpret it differently.

listening.teaching: At today's library meeting I want to clarify the costed evening proposal. We are considering Wednesday opening, not a permanent extension across the week. Each evening needs two desk staff and a security officer. The additional cost is estimated at 180 pounds. For six evenings that is 1,080 pounds, but the council has offered 900. We therefore cannot advertise six fully funded sessions yet. One option is to run five; another is to secure the remaining 180 pounds before launch. Volunteers can assist visitors, but they cannot replace the security officer required by our operating arrangements. Please do not describe them as a free substitute. We will record attendance and ask whether the later opening enabled a visit that otherwise would not have happened. The questions will be optional, and a person may decline without affecting access. We also want to record people arriving shortly before the current closing time. That could help us understand whether the extension addresses an existing difficulty. It will not tell us about everyone who never reaches the building. Before publicity goes out, the finance officer must confirm the final number of evenings. I will send the proposed rota tomorrow. Staff should identify clashes by Friday rather than assume that the usual daytime arrangements will cover the extra hours.
listening.test: This is a message for members using the harbour sports centre. From next Monday, the small exercise room will be available for supervised rehabilitation sessions on Tuesday mornings. There will be eight places in each session, with a qualified instructor present. That is the maximum number the instructor can supervise under the agreed plan; it is not a promise that every member will be offered a place immediately. You must have an initial discussion with the coordinator before booking your first session. The discussion is free and can take place by telephone. We originally planned to provide transport from the main car park, but that service has not been funded. Please make your own arrangements or ask the coordinator about the accessible drop-off point. The fee of twelve pounds covers the session and use of the changing facilities. It does not include individual treatment or an exercise programme outside the centre. Members who cannot attend should cancel by noon on the preceding day so that the place can be offered to someone else. If the instructor is unavailable, the session will be cancelled rather than run without supervision. We will review demand after four weeks. A full waiting list may justify considering another session, but no additional day has yet been approved.

sourceA.title: What a shorter queue really means — extended case review
sourceA.text:
The fictional Brookside advice centre has reorganised its reception system. Managers want to explain the early figures without exaggerating what they establish. Queue length, waiting time and the quality of advice are related, but they are not identical measures. Some appointments now take place by telephone, which changes who appears in the reception data. The centre has prepared language for a cautious progress briefing rather than a celebratory announcement.

A person receiving detailed advice may need a longer appointment, so faster service is not always better service. The centre should examine whether clients understand their next step. It should also check whether telephone users and people visiting in person face different barriers before describing the system as an improvement for everyone.

A shorter queue does not necessarily imply faster individual service. The figures suggest improvement but do not prove its cause. Telephone appointments may account for part of the apparent decline. The reduction was modest rather than dramatic. We should distinguish an accurate count from a representative sample. Some clients described the new reception process as convenient.

Convenience alone does not establish that the advice was appropriate. The manager acknowledged limitations without dismissing the positive results. A plausible explanation still needs independent checking. The evidence is consistent with a benefit, although alternatives remain. We need comparable figures from a similar period. The final statement should reflect the uncertainty in the findings.

At the advice centre, the first comparison covered 120 appointments before the change and 118 afterwards. Median visible waiting fell from 24 to 17 minutes. However, the later group included 35 telephone appointments, which did not create a queue in reception. A staff member proposed excluding them, but the manager pointed out that this would answer a different question about the remaining in-person service. The revised briefing reports both the overall figures and the separate appointment types. It also notes that no check of clients' understanding was conducted. The next review will therefore include an optional follow-up question about whether people knew what to do after the appointment.

sourceB.title: A headline about lecture recordings
sourceB.text:
A university department trialled recordings in one first-year lecture course. A student newspaper reported that recordings had transformed attendance because fewer empty seats were visible in the final month. The lecturer objected to the word transformed. The course register showed a small increase in attendance, but the final month also included revision sessions and an assessed group activity. The newspaper's observation was not necessarily false; its explanation was stronger than the evidence justified.

The department had introduced recordings primarily to help students revisit difficult explanations. It had not designed the trial as a test of attendance. Sixty-two students answered an optional survey, and forty-nine said they had used a recording at least once. Those figures showed use among respondents. They did not establish how frequently the entire class listened, whether students watched complete lectures, or whether listening improved examination performance. Some respondents described the recordings as reassuring even when they rarely replayed them.

A teaching committee asked the lecturer to distinguish availability, actual use and learning benefit in the report. She proposed collecting anonymous viewing patterns alongside samples of students' explanations of key concepts. The committee accepted that these sources might illuminate how recordings were used, while noting that an improvement in explanations could have several causes. Students would be informed about the collection and allowed to decline the research component without losing access to recordings.

The newspaper revised its headline to say that students welcomed the recording trial. Even that statement was qualified in the article by reference to the voluntary survey. The editor retained an account of the attendance discussion because the uncertainty was informative. A responsible report need not suppress encouraging findings; it must avoid allowing a vivid phrase to imply a causal result that nobody has actually demonstrated. The lecturer would review the revised measures with students before collecting new information.

listening.teaching: Let us look at the advice-centre comparison before choosing a headline. Before the change, there were 120 recorded appointments and a median visible wait of 24 minutes. Afterwards there were 118 appointments and the median was 17 minutes. That looks encouraging. However, 35 appointments in the later period were by telephone. Those clients were not standing in the reception queue. If we describe the result as a faster service for everyone, we would be combining different experiences. We could report the overall change, but we should also show appointment type and explain the limitation. Removing telephone appointments entirely is not automatically wrong; it simply changes the question to the experience of people who still attend in person. Another issue is quality. A shorter wait does not tell us whether clients understood the advice. We have not measured that yet. The next review will offer an optional question asking whether people know their next step. Staff should avoid suggesting that a positive answer proves the advice solved the underlying problem. It is a more limited measure of understanding. My preferred wording is that the early figures suggest a change in access and waiting patterns. They justify further checking, not an announcement that the new system has conclusively improved every part of the service.
listening.test: The town's swimming club has asked me to explain the results of its membership survey. We sent the questionnaire to 240 current members and received 84 replies. Sixty-three respondents said they preferred Saturday morning lessons to Sunday afternoon lessons. That is three quarters of respondents, not three quarters of everyone in the club. We did not ask former members or people currently on the waiting list. Their preferences may be different. The committee is therefore using the result to plan a small Saturday trial, not to cancel all Sunday classes. The trial will last four weeks and use one instructor who is already available. Members will be invited to book through the usual system, and we will record bookings, attendance and cancellations separately. A full booking list can still leave spaces if people do not attend. At the end, the committee will compare the sessions and ask whether the time created new opportunities or merely moved existing swimmers from another day. The survey does show a clear preference among the people who replied. It does not establish how large the demand would be across the wider community. Please retain that distinction when discussing the decision with other members. The committee will publish the review date in advance.

sourceA.title: Rewriting a housing notice — extended case review
sourceA.text:
A fictional housing cooperative needs access to residents' kitchens to inspect shared water pipes. Its first notice sounded abrupt and gave no way to discuss individual circumstances. A revised version must remain clear about the inspection while respecting privacy and making the required action easy to identify. The team is preparing both a formal letter and a short reminder message. Each version must preserve the same deadline and contact arrangements.

Privacy is central to residents' response. The letter should explain what staff will inspect, how identity will be checked and how a different appointment can be requested. A shorter reminder can omit background discussion, but it must not drop the action that residents are expected to take.

We would appreciate access to your kitchen during the inspection window. Please contact the office if the proposed time is unsuitable. The inspection is required, but alternative appointments are available. Residents are requested to reply by Thursday afternoon. For clarity, the visit does not involve opening personal cupboards. A member of staff will show identification before entering.

Could you let us know whether anyone requires additional support? The reminder should retain the deadline stated in the formal letter. Friendly wording must not obscure what residents need to do. We apologise for the inconvenience caused by the inspection. If you have already replied, no further action is needed. A firm request can remain respectful and specific.

The cooperative tested its revised letter with eight residents before sending it to all 64 households. Five could identify the reply deadline immediately, but three thought that access was compulsory at the first proposed time. The team therefore moved the alternative-appointment information into the opening paragraph. It kept the explanation of the inspection's purpose, rather than relying on a threatening reminder of the rules. The office will accept replies by telephone as well as email. Residents who need support may discuss it privately, and the public booking sheet will show appointment times without names or health details.

sourceB.title: Explaining a payroll correction
sourceB.text:
A small research organisation discovered that a travel allowance had been calculated incorrectly for nineteen employees. The finance manager's first draft email said that an adjustment would be processed in due course. It did not explain whether employees owed money, would receive money or needed to submit a form. Staff representatives warned that the phrase was likely to create anxiety precisely because it avoided the information readers needed.

The error had resulted in underpayments, not overpayments. The revised email stated this in the opening paragraph. It explained that the missing amounts would be added to the following month's salary and that affected employees would receive an individual calculation through the secure payroll portal. Nobody needed to send bank details by email. People who thought that their calculation was wrong could contact a named payroll officer within ten working days. A separate technical note described the formula for managers who needed to review the process.

The organisation did not publish individual sums on the staff website. Although transparency mattered, it did not justify exposing personal financial information. Instead, the public internal notice reported the number of affected employees, the correction timetable and the checking procedure. It also acknowledged that some staff might have incurred costs because of the delay and invited them to discuss these privately, without promising automatic reimbursement before the circumstances were reviewed.

The staff representatives supported the message because it distinguished a confirmed remedy from a request that still required consideration. They asked that the phrase in due course be avoided when a date was already known. Formal language can help maintain a professional relationship, but vagueness is not the same as tact. The finance manager agreed to have future notices checked by a colleague outside the department, whose unfamiliarity with payroll terminology would reveal assumptions that specialists might otherwise overlook.

listening.teaching: We have tested the inspection letter with eight residents. Five found the deadline immediately, but three thought they had no choice about the first appointment time. That is not what we intend, so the revised opening now says that alternative appointments can be arranged. Please keep that sentence near the request for access. Moving it to a footnote would recreate the problem. The letter will go to 64 households, with replies accepted by telephone or email. The office should not ask people to explain private circumstances on the public booking sheet. That sheet will show available times only. A member of staff will discuss support needs individually. Another point concerns identification. Residents should know that the inspector will show an identity card before entering. We do not need a long description of every tool used during the visit, but we do need to explain that personal cupboards will not be opened. The short text reminder must preserve the Thursday deadline and the office contact route. It can omit background about the pipe system. Please compare the two versions before sending them: shortening is useful only if the essential action and the choice of appointment remain clear. If someone has already replied, the reminder should explicitly say that no further action is required.
listening.test: I am calling about the changes to tomorrow's training assessment. The practical session will begin at nine thirty in workshop four, not workshop two. The written section remains in the upstairs classroom at eleven. Please arrive fifteen minutes before the practical session so that the assessor can check your identification. You should bring protective footwear; gloves and eye protection will be provided. If you do not have suitable footwear, contact the training office this afternoon rather than arriving and hoping to borrow some. The centre has only a limited number of spare pairs. The email sent yesterday used the phrase mandatory rescheduling. That was unclear: you must use the new room, but anyone whose travel arrangements make the new practical start impossible may request another date. The office will discuss those requests individually. No fee will be charged for a change caused by this timetable correction. However, please do not simply fail to attend without contacting us. The written assessment result will be sent through the learner portal, not read out to the group. If you cannot access the portal, we can arrange a private collection appointment. Thank you for checking the details before travelling. Staff will answer questions through the training office today.

sourceA.title: A lecture on urban shade — extended case review
sourceA.text:
In a fictional public lecture, landscape researcher Elena explains why a city should not judge its tree programme by planting totals alone. A young tree offers little shade immediately, and survival depends on soil, watering and protection. Her lecture moves from the problem of summer heat to the practical choices a maintenance team must make. The briefing below preserves that sequence so that listeners can reconstruct the argument rather than merely remember isolated statistics.

For a school route, the location of shade can matter more than a distant increase in canopy cover. Elena therefore asks the audience to connect measurement with the intended benefit. Her practical conclusion is to care for existing trees while choosing new sites in relation to people's daily movements.

The speaker first establishes why planting totals can be misleading. She then turns to the conditions required for young trees to survive. The shaded playground is an illustration, not the entire argument. Although mature trees provide shade, benefits develop over many years. Maintenance should be treated as part of the investment. The proposal depends on reliable summer watering.

A survival rate tells us more than an initial planting count. The lecturer qualifies her recommendation rather than withdrawing it. In this context, shade distribution matters as much as total cover. The conclusion returns to the neighbourhoods with the least protection. My notes separate the central claim from supporting examples. A useful summary preserves the conditions attached to the recommendation.

The city has now identified twelve possible planting sites near schools. Six have adequate soil volume, four would require reconstruction of the pavement, and two are unsuitable because of underground services. Elena uses this classification to show why a target of twelve new trees cannot be treated as twelve equivalent projects. The maintenance team can support eight new sites this year. Rather than selecting the easiest eight automatically, the council will compare current shade, walking routes and preparation costs. The lecture ends by asking students to write a recommendation that retains those competing criteria instead of copying the planting target.

sourceB.title: Why a materials lecture begins with failure
sourceB.text:
Professor Chen opened a lecture on reusable packaging by showing a damaged container rather than a successful product. A hinge had cracked after repeated washing. Several students assumed that the example proved reusable packaging was environmentally inferior to disposable packaging. Chen explained that the failed hinge raised a design question; it did not settle the wider comparison. The environmental balance depended on production, washing, transport, the number of uses and what happened at the end of the container's life.

The demonstration came from a pilot in a college cafeteria. Two hundred containers had been supplied, and 146 were returned during the first month. Some missing containers might still have been in students' rooms, so the remaining fifty-four could not all be described as permanently lost. Nor did the number returned reveal how many times each container had been reused. Without that information, a simple average environmental claim would be premature.

Chen then distinguished durability from return behaviour. Improving the hinge could extend physical life, but it would not encourage people to bring containers back. A convenient return point might improve return behaviour without changing the material at all. The cafeteria therefore planned two separate changes: a redesigned hinge and a return station near the library. Testing both at once could improve the service, yet would make it difficult to isolate the contribution of each change.

The lecturer did not argue that practical decisions must wait for perfect experiments. Instead, she asked students to state whether they were recommending a service improvement or claiming a measured causal effect. Those were different tasks. Her final slide showed a diagram linking manufacture, use, return and cleaning, with unknown quantities marked explicitly. Students were asked to reconstruct the chain in their notes, placing the broken hinge within it rather than allowing the vivid opening example to dominate the conclusion.

listening.teaching: I would like you to reconstruct the argument of the shade lecture rather than write down every sentence. Start with the city's proposed twelve planting sites near schools. They are not twelve identical opportunities. Six already have adequate soil volume. Four need pavement reconstruction, and two conflict with underground services. Elena used that classification to challenge a simple planting target. The maintenance team can support only eight additional sites this year. That does not automatically mean choosing the six easy sites plus the two cheapest remaining ones. We also need to consider where children walk and which routes currently have little shade. In your notes, separate the target, the capacity limit and the selection criteria. The example of a playground illustrates where shade may be useful; it does not prove that every playground is the best site. Elena's wider argument is that the benefits develop over time and require care. A tree counted on planting day may not survive to provide substantial shade. You may take a position, but explain which trade-off supports it. A list of twelve locations without those conditions would miss the structure of the lecture.

The site has poor mobile reception, so download the map before leaving. If the weather makes the path unsafe, both groups will stay at college and examine the archive photographs instead. We will decide by seven thirty and send a message through the course portal. Do not travel directly to the mill before checking it.

sourceA.title: An organiser reflects on a crowded festival — extended case review
sourceA.text:
In this fictional interview, an arts organiser discusses a neighbourhood festival that attracted more people than expected. The interviewer asks whether the event should simply become larger next year. The organiser welcomes interest but is cautious about treating attendance as the only sign of success. Her comments concern staff capacity, access and the experience of nearby residents. Listeners should distinguish what she says directly from what her careful qualifications allow us to infer.

The organiser wants residents to remain partners in the festival rather than become an audience for a decision already made. Her cautious phrases keep that possibility open. A reliable interpretation must retain both her pleasure at public interest and her concern that a larger programme would require stronger support.

The organiser sounds pleased with attendance but uneasy about expansion. Her phrase “a useful beginning” stops short of declaring success. She concedes that a larger event could attract more funding. However, she questions whether the volunteer team could sustain it. The interviewer interprets hesitation as opposition, which is too strong. Her answer implies a preference for improving access before expanding.

She does not claim that nearby residents opposed every performance. The qualification concerns evening noise rather than daytime attendance. A warm tone alone does not establish agreement with a proposal. We should support an inference with specific words and context. She recommends consultation before making next year’s programme public. Her position is conditional support, not an outright refusal.

The organiser later clarified what further support meant. The festival had used 42 volunteer shifts, and six had been covered at the last minute by committee members. A sponsor offered money for another performance but not for volunteer coordination. The organiser said this was welcome, although it did not solve the difficulty she had identified. She also described a resident consultation as overdue, rather than optional. Learners should ask whether these details support an inference of opposition or a more specific concern about conditions. A useful analysis does not treat her refusal to celebrate expansion immediately as evidence that she dislikes the festival.

sourceB.title: A curator speaks about an unexpected donation
sourceB.text:
When a private collector offered a local museum 180 photographs, the regional radio presenter described the donation as a remarkable gift that must be accepted. Curator Helen responded that the offer could be valuable. Her choice of could was deliberate. The museum had seen digital previews of sixty images, but it had not checked the physical condition of the full collection or established whether the donor held the rights needed for public display.

The presenter asked whether those checks were merely bureaucratic obstacles. Helen replied that an image could be historically interesting and still be expensive to conserve or difficult to exhibit lawfully. She pointed out that the museum had storage for approximately ninety additional photographs under suitable conditions. Accepting the entire donation would therefore require either more storage or a carefully agreed selection. Her explanation was not a judgement that the remaining images lacked value.

When asked whether she was worried about offending the donor, Helen said that a clear conversation now would be kinder than an enthusiastic acceptance followed by years in an unsuitable cupboard. The remark implied that she preferred honest limits to a flattering promise. It did not establish that the donor had behaved unreasonably. Indeed, Helen described the donor as willing to discuss the practical arrangements and share information about where the photographs had come from.

The museum proposed a preliminary review by a conservator and a rights specialist, followed by a meeting to decide what could be accepted. Helen resisted the presenter's invitation to call this a rejection. The process was still open, subject to information that the museum needed before making a responsible commitment. The interview left listeners with a qualified position: interest in the material, gratitude for the offer and caution about obligations. Treating any one of these as the whole answer would distort the curator's view.

listening.teaching: Listen to how the festival organiser qualifies her support. She says the sponsor's offer is welcome, which directly expresses appreciation. But the offer pays for an extra performance, not for coordinating volunteers. The organiser has already described coordination as the main constraint. Forty-two shifts were required last year, and six had to be filled at the last minute by committee members. That is why her positive response to the money does not amount to approval of expansion. We should also notice her description of consultation as overdue. It implies that a discussion with residents should have happened earlier, not merely that it might be pleasant in future. However, do not infer that all residents oppose the festival; she has not said that. Her concern is that the next programme should be discussed before it becomes a public commitment. In your analysis, quote or paraphrase the words supporting each inference. Separate an explicit fact, such as the number of shifts, from an interpretation of her attitude. If a classmate calls her ungrateful, ask which part of the interview supports that label. She can appreciate the sponsor's money while pointing out that it does not pay for the work needed to use it responsibly. Those positions are compatible, rather than contradictory.
listening.test: Thank you for inviting me to discuss the village history project. Yes, the response to our first exhibition was encouraging, although I would hesitate to call it a complete account of village life. Most of the material came from three families who had already kept organised archives. That was useful, but it means we heard less from people who moved here recently or never kept photographs. Next time, I would like to hold an open story-collecting afternoon before choosing the display. No, I am not suggesting that the first contributors were overrepresented deliberately. We worked with what was available, and they were generous. I simply do not want convenience to determine the whole story. The council has offered the hall for one Saturday. We still need trained people to record contributions and explain consent. A microphone on a table is not enough. We must agree how recordings can be used and allow contributors to decline public release. If we cannot organise that properly this month, I would rather postpone than collect material under unclear conditions. The aim is a more inclusive account, not a bigger pile of recordings. I hope existing contributors will help invite neighbours whose experiences have not yet been heard.

sourceA.title: A team negotiates a shared workspace — extended case review
sourceA.text:
Four members of a fictional cooperative discuss converting a storeroom into a shared workspace. The finance coordinator favours a small pilot, the designer wants flexible furniture, the access representative raises doorway clearance, and the caretaker explains maintenance constraints. Their first preferences differ, but the conversation is not a competition to find a single winning speaker. The aim is to identify a proposal everyone can accept without pretending that every concern has disappeared.

A plan can look acceptable on a drawing while leaving a practical problem unresolved. For example, movable furniture still needs a safe storage position. The manager should ask participants to test the proposed arrangement in the room itself and report whether access, cleaning and rehearsal can coexist.

The finance coordinator supports a pilot rather than full conversion. The designer builds on that suggestion by proposing movable desks. The access representative asks whether the doorway remains unobstructed. The caretaker accepts the layout provided that cleaning remains practical. Nobody has agreed to remove the storage shelves permanently. The group distinguishes a temporary arrangement from a lasting commitment.

I take your point about cost, but access is also essential. Could we combine the pilot with a review after six weeks? That would address maintenance without ruling out later improvements. The minutes should identify unresolved questions as well as agreements. Silence should not automatically be recorded as consent. Before closing, the chair checks who will carry out each action.

The cooperative tested the proposed furniture in the storeroom. A clear doorway could be maintained with four desks, but the first six-desk arrangement obstructed access to the cleaning cupboard. The designer accepted four desks for the pilot while reserving the possibility of a different six-desk layout later. The caretaker asked for fifteen minutes at the end of each day to reset the room. The finance coordinator agreed to fund movable desks only if they could be used elsewhere when the pilot ended. The access representative supported the trial after checking the route in person. These are conditional agreements, not evidence that everyone prefers the same final design.

sourceB.title: A department negotiates presentation time
sourceB.text:
A university department planned a public research evening with five presentations. The chair suggested twelve minutes for each speaker, followed by a joint discussion. A postgraduate representative wanted shorter presentations so that visitors could ask questions after every topic. A senior researcher objected that complex work could not be explained responsibly in six minutes. Their first exchange treated duration as if it were the only issue.

The outreach coordinator asked what audiences were expected to understand. The senior researcher said that listeners needed enough context to avoid mistaking an early result for an established conclusion. The postgraduate representative said that visitors often forgot questions while waiting for a long discussion. These concerns were not necessarily incompatible. The group considered a nine-minute presentation followed by three minutes of clarification, with broader debate saved for the end.

The technician pointed out that changing speakers also took time. With five presentations, introductions and transitions would add approximately ten minutes. The original ninety-minute booking therefore left little room for a final discussion. Rather than silently exceed the venue slot, the chair proposed four presentations and a separate online feature for the fifth team. That team would decide whether the alternative met its needs; the chair would not claim its consent before consultation.

The minutes recorded a provisional programme and named the people responsible for checking it. The outreach coordinator would test the explanation level with two non-specialist readers. The technician would confirm the transition schedule. The fifth team would reply within three working days. Nobody had approved a permanent rule limiting every departmental talk to nine minutes. The agreement concerned this event and its constraints. The group had progressed by identifying the interests behind positions and translating them into a bounded arrangement, while leaving one participant's decision genuinely open. The chair would circulate the corrected minutes for confirmation.

listening.teaching: Here is the outcome of the workspace layout test. Six desks did not fit in the first arrangement because the cleaning cupboard became inaccessible. Four desks allowed the doorway and cupboard route to remain clear. The designer accepts four for the pilot, but still wants to explore another six-desk plan later. Please do not record that as a permanent rejection of six desks. The caretaker also needs fifteen minutes at the end of the day to return the furniture to its agreed position. That time must appear in the timetable. The finance coordinator will fund movable desks provided they can be used elsewhere if the pilot stops. This is important because the budget cannot support equipment with no alternative use. The access representative has now walked the route and supports the trial under the four-desk layout. We therefore have enough agreement to proceed with a limited test, not unanimous preference for one final design. In the minutes, record each condition beside the action it affects. Then name who will check the daily reset and who will arrange the review. A summary saying everyone approved the workspace would omit the main work of the discussion. The next meeting should examine how the arrangement functions, rather than assume that the drawing alone settled every practical concern.
listening.test: Before we leave, I want to summarise the reading-circle discussion. We will test a shorter meeting on the second Thursday of next month, beginning at seven and ending at eight fifteen. The usual two-hour format remains for the other meetings. sourceA.title: Who owns the public square? — extended case review
sourceA.text:
A fictional local commentary examines a plan to lease part of a public square to a café. The author recognises that seating and maintenance could improve the space, but questions whether commercial activity should become the default test of public value. Readers should follow the argument beyond the opening contrast: the article considers practical arrangements as well as principles. Its purpose is to invite a better agreement rather than to reject every partnership with a business.

The central question is whether people retain a right to occupy the square without buying anything. A lease could address that explicitly through marked public seating and enforceable hours. The author asks readers to consider these terms, rather than assume that every improvement funded by a business necessarily benefits every user.

The author concedes that café income could support maintenance. Her objection concerns exclusive control rather than coffee itself. The opening contrast frames the square as a shared resource. A rhetorical question invites readers to reconsider an assumption. The example illustrates a risk without proving it will occur everywhere. The proposed agreement would protect seating for non-customers.

Public value cannot be reduced to the amount of money spent. Nevertheless, funding constraints deserve a practical response. The conclusion qualifies the opening criticism rather than abandoning it. I find the access argument stronger than the prediction about noise. The prediction needs evidence about hours, layout and expected use. A fair response should engage with the author’s strongest reason.

A draft café lease would reserve twenty seats for customers and leave sixteen publicly available. However, the public seats were initially all in the unshaded part of the square. The author argues that counting seats alone would miss a meaningful difference in access during summer. The business offers to maintain planting and keep public toilets open until eight. Residents welcome these benefits but ask who would enforce the public seating condition if staff discouraged non-customers. The council is therefore considering a published complaint route and a review after one season, rather than relying entirely on the operator's description of its intentions.

sourceB.title: The argument for a slower shopping street
sourceB.text:
A proposal to reduce traffic speed on Westbridge High Street has produced two apparently opposing slogans: protect local trade and protect public space. Both express legitimate interests, but neither tells the council exactly what it should do. A shopping street is a place to reach by car, bus, bicycle or foot, as well as a place where people spend time. Treating one function as the entire purpose can make the debate more dramatic and less useful.

Retailers fear that customers will find access inconvenient if the street is redesigned. That concern deserves examination, particularly for customers carrying heavy goods or needing an accessible drop-off point. Yet a claim that every parking space creates a fixed amount of spending would require evidence. The current consultation contains individual experiences, not a reliable calculation of lost sales. Equally, supporters of redesign cannot assume that making a street look attractive will automatically help every business.

The proposed plan lowers the speed limit, widens two crossing points and retains timed loading bays. It does not close the street to all vehicles. An early leaflet used the term traffic-free, causing both unnecessary alarm and unrealistic expectations. Correcting that phrase helped reveal the actual decisions: how buses move through the street, where deliveries stop and whether pedestrians can cross safely.

The strongest case for the plan is not that one group has more moral value than another. It is that the existing arrangement makes some ordinary activities unnecessarily difficult, and targeted changes may improve them without removing all access. The council should measure journey times, crossing use, delivery problems and the experience of people with mobility limitations. Sales data could inform the review if businesses choose to provide it under suitable privacy arrangements. A fair trial would specify what evidence might justify adjustment, rather than invite each side to interpret every event as proof that it was right from the beginning.

listening.teaching: In the public-square commentary, the new lease figures appear helpful at first: twenty customer seats and sixteen public seats. But all sixteen public seats were initially in the unshaded area. In summer, that could make the formal right to sit less useful for some visitors. The author is asking us to evaluate the quality and location of access, not merely count furniture. The café offers maintenance of planting and toilet opening until eight. Those are genuine potential benefits, and a fair response should acknowledge them. The next question is enforcement. If staff discourage a non-customer from using public seating, who can correct the problem? A general statement of good intentions may not be enough. The council is considering a published complaint route and a seasonal review. When you write your response, reconstruct the strongest argument before criticising it. Do not say that the author opposes every commercial partnership; the concern is about the terms of this one. You might support the lease if shaded public seating and enforceable access conditions are included. Alternatively, you might argue that those safeguards remain inadequate. Either position needs to explain how the actual arrangement affects users. A prediction about noise or spending should be marked as a prediction unless supporting evidence is supplied.
listening.test: The council is inviting comments on the proposed river path, and I want to clarify what is being consulted on. The current proposal links the footbridge to the railway station along the northern bank. It does not include the southern bank, which remains privately owned. The path would be shared by walkers and cyclists, with a lower-speed section near the playground. Some residents have described it as a cycle-only route, but that is incorrect. We are particularly interested in views about the two narrow sections and access for people using mobility aids. You can comment online or collect a paper form from the library. Responses close on the eighteenth of March. This is not a vote in which the most repeated sentence automatically wins. The planning team will consider practical concerns and explain how they influenced the design. No construction date has been approved. If the design proceeds, a separate funding decision will be needed. Please identify the location you are discussing, since a concern about one entrance may not apply to the whole route. We will publish a summary without personal names, although you may choose to be contacted for clarification. The library will retain paper copies of the consultation documents.

sourceA.title: Why stored rainwater needs monitoring — extended case review
sourceA.text:
An original fictional science briefing explains a school rainwater project. The school collects roof runoff for garden irrigation, not for drinking. The article follows the path from roof to storage tank and identifies where leaves, sediment and sunlight could affect water quality. Its educational aim is to connect a physical mechanism with an appropriate monitoring plan. No health claim is made about untested water, and the case should not be treated as engineering advice.

Monitoring should follow the route the water actually takes, rather than rely on its appearance at one outlet. The school can use the project to explain filtration, storage and measurement limits. Any description of results must remain within the intended irrigation use and must not imply that visual clarity establishes safety.

Leaves are intercepted before water enters the storage tank. Sediment may accumulate even when the incoming water looks clear. An opaque cover limits the amount of light reaching the water. A plausible mechanism must be distinguished from a measured effect. The tank supplies irrigation water rather than drinking water. The team records rainfall because weather affects the observations.

A single clear sample cannot establish quality throughout the tank. Repeated measurements reveal variation over time. The explanation follows the sequence from collection to storage. We should identify which link in the causal chain was tested. The conclusion remains limited to the conditions actually observed. Further testing is required before any wider claim is justified.

The school recorded tank readings after four rainfall events. A sample taken immediately after heavy rain looked clearer than one taken after three dry weeks, but the team had not standardised the sampling depth. Pupils initially attributed the difference entirely to time in storage. The teacher asked them to consider whether location in the tank could also affect the result. The next plan specifies a consistent sampling point and records the date, recent rainfall and cleaning activity. A maintenance volunteer also noted that the leaf screen had been cleaned between two readings. That intervention must be recorded rather than treated as irrelevant background.

sourceB.title: Testing the effect of classroom ventilation
sourceB.text:
A college installed monitors in three classrooms to examine how indoor carbon dioxide levels changed during teaching. The facilities team wanted to understand ventilation patterns, not diagnose illness or judge individual teachers. Each monitor recorded a reading every five minutes. Classroom A held thirty students, classroom B held eighteen and classroom C was used irregularly for tutorials. Comparing the highest reading from each room without considering occupancy would therefore be misleading.

During the first week, classroom A often showed a rapid increase near the end of a lesson. Staff opened a high window during the second week and observed lower readings on several days. A newsletter draft announced that the window change had solved the air-quality problem. The project leader asked for a more limited statement. Weather, lesson duration and attendance had also changed, and one monitor had been moved from a shelf to a wall position. The observation was useful, but the comparison did not isolate a single cause.

For the next phase, the team would keep monitor positions constant, record attendance and note when doors and windows were opened. The report would distinguish room conditions from direct evidence about health or concentration. Students' comments about feeling less sleepy might be worth collecting, but they would not establish a physiological mechanism on their own. Participation in any questionnaire would be optional and separate from normal classroom access.

A lecturer worried that these qualifications would make the project sound indecisive. The leader replied that the practical action and the scientific claim could have different levels of certainty. Opening a suitable window might be a sensible immediate measure even while the explanation was being investigated. The important point was to avoid representing a small observational exercise as proof of a universal effect. Better records would support a more informative discussion about each room and the constraints affecting its use.

listening.teaching: The rainwater observations give us an opportunity to examine the difference between a pattern and an explanation. After four rainfall events, pupils compared water taken following heavy rain with water sampled after three dry weeks. The later sample looked less clear. It is tempting to say that storage time caused the difference, but the depth of sampling had not been standardised. Water from different parts of the tank may not contain the same amount of sediment. We must also note that a volunteer cleaned the leaf screen between two readings. That is an intervention, not an irrelevant detail. In the next round, use one agreed sampling point, record the date and recent rainfall, and note cleaning activity. The aim is not to keep measuring until a preferred explanation appears. It is to make competing explanations easier to examine. Visual clarity remains only one observation. Do not extend the finding into a claim that the water is suitable for drinking. The project is about irrigation and scientific reasoning. In your account, trace the physical route from roof to screen to storage, then identify which part of that route each observation concerns. A good diagram can show where measurements were taken and where information is still missing.
listening.test: For the seed-growth project, please use the revised recording sheet from Monday onwards. We are comparing two soil mixtures, not testing different watering schedules. Each tray should receive the same measured volume of water unless a problem is reported to the supervisor. There are twelve trays in total, six for each mixture, and their positions on the bench will be rotated twice a week to reduce the effect of uneven light. Measure shoot height from the soil surface to the highest living point, using the same method each time. Do not remove a weak plant simply because it would lower the average. Record its condition and ask before making any change. If a tray is accidentally knocked over, mark the event clearly rather than inventing a replacement measurement. Photographs can support your notes but do not replace the numerical record. We will discuss the findings after three weeks. A difference between these trays would justify further investigation; it would not establish that one mixture is best for every species or climate. Please keep that limit in mind when preparing your poster, and distinguish the result you observed from the explanation you think may account for it. Use the same ruler throughout the project.

sourceA.title: Two ways to describe a cycle route — extended case review
sourceA.text:
A fictional transport team is preparing a public briefing on a protected cycle route. It has a rider survey and a set of junction observations. The sources answer different questions: the survey describes reported experience, while the observations record behaviour at selected locations and times. Neither source is useless, but neither should be asked to establish everything. The briefing needs to show what can be compared fairly and where uncertainty remains.

The team should begin by writing the precise question above each result. A statement about comfort, a count of riders and an observation of turning behaviour can all be valuable without measuring the same thing. Understanding that difference prevents an attractive headline from replacing a careful account of the evidence.

The rider survey measures reported experience rather than collision risk. Junction observations cover selected hours, not the entire week. Before comparing percentages, we need to inspect their denominators. A source may be accurate within a narrow scope. Different definitions can create an apparent contradiction. The team should attribute each claim to the relevant evidence.

An interested organisation can still provide useful data. Its role is a reason for scrutiny, not automatic dismissal. The two sources overlap without being interchangeable. Missing evening observations limit conclusions about night-time use. We should report uncertainty instead of forcing agreement. A stronger briefing combines findings while preserving their boundaries.

The transport team has now compared the survey and observation schedules. The survey received 210 responses, of which 156 came from people who already cycled at least weekly. The observations covered three junctions between seven and nine on two weekday mornings. Neither source adequately represents people deciding whether to start cycling after dark. A local shopkeeper offered a list of delivery conflicts but had recorded only incidents that disrupted the business. The team will treat this as evidence of specific operational problems, not as a complete count of conflicts. Its public briefing will identify each source's population, timing and purpose before combining findings.

sourceB.title: Two accounts of a neighbourhood food scheme
sourceB.text:
A newspaper reported that a neighbourhood food scheme had doubled its reach. The operator said it distributed 1,200 parcels in April, compared with 600 in January. A volunteer group responded that only a small number of additional households had joined. The claims seemed inconsistent until the reporting units were examined. Parcels were distributed weekly in April but only twice during January, and some households received more than one parcel in a week.

The operator had not invented its figures. They accurately counted parcels leaving the depot. However, the word reach suggested something about the number of people or households supported, which those figures alone could not establish. The volunteer group held a household register, but that register included people who had signed up and never collected anything. Its total was therefore not a direct measure of actual use either. Both organisations needed clearer labels rather than an argument over which number sounded more impressive.

A joint audit proposed reporting parcels, distinct collecting households and distribution days separately. Where households shared a collection, volunteers would note the arrangement without demanding intrusive personal information. The audit also identified a gap: neither dataset described people who needed support but found collection times impossible. A short consultation through trusted community contacts could explore that issue, although voluntary accounts would not immediately establish its prevalence.

The newspaper corrected the headline to describe an increase in parcel distribution. It explained the difference between volume and coverage in the article. The operator welcomed the correction but worried that readers might assume wrongdoing. The editor made clear that the issue was interpretation, not evidence of fabricated records. This distinction mattered for public trust. Accurate scrutiny should identify what a source measures, what a headline implies and what remains unknown, rather than turn every mismatch into an allegation of dishonesty.

listening.teaching: Before combining the cycle-route evidence, write down the population and time period for each source. The survey has 210 responses, and 156 respondents already cycle at least once a week. That is useful information about existing riders, but it does not fully represent people who are considering starting. The observations cover three junctions between seven and nine on two weekday mornings. They can describe behaviour at those locations and times, not the entire week. We also have a shopkeeper's record of delivery conflicts. The record contains incidents that disrupted the shop, so it was created for a different purpose from the junction observation. We should investigate those incidents without pretending that the list is a complete count. The major remaining question concerns use after dark. Neither the survey profile nor the morning observation answers it well. In the public briefing, put each claim beside its supporting source. If sources disagree, first check definitions and coverage. Do not assume that one must be dishonest. A narrower source can be accurate within its scope. Your recommendation should explain which information can be combined and which gap requires a new check. That is more informative than averaging incompatible figures to produce a reassuring single result.
listening.test: The local employment office has asked us to clarify this month's training figures. The poster says that 75 people completed workshops, but this is actually a count of workshop attendances. A person attending three different workshops appears three times. The separate registration system lists 48 people who attended at least one session. We will correct the poster before printing more copies. This is a reporting error, not a suggestion that the sessions did not take place. The office wants to know whether the programme is reaching new jobseekers, so the next report will show both total attendances and distinct participants. We will also distinguish first-time users from returning participants where consent allows. Completion of a workshop is not evidence that a person subsequently found work. Employment outcomes require a different follow-up, and some participants may not be available to answer. Please do not fill missing responses with assumptions. If you cannot contact someone, record that the outcome is unknown. The revised figures are due by Thursday, but accuracy takes priority over producing a flattering increase. Contact the data coordinator if the two systems cannot be reconciled, and retain the original entries so that the correction can be traced. Please check the unit before approving any new poster.

sourceA.title: A balanced plan for a learning garden — extended case review
sourceA.text:
A fictional college wants to turn unused land into a learning garden. Its planning dossier combines students' requests, a caretaker's maintenance estimate and a teacher's ideas for practical lessons. The writer must develop a recommendation from these different perspectives without inventing consensus. A garden could serve several purposes, but the plan has to make trade-offs visible. The report will go to a committee that has not read the original discussion notes.

The garden proposal should state which activities have priority when space or supervision is limited. Access to a raised bed means little if nobody is available to support a planned class. A phased arrangement allows the committee to investigate real demand while avoiding a promise that every requested activity will begin immediately.

The requests identify desired uses but do not establish maintenance capacity. The caretaker’s estimate assumes volunteers will water the beds. That assumption should be checked before the budget is approved. The teacher proposes practical lessons rather than unrestricted public access. These purposes can coexist if responsibilities are clearly assigned. I recommend a smaller first phase with accessible raised beds.

The report should acknowledge the opportunity cost of using the land. A synthesis explains relationships between sources instead of listing summaries. Where accounts differ, I would identify the underlying question. The committee needs a decision rule for continuing the project. My conclusion is provisional because summer staffing remains uncertain. The next report should show what happened as well as what was planned.

The garden committee has received three costed options. A simple bed layout costs 1,400 pounds, accessible raised beds cost 2,100, and a paved teaching area with beds costs 3,600. The available grant is 2,500. Students favour the third option because it allows group teaching after rain, while the access representative prefers the second to a cheaper inaccessible start. The caretaker notes that every option still requires watering during the summer break. A nearby association has offered volunteers for two weeks but not the whole holiday. The writer must not count that offer as complete maintenance coverage. A phased recommendation should explain which need is protected now and what remains unresolved.

sourceB.title: Choosing the first phase of a digital archive
sourceB.text:
A regional history society planned to make its collection easier to consult. Three sources shaped the proposal: a researcher survey, an archivist's condition report and a small technical estimate. Researchers wanted searchable documents available from home. The archivist warned that some fragile volumes could not be scanned using the inexpensive machine in the estimate. The technical volunteer had priced file storage but had not included the time needed to describe items accurately.

The society had a grant of 8,000 pounds. Scanning the most requested material was estimated at 5,500, provided the pages were already stable. Conservation of two damaged volumes would cost another 4,000. Creating basic catalogue descriptions for a smaller selected set would cost 2,000 in paid time. These were not three independent extras that could all be funded. The committee needed to choose a coherent first phase rather than combine the most attractive parts of incompatible plans.

A researcher representative initially favoured scanning everything that could be handled safely. The archivist pointed out that images without useful descriptions might be difficult to discover, even if technically online. A second proposal therefore selected stable material, included basic descriptions and deferred the damaged volumes until conservation funding was available. It would not satisfy every request immediately, but it connected access with preservation and the practical work of finding information.

The report recommended a limited collection with clear selection criteria and a published explanation of exclusions. It also proposed recording unsuccessful searches, because download counts alone would show only material people had already found. The researcher survey informed priorities but did not represent every possible future user. The final judgement was therefore provisional. Combining sources meant preserving their different contributions: demand, physical constraints and implementation cost. A useful synthesis did more than list three opinions; it explained why one achievable sequence followed from their relationship.

listening.teaching: We now have three garden options and a fixed grant of 2,500 pounds. The simple bed layout costs 1,400, the accessible raised beds cost 2,100, and the paved teaching area with beds costs 3,600. The students favour the paved area because it would support classes after wet weather. That is a relevant educational benefit, but the current grant does not cover it. The access representative argues that the cheaper option should not begin by excluding people who need raised beds. The caretaker adds a different constraint: every option needs summer watering. A nearby association offers volunteers for two weeks, not for the whole holiday. We must not expand that offer when writing the budget. Your synthesis should show how the sources relate. One possible recommendation is accessible raised beds as a first phase, leaving 400 pounds that might contribute to maintenance. But do not assume that 400 is enough without a costed plan. Another option is to delay construction until maintenance is confirmed. Either judgement needs to state what it protects and what it postpones. The committee wants a reasoned sequence, not a paragraph praising each option separately and leaving the actual decision unexplained. Explain who would carry out that next check.
listening.test: The community music project must choose its first purchase before the grant deadline. We have 1,800 pounds. A set of portable keyboards would cost 1,200, storage cases another 250, and a suitable lockable cupboard 500. Buying all three would exceed the grant by 150 pounds. The tutor prefers the keyboards because several learners currently share instruments. The centre manager says the equipment cannot be left unsecured overnight. A parent has offered to lend two keyboards, but only until the end of the term. That offer may help a short pilot; it cannot be counted as a permanent replacement for purchased instruments. We could begin with borrowed equipment and use some funding for secure storage, provided the lender accepts the arrangements. Alternatively, we could buy a smaller set and postpone the cases. The decision should consider how instruments will be moved and protected, not just how many can be advertised. Please bring a written recommendation to Friday's meeting, with costs and conditions stated separately. The grant officer will allow a revised item list but not a purchase made after the deadline. Do not place an order before we agree on a complete workable option. Include the lender’s conditions in your written recommendation.
