sourceA.title: Should a club remove late fees? — extended case review
sourceA.text:
A fictional community sports club is debating whether to remove late cancellation fees. Supporters say fees discourage people facing unpredictable caring duties. Opponents argue that empty spaces prevent others from joining. The workshop asks learners to engage with both concerns rather than label one side selfish. A persuasive response should identify the purpose of the current rule, test its assumptions and offer a workable alternative with limits.

The club should record when notice is given and whether a place is subsequently filled. Those measures would help distinguish unavoidable last-minute changes from a pattern that a different booking rule might address. A fair discussion should avoid demanding private details from carers merely to establish that their responsibilities can change.

The strongest objection is that unused places deny others an opportunity. That concern is legitimate even if we reject the current fee. I agree that cancellations have costs, but the burden is uneven. People with caring duties may face changes beyond their control. Removing the fee need not mean removing every consequence. A waiting list could fill some places if notice is prompt.

The alternative must be judged against the same practical objective. One example does not establish how frequently the problem occurs. We should avoid treating a disagreement as a personal failing. If repeat absences increase, the trial may require adjustment. My support is conditional on keeping a clear attendance record. A fair reply addresses the concern rather than attacking its speaker.

The club reviewed four weeks of bookings. There were 18 late cancellations, but eleven places were filled from the waiting list when notice arrived at least two hours before the session. The remaining seven places stayed empty. A member argued that the waiting list had therefore solved the problem. The secretary disagreed: it had helped under certain conditions, while people cancelling very near the start still left gaps. The committee is considering a reminder system and a limited number of fee-free cancellations for unforeseen caring duties. It must also explain how that policy can be applied without demanding public disclosure of private circumstances.

sourceB.title: A workplace debate about fixed office days
sourceB.text:
A consultancy proposed requiring every employee to attend the office on the same three weekdays. Management argued that shared attendance would make mentoring and informal collaboration easier. Some staff opposed the plan because their work involved long periods of individual analysis and their journeys were expensive. The disagreement was initially framed as a choice between commitment to colleagues and personal convenience, which obscured the actual question of how different tasks were best supported.

A junior analyst said that remote work had sometimes left her unsure whom to ask for help. Her account supported the need for reliable mentoring access, but not necessarily a rule covering every employee on identical days. A project manager reported that scheduled online consultations worked well for his team. That example did not establish that online support met every beginner's needs. Both accounts were informative without being universal proof.

The staff group proposed two common collaboration days and a third day arranged by each team according to its tasks. Management worried that team arrangements would become inconsistent and hard to coordinate. In response, the group suggested published expectations for mentoring availability and a review of missed consultations, rather than leaving attendance entirely to individual preference. The proposal therefore addressed the purpose of the rule instead of merely asking for an exemption.

A three-month trial would record access to advice, delays in joint tasks and employee travel difficulties. It would not treat desk occupancy as the sole measure of collaboration. Employees with agreed access adjustments would continue to discuss those privately. The final recommendation acknowledged that no arrangement would remove every conflict. Its strength lay in a testable alternative that preserved common working time while allowing tasks to influence the remaining schedule. A fair argument had to engage with the genuine mentoring concern, not portray managers as simply distrustful or staff as unwilling to work.

listening.teaching: We have new information for the cancellation-fee debate. During four weeks, eighteen bookings were cancelled late. Eleven places were filled from the waiting list when at least two hours' notice was available. Seven remained empty. These results show that the waiting list can help, but they do not show that it solves every cancellation problem. Very late notice may leave insufficient time to contact someone else. When responding to the fee's supporters, acknowledge their strongest concern: an empty place can deny another member an opportunity. Then examine whether the current fee addresses that concern fairly and effectively. The committee is considering reminders and a limited number of fee-free cancellations for unforeseen caring duties. A practical policy must define the process without requiring members to share private details publicly. It should also avoid promising that every absence will be excused. If you favour the alternative, explain what evidence would make you reconsider it. For example, repeated absences might increase despite reminders. If you favour retaining a fee, explain why the benefits cannot be achieved through a less burdensome arrangement. Neither side should use one sympathetic or frustrating example as proof of the whole pattern. Your task is to develop a response that changes the decision, not simply to restate your preference more forcefully.
listening.test: The residents' committee is reviewing the rule that meeting rooms must be booked in four-hour blocks. Supporters say the blocks simplify staffing and cleaning. Several small groups say they need only ninety minutes and cannot afford to pay for unused time. We are not deciding that one concern is imaginary. The caretaker has explained that some setup work is required regardless of meeting length, but cleaning does not always take the same time. A proposed alternative is a two-hour minimum with an additional fixed setup charge. That would be tested on weekday afternoons only, when staffing is already available. Evening bookings would remain unchanged during the trial. We need to know whether shorter sessions attract new users and whether transitions between groups create delays. We will therefore record actual finishing times and preparation work, not just the number of bookings. Please send comments by Friday, identifying a practical difficulty or benefit. A message saying that all rules are unfair will not answer the staffing question; a message saying that all users can afford four hours will not answer the access question. The committee will compare the alternative with the current arrangement after six weeks before deciding whether to extend it.

sourceA.title: Negotiating use of a rehearsal room — extended case review
sourceA.text:
Two fictional groups want the same community rehearsal room on Thursday evenings. A choir needs stable weekly practice, while a youth theatre needs occasional longer sessions before performances. The building manager cannot create another room or ignore the closing time. Learners will negotiate around the interests behind the requests, making proposals specific enough to check. Agreement should not rely on a vague promise that somebody will somehow be flexible later.

The building manager can help by identifying the calendar dates that genuinely create a clash. Once those are known, the groups may trade a small number of sessions instead of disputing an entire term. The written agreement should preserve that limited scope so that an occasional exception does not become an assumed permanent entitlement.

The choir’s underlying interest is a predictable weekly schedule. The theatre needs extra time before performances, not every Thursday. Would you consider an earlier start in exchange for two longer sessions? We could accept that provided the dates are agreed in advance. The closing time is a fixed constraint rather than a bargaining point. Let us separate what is essential from what is merely preferred.

A tentative agreement still needs confirmation from both coordinators. Who would notify members when the usual timetable changes? We should record a procedure for handling an unforeseen clash. I cannot commit the other group without consulting its organiser. To confirm, the exception applies only to the two named dates. A workable agreement makes responsibilities and review dates explicit.

The room calendar now shows three actual clashes rather than an entire term of conflict. The choir needs all Thursdays before its June concert, while the theatre needs two longer rehearsals in May. A possible exchange gives the theatre an earlier start on those two dates and the choir an additional Sunday session. The building manager can provide Sunday access only if a trained keyholder is present. Neither group currently has one available. A vague promise to find somebody would therefore leave an essential condition unresolved. The negotiators need either a named trained person, a different exchange or a timetable that stays within confirmed access.

sourceB.title: Agreeing responsibilities in a translation contract
sourceB.text:
A charity commissioned a freelance translator to prepare a public information booklet in two languages. The charity wanted delivery within three weeks, while the translator requested a stable source text before agreeing to the deadline. The project manager initially described this as inflexibility. On closer discussion, the translator explained that changing a paragraph after translation could require checking terminology and layout in both versions, not merely replacing a few words.

The parties separated the main interests. The charity needed a usable booklet before a community event. The translator needed a defined workload and a reliable review process. They agreed that the source text would be frozen on the fifth of the month. One round of minor factual corrections would be included, but additional sections or substantial rewriting would require a revised quotation. The charity would appoint one reviewer to consolidate comments instead of sending contradictory instructions from several volunteers.

A remaining issue concerned approval. The translator could guarantee a checked translation of the approved source, but could not certify the accuracy of the charity's underlying policy. The charity retained responsibility for that content. The contract would state this distinction and identify the final approval date. If approval was late, the delivery schedule would be adjusted rather than leave the translator responsible for an impossible unchanged deadline.

Both parties accepted a short initial section to test terminology before the full document proceeded. The fee included that pilot section and one agreed revision, not unlimited future updates. Neither side obtained unlimited flexibility. Instead, the agreement connected each promise to a condition the relevant party could control. The project manager later said that the conversation had become easier when they stopped debating whether the translator was helpful and began specifying which changes, decisions and delays the contract actually covered. The charity recorded those responsibilities in its project file.

listening.teaching: The rehearsal negotiation has become more specific. We no longer have a conflict covering every Thursday. There are three actual clashes. The choir needs its regular practice before the June concert, and the theatre needs two longer rehearsals in May. One proposed exchange gives the theatre an earlier start on those two dates and the choir an extra Sunday session. That sounds workable until we check access. The building manager can open on Sunday only if a trained keyholder is present. Neither group currently has a named person available. We must not write the agreement as if that condition were already satisfied. We could ask whether a trained person can be confirmed by a stated deadline. If not, the parties need a different exchange. In the role-play, distinguish the choir's interest in predictable preparation from its opening demand for every Thursday. Distinguish the theatre's interest in enough rehearsal time from its preferred timing. Then make a conditional offer that preserves the fixed closing time. Before accepting, check who notifies members and what happens if the condition fails. A successful negotiation is not merely one in which everyone says yes. The written version must describe an arrangement that the people involved are actually authorised and able to carry out.
listening.test: I am calling to confirm the provisional agreement for your association's weekend workshop. We can hold the large room for Saturday from ten until four, provided we receive the signed booking form and deposit by Tuesday noon. The room is not yet confirmed, so please wait before advertising tickets. The fee includes tables, chairs and ordinary cleaning. It does not include the sound technician you requested; that is a separate service costing eighty pounds. If you choose not to book the technician, you may use the small portable speaker after a short instruction session with the caretaker. You cannot operate the main sound desk yourselves. Access for setting up begins at nine thirty, and the room must be clear by four thirty. The programme should therefore finish before four if you need substantial packing time. We can cancel the sound-technician booking without charge until Thursday, but the room's cancellation conditions are different and appear on the form. Please check both rather than assume one deadline applies to everything. If another committee member will sign, make sure that person has read the equipment restrictions. Call me if any term needs discussion before you return the form. I can clarify the separate conditions before Tuesday.

sourceA.title: Reporting on a study-room trial — extended case review
sourceA.text:
A fictional college committee has asked for a report on reservable study rooms. The writer has booking records, staff observations and comments from students who could not find a place. A useful report must distinguish the questions these materials answer and make practical recommendations. Headings should guide a busy reader without becoming a substitute for connected argument. The report is intended to support a decision, not merely demonstrate that data have been collected.

The committee needs to know whether a proposed change addresses empty reservations, lack of space or both. The report should not assume that visible empty rooms are available for immediate use without checking their status. A practical recommendation can begin with the booking rule while leaving broader capacity questions open.

The purpose of this report is to evaluate the booking trial. The records cover completed bookings but not every unsuccessful attempt. It was observed that some rooms remained empty after being reserved. Student comments indicate frustration, although their frequency is uncertain. These findings should be interpreted within the limited observation period. An automatic release rule could reduce unused reservations.

It is recommended that the rule be tested before wider adoption. The facilities team should be responsible for monitoring room availability. The report separates immediate actions from questions requiring further study. A finding should be traceable to the material that supports it. Headings help the reader locate evidence and recommendations. The conclusion should not introduce an unsupported new claim.

The study-room review now distinguishes reservation time from actual occupancy. Of 160 bookings over two weeks, staff observed 38 rooms still empty twenty minutes after the reserved start. However, observations occurred only at fixed rounds, so the records cannot establish whether every room remained unused for its entire slot. Students propose a fifteen-minute release rule, while staff warn that visitors may be delayed by inaccessible lifts or timetable changes. A report should therefore examine a simple check-in option and a route for agreed exceptions. It should not assume that the largest possible release count is automatically the fairest measure of success.

sourceB.title: Reporting on a college equipment-loan service
sourceB.text:
A college commissioned a report on the service through which students borrowed laptops. The review covered four weeks and used loan records, observations at the collection desk and twelve voluntary interviews. Its purpose was to identify operational improvements, not to judge the academic performance of borrowers. The report stated this scope explicitly because some readers had expected a wider evaluation of whether loaned computers improved attainment.

The most frequent recorded problem was a mismatch between collection times and students' timetables. Of 95 reservations, 21 were not collected during the original slot. However, staff later arranged collection for fourteen of those students. Describing all 21 as unused demand would therefore exaggerate the problem. Interviews suggested that some students could not leave classes during the advertised collection period, while others had found alternative equipment. The small voluntary sample could illustrate these reasons but not establish their exact prevalence.

The report recommended two immediate changes: a clearly advertised late-afternoon collection window and a message asking students to cancel reservations they no longer needed. It did not recommend buying additional laptops before checking how the existing stock circulated. A technician also identified six chargers requiring replacement. That issue was assigned to the equipment team with a deadline, rather than buried inside an overall satisfaction score.

For a longer review, the report proposed recording waiting time for a device, actual loan duration and the number of students unable to obtain suitable equipment. It also requested a separate process for access requirements, since a laptop available on paper might not meet every learner's needs. The conclusion distinguished urgent maintenance, communication changes and questions about future capacity. The college could act on the first two without claiming that four weeks of limited evidence justified every possible investment. Each recommendation named an owner and explained which finding it addressed, making the report useful for a decision rather than merely descriptive.

listening.teaching: The study-room report should distinguish reserved time from actual occupancy. We have 160 bookings across two weeks, and staff observed 38 rooms still empty twenty minutes after the start. That does not mean 38 complete slots were unused. Staff checked at fixed rounds, so somebody may have arrived later. A proposed fifteen-minute release rule could make space available, but we need to examine exceptions. A student delayed by an inaccessible lift may have a different problem from someone who simply forgot the booking. The report should not label both cases as irresponsible. Consider a check-in option and a clear route for agreed adjustments. We also need to know who would administer the rule and how quickly a released room could be booked by someone else. Your findings section should state what was observed and the limits of observation. Your recommendation can then propose a test, with responsibility assigned to the facilities team. Do not introduce an unsupported new claim in the conclusion, such as saying that the college never needs more rooms. The current material may justify improving how existing space is used while leaving the capacity question open. A strong report connects an action to evidence and explains what further review is needed.
listening.test: I am outlining the report requested by the warehouse manager. Please review the equipment-return desk during the next ten working days. We need to know whether the new return procedure reduces missing items without creating long queues. Do not review the purchasing system; that is a separate project. Record the time each sampled customer joins the queue and leaves the desk, and note whether the return was complete or needed follow-up. Do not record customer names on the observation sheet. If an item appears damaged, normal staff must handle it; you are observing, not inspecting technical safety. We would like a short interim note after the first five days if an urgent operational issue appears. The final report is due on the following Wednesday. Please separate observed facts, staff comments and your recommendations. A photograph of a queue is not a reliable measure of average waiting, so numerical timing matters. The manager also wants to know if the desk arrangement causes access difficulties. You can describe a specific obstruction without identifying the person affected. We will decide on any permanent layout change after reading the report and discussing it with staff who operate the desk. Keep your timing records with the final report.

sourceA.title: Proposing a practical mentoring scheme — extended case review
sourceA.text:
A fictional adult college is considering peer mentoring for new students. The proposal should explain who would benefit, what mentors could realistically provide and where professional support remains necessary. Enthusiasm alone cannot establish capacity. The writer must specify recruitment, training, supervision and a modest first phase. The intended reader is a budget committee deciding whether the scheme is ready for a trial, not a publicity team seeking a slogan.

A mentor's value may lie in helping a student locate the right service, not in answering every question personally. Training should therefore include how to recognise a concern outside the mentor's role. The committee can authorise a bounded trial while requiring a coordinator to check the quality of referrals and contact.

The proposed scheme would help new students navigate routine college life. Mentors would offer guidance rather than replace professional advisers. A small first cohort would keep supervision manageable. The budget must include training as well as publicity. Potential benefits depend on consistent contact and clear boundaries. Participation should be voluntary for both mentors and new students.

We should specify how a mentor can refer a difficult concern. The proposal identifies a coordinator rather than assuming shared responsibility. A review after one term would inform any expansion. The alternative is to improve existing induction sessions first. A persuasive proposal acknowledges what it cannot yet establish. Funding should be released only when the training plan is agreed.

The mentoring pilot has been costed for twelve mentors and twenty-four new students. Training costs 360 pounds, coordinator time 600 and accessible meeting materials 140, bringing the requested grant to 1,100. A proposed publicity campaign would cost another 300, but the committee asks whether recruitment through existing induction sessions could serve the first cohort. The student representative supports saving publicity costs only if the approach still reaches people who do not attend induction. The safeguarding adviser adds that mentors need a named referral route before recruitment begins. The proposal must therefore explain how a smaller budget preserves essential supervision rather than merely reducing every line by the same percentage.

sourceB.title: A proposal for an employer-learning partnership
sourceB.text:
An adult college and a local manufacturing firm discussed a short numeracy programme for employees. The firm offered a meeting room and paid release time for two hours each week. The college would provide a tutor and learning materials. At first, the partnership sounded almost cost-free because both sides described their contributions as existing resources. A detailed proposal showed why that wording was misleading: the tutor's time displaced other teaching, and production teams needed cover while employees attended.

The first phase would involve sixteen volunteers over eight weeks. The proposal distinguished practical learning from staff appraisal. Individual work would not be shared with line managers, although attendance arrangements and an anonymous programme summary would be available. Employees could discuss access needs privately with the college coordinator. The firm wanted evidence of improved productivity, but the college explained that such a claim would require a different evaluation and could not be inferred from completion alone.

The budget included preparation, teaching, travel and one joint review meeting. It did not assume that a successful pilot could continue indefinitely under the same staffing arrangements. Before expansion, the partners would examine demand, learner work and the effect on other provision. A possible evening alternative was also considered, but employees working rotating shifts said that fixed evening attendance might exclude them. The proposal therefore retained paid daytime release as an essential condition rather than treating it as a convenient extra.

The final document named a college coordinator and a firm contact responsible for timetable changes. If release time was withdrawn, the programme would pause while the partners agreed a workable alternative. The proposal was persuasive because it made the exchange explicit, acknowledged opportunity costs and protected the educational purpose. It did not promise that eight weeks would solve every workplace difficulty. The partners agreed to judge the pilot against the aims it could reasonably address and to state separately any wider benefit that remained untested.

listening.teaching: For the mentoring proposal, we now have a budget for twelve mentors and twenty-four new students. Training is 360 pounds, coordinator time 600 and accessible materials 140. The total request is therefore 1,100 pounds. Publicity would add another 300, but the committee asks whether existing induction sessions could recruit the first group. That may be reasonable, provided we do not miss students who cannot attend induction. The student representative wants a second contact route for them. The safeguarding adviser also makes a clear point: mentors need a named referral route before recruitment begins. We should not save money by removing supervision and then describe the scheme as unchanged. If the grant is reduced, identify which activities are essential to the purpose and which can be postponed. A smaller publicity campaign may be possible; an unsupported group of mentors would be a different and potentially unsuitable service. Your proposal should explain the alternative, not simply reduce every budget line by the same proportion. It should also name the coordinator and the review date. Completion of mentoring meetings is one measure of participation, but it does not show that every student's underlying difficulty was resolved. The first review should examine whether students could reach the support they needed and whether mentors understood the limits of their role.
listening.test: Thank you for discussing the mobile language workshop with our association. We can provide a room on four Saturday mornings and help contact residents, but we cannot guarantee a minimum number of learners. The tutor will need to confirm what level the sessions are intended for. Advertising them simply as suitable for everyone may create unrealistic expectations. The grant available is 900 pounds. Your draft budget lists 640 for teaching, 160 for travel and 180 for printed materials, which totals 980. Please send a revised proposal rather than assume that the difference will be covered later. We may be able to use digital handouts, but participants without devices will still need an accessible alternative. The venue has a projector; it does not have loan tablets. The committee also wants a named contact if a learner requires support beyond the tutor's role. We would like the first session in February, subject to the agreement being signed by the twentieth of January. Do not begin publicity before the level, access arrangements and final budget are confirmed. After the four sessions, we will review attendance, learner feedback and work samples before considering another grant. We are funding a bounded pilot, not promising a permanent weekly service.

sourceA.title: Designing an accessible community learning weekend — extended case review
sourceA.text:
The original integrated project concerns a fictional learning weekend combining practical workshops, talks and peer support. Learners act as an advisory team, not as event promoters. They must compare demand with capacity, identify access requirements and propose a limited programme with an evaluation plan. The project brings together reading, explanation, negotiation and revision. Completing it provides evidence for review but does not by itself certify C1 proficiency.

A single weekend cannot demonstrate every long-term educational outcome. It can nevertheless provide evidence about access, participation and the feasibility of activities. The advisory team should identify which findings would support repetition, which would require redesign and which questions would remain unanswered even if visitors enjoyed the event.

Our central purpose is accessible learning rather than maximum attendance. The first programme should match the number of trained facilitators. We have distinguished confirmed resources from requested support. The access plan includes a route for requesting individual adjustments. Demand remains uncertain because the survey reached existing members only. The project can proceed in a limited form while that gap is investigated.

I would respond to that challenge by narrowing the claim. The proposed measure captures participation, not learning by itself. A review should include work produced as well as participant comments. Our report records the reasoning behind each significant trade-off. The final presentation should invite questions about uncertain assumptions. Independent language review remains necessary before claiming a C1 level.

The weekend team has narrowed its proposal to six workshops and two public talks, with a total capacity of 96 workshop places. A person attending two workshops would occupy two places, so the figure must not be advertised as 96 distinct learners. Four facilitators are confirmed and two are still being approached. The team has also reserved one quiet room rather than scheduling activities in every available space. A reviewer questions whether this is an inefficient use of the venue. The response should explain the room's access function and the evidence needed to judge demand, while acknowledging the opportunity cost of not using it for another workshop.

sourceB.title: Defending a cross-campus research showcase
sourceB.text:
A student team submitted a proposal for a research showcase linking three campuses. The plan included twelve short presentations, a travelling exhibition and an online discussion. During the review, the panel asked what the project was primarily intended to achieve. The team said it wanted researchers from different departments to understand one another's methods. The panel then questioned whether moving display boards between campuses was the best use of the limited budget.

The original budget allocated 2,400 pounds to transport and installation, 900 to access support and 700 to facilitation. The available grant was 3,500, leaving a 500-pound gap. One team member proposed cutting access support first because transport had already been discussed with a supplier. Another argued that a conversation with a supplier was not a binding obligation and should not determine the project's priorities. The panel asked the team to reconsider the sequence rather than treat the first estimate as fixed.

A revised plan kept the online discussion and six presentations, produced digital displays and retained access support. Transport costs fell, but the team acknowledged that not every researcher would receive an in-person platform during the first phase. Selection criteria would therefore be published, and those not selected could contribute questions and material to the online discussion. The project would record whether participants could explain a method from another department afterwards, not merely whether they liked the event.

The panel requested a revised budget and confirmation of facilitator availability before deciding. It did not certify the educational value of the project simply because the presentation was fluent. In a reflection, the team explained which assumptions changed during questioning and which core purpose remained. The review demonstrated why effective advanced communication includes revising a defensible plan under challenge. A polished opening can introduce a project, but the quality of reasoning becomes clearer when resources, access and competing priorities must be reconciled in conversation.

listening.teaching: Let us prepare for the learning-weekend review. The revised programme has six workshops and two public talks. The workshops provide 96 places, but not necessarily 96 different learners, because one person may attend more than one session. Use the correct unit in the publicity. Four facilitators are confirmed and two are only being approached. If you present all six as secured, the panel will be unable to assess whether the programme is ready. We have also reserved a quiet room. That means one fewer activity room, so it has an opportunity cost. The team should explain its access function rather than pretend that reserving it has no trade-off. A reviewer may ask how demand will be judged. You could propose confidential feedback and observation of whether the arrangement supports participation, without requiring people to disclose private information publicly. During the presentation, begin with the central purpose and recommendation. Then show how the programme fits the confirmed resources. If a question reveals that a claim is too broad, narrow it explicitly. Do not defend a misleading figure because it appeared on your first slide. After the review, your reflection should explain any change to the proposal and the reasoning behind it. That is evidence of responsive communication, not an admission that preparation was pointless.
listening.test: The project panel has reviewed your proposal for a neighbourhood oral-history event. We are inviting a revision rather than rejecting the idea. Please reduce the first event to one venue and explain how recorded contributions will be stored and used. Your draft budget allowed 300 pounds for recording equipment, but it did not include transcription or the time needed to explain consent. Those tasks are essential if the recordings are to become a usable archive. You may borrow equipment from the college, subject to training, which could release funds for those activities. We also need confirmation that the venue has a private space for contributors who do not want to speak in front of a group. The panel does not require a target of fifty recordings. It would prefer a smaller number collected responsibly with clear information about future use. Submit the revised budget and access plan by the tenth of June. Two reviewers will then ask you questions online for fifteen minutes. You may bring notes, but please be ready to explain alternatives rather than read the proposal aloud. If the revised conditions cannot be met by that date, contact the coordinator to discuss postponement before making public commitments.

sourceA.title: Building a defensible language portfolio — extended case review
sourceA.text:
The final original briefing concerns a fictional learner preparing an independent review. A portfolio can show completed tasks and responses to feedback, but familiar work alone does not establish how the learner handles new material. The review therefore includes unseen listening and reading, independent writing and interaction with another person. It reports strengths and limitations separately. Neither course completion nor a local transcription score is treated as an official CEFR or IELTS result.

A reviewer needs enough information to distinguish a stable ability from a successful rehearsed performance. The learner should therefore label assistance, revisions and repeated tasks honestly. The resulting profile can guide further practice even when the evidence is too limited to support a single confident level for all four skills.

My portfolio distinguishes first attempts from revised work. Familiar material can show learning without proving general transfer. I need evidence from tasks that I have not rehearsed. Listening, reading, writing and interaction should be reviewed separately. A transcript cannot establish every aspect of spoken performance. An external reviewer should know what help was permitted.

A disagreement between reviewers calls for examination of the evidence. I would treat an uneven profile as information for planning. The next plan should target recurring weaknesses rather than every possible error. A delayed task with new material helps check retention and transfer. Course completion is not an official proficiency certificate. Any score estimate should state its evidence and uncertainty.

The learner's portfolio now contains six revised essays, three unrehearsed recordings and two reading tasks completed with a dictionary. The index labels the conditions for every item. An assessor notes that the revised essays show useful editing skill but cannot be treated as unaided timed writing. One spoken task was repeated after feedback, so the first and second versions remain together. The learner proposes a new unfamiliar task after two weeks to check whether the improvement transfers. The review will report skill-specific strengths and gaps. It will not convert the number of completed items into a guaranteed examination result or a single automatically awarded C1 level.

sourceB.title: Evaluating a workplace communication course
sourceB.text:
A company reviewed an English communication course for its international project teams. The training provider reported that 92 percent of participants had completed all online units. Managers wanted to know whether meetings had become clearer. Completion data could answer a participation question, but it did not directly establish how employees handled spontaneous disagreement or explained technical uncertainty to unfamiliar colleagues.

The review used three additional sources: samples of written updates, role-play meetings with new scenarios and voluntary accounts from colleagues. Written samples were labelled according to whether they had been revised with tutor support. A polished update remained evidence of editing and learning, but it was not described as an unaided first attempt. The role-plays introduced a change halfway through so that participants could not rely entirely on a prepared explanation.

Two reviewers assessed the same selected performances using agreed criteria. They considered clarity, relevance, organisation, language control and interaction. When their judgements differed substantially, they returned to the recording and identified the evidence supporting each view. In two cases they requested another sample instead of hiding the disagreement inside an average. They also noted that a transcript could not fully show timing, intelligibility or how a speaker responded to interruption.

The report found uneven profiles. Some participants wrote clear updates but needed support in rapid discussion; others interacted effectively while producing ambiguous written instructions. Each received a targeted plan and an opportunity to complete a new task after several weeks. The company did not translate course completion into an official examination band. Its purpose was to identify usable communication strengths and remaining risks in relevant work. The provider supported this distinction and retained completion as one measure among several. A credible evaluation explained the limits of its evidence, rather than making its conclusion sound more certain by combining different kinds of progress into one impressive score.

listening.teaching: Before the independent review, check the conditions attached to every portfolio item. We have six revised essays, three unrehearsed recordings and two reading tasks completed with a dictionary. Those are different forms of evidence. The revised essays can show editing skill, but they should not be labelled unaided timed writing. The reading tasks also need their dictionary use recorded. That does not make the work worthless; it tells the reviewer what can reasonably be inferred. One speaking task was repeated after feedback. Keep both versions so that the change can be examined. Then use a new unfamiliar task after two weeks to see whether the improvement transfers. If the learner simply repeats the same response, we cannot separate memory for that answer from a more general ability. The final report should describe listening, reading, writing and interaction separately, including any gaps in the sample. A local transcription score does not establish every aspect of pronunciation or conversational performance. A completion badge is not an official language certificate. You may use the profile to decide what to practise next, but do not convert the number of finished activities into a guaranteed examination result. Honest labels make the portfolio more informative, not less valuable.
listening.test: Your independent review appointment is confirmed for Monday at nine forty-five. Please bring identification and a short index of your work, but do not bring a prepared answer to the speaking question. The first task will be an unfamiliar reading passage. You may make notes, but a dictionary is not permitted in that particular task. The listening task follows after a five-minute break. Writing will be completed independently in forty minutes. If you need an agreed access adjustment, contact us before Friday so that the conditions can be recorded consistently. The spoken interaction includes another participant, and the assessor may introduce a new practical constraint during the discussion. We want to see how you respond, not whether you remember a fixed script. Your report will distinguish observed performance from areas where the sample is insufficient. It is an internal review and will not issue an official examination certificate. If two assessors disagree materially, we may invite an additional short sample before finalising the profile. You will receive feedback within ten working days and can request clarification of a comment. A later retest will use new material so that it can examine transfer rather than familiarity with this appointment. The coordinator can explain the recorded assessment conditions.

sourceA.title: 教学案例：a neighbourhood water laboratory：扩展论证
sourceA.text:
At a neighbourhood water laboratory, participants considered whether to describe its new filter as effective under the conditions tested. The background was specific: twelve household samples became clearer after filtration, although the trial did not measure dissolved contaminants or long term maintenance. However, clear water was being mistaken for safe water in the public demonstration. The proposed response was to publish the measured outcomes beside the unmeasured risks and remove the unqualified word safe.

The public demonstration creates a particular responsibility. Spectators can see a change in appearance immediately, whereas the untested chemical properties remain invisible. The institution should not rely on a small disclaimer to undo a striking visual suggestion of safety. I would place the measured outcome beside the demonstration itself and explain which tests were not conducted. The laboratory could then decide whether additional testing is feasible. If it is not, the narrower claim can still be useful. People may value a filter that removes visible particles, provided they do not confuse that benefit with protection from every contaminant. Responsible communication makes the boundary part of the main message rather than an inconvenient technical footnote. A plausible account is not necessarily the most probable one. The filter reduced visible particles without establishing that the water was safe. We should qualify the claim before it acquires a life of its own. The result holds under the conditions specified in the report. Absence of detected harm does not amount to evidence of harmlessness. Her wording conveys confidence without implying that the question is settled. The observation substantiates a narrower claim than the advertisement makes.

The laboratory subsequently receives a request to supply filters for a school event. This changes the decision without changing the original result. A classroom demonstration of clearer water and advice about what pupils may drink carry different responsibilities. The team should explain that the test did not establish drinking safety before accepting the invitation. It could still demonstrate particle removal using water clearly labelled as unsuitable for consumption. Naming that boundary does not weaken a scientific lesson; it teaches why a visible effect and a practical guarantee are not interchangeable. The organisers should confirm the wording on signs as well as in the spoken introduction, since spectators may arrive after the explanation.

sourceB.title: The Quiet Label
sourceB.text:
A fictional company designs sound absorbing panels for shared offices. In a small demonstration room, visitors find recorded speech less distracting after the panels are installed. The company proposes the label concentration guaranteed. Its engineer objects: the demonstration measured visitors immediate impressions, not their performance on sustained work. The recorded speech also came from a fixed speaker, whereas real offices contain moving conversations, telephone calls and unpredictable interruptions.

The marketing team argues that customers understand guaranteed as enthusiasm rather than a technical promise. That assumption is precisely what needs scrutiny. A customer deciding whether to spend money may reasonably treat the word as a claim about a result. A phrase that attracts attention by sounding stronger cannot be defended merely by insisting that attentive readers should interpret it weakly.

The engineer does not recommend discarding the observation. The panels may genuinely improve perceived comfort under the tested conditions. That finding can be described accurately, with the room dimensions and type of sound identified. The firm could also arrange a practical trial in a working office and decide in advance which outcomes to assess. Task performance, self reported distraction and employee preference would provide different kinds of information rather than interchangeable measures of concentration.

A purchasing manager adds another concern. Some workers need to hear colleagues calling across the room. A reduction in audible speech could help one activity while hindering another. This does not refute the comfort result; it shows why a universal benefit is unlikely to follow from a narrow demonstration. The recommendation must connect the product with the use for which it is appropriate.

The final proposal replaces the guarantee with a description of reduced perceived speech distraction in the demonstration. It invites purchasers to test a limited installation before expanding. The wording is less memorable, but it lets customers distinguish a measured impression from a promised improvement in work. If later testing supports a stronger claim, the company can revise it. Until then, precision protects the useful result from being undermined by an ambition the evidence cannot carry.

Purchasers should be able to discover these boundaries before committing funds, not only after a disappointing installation.

listening.teaching:
When our archive described a scanned collection as complete, we meant that every item in the box had been scanned. Several readers understood the word differently. They assumed that the collection contained every letter written by the person whose name appeared on it. We had not established that, and some correspondence was known to be held elsewhere.

The problem was not solved by saying that complete was technically accurate from our perspective. The relevant question was what a reader could reasonably take the label to mean. The catalogue title provided a persons name but did not name the physical box. Our internal boundary was therefore invisible to the audience.

We changed the description to say that all items in the donated box were available digitally. We also added a note explaining that this did not constitute a complete record of the correspondence. The scans themselves did not change, and their value was not reduced. What changed was the scope of the claim made around them.

This distinction matters when institutions communicate with people who do not know their working conventions. A familiar internal term can carry an unexpected public implication. We now review prominent labels before adding detailed notes, because a note hidden several pages away cannot reliably correct the first impression. Precision is not simply a matter of avoiding false sentences. It also requires examining the boundary an ordinary reader is likely to infer and deciding whether the available evidence supports that boundary.
listening.test:
A community programme advertised its evening workshop as accessible to everyone. The room had a step free entrance, and the organiser believed the description was justified. A prospective participant asked about the hearing loop. Another asked whether the last bus left before the workshop ended. Neither question had been considered when the advertisement was written.

The organiser initially replied that accessible referred to the entrance. That explanation revealed the narrow sense intended, but it did not establish that the public wording conveyed that sense. Everyone suggested a broader range of needs. A reader could reasonably expect information about participation, not only entry into the building.

The team revised the advertisement to describe the entrance specifically, state what equipment was available and invite questions about other requirements. They also moved the finishing time so that public transport remained practical. This did not prove that every possible barrier had disappeared. It made known conditions visible and created a way to discuss needs not yet identified.

I would preserve the organisers useful work on physical entry while qualifying the original universal claim. Calling the entire programme a failure would ignore the improvements. Repeating the claim unchanged would ignore what the questions had revealed. The stronger response is to distinguish established provisions from unresolved requirements, identify who can answer further questions and update the description as information changes. A practical invitation can be welcoming without promising a level of inclusion that nobody has yet checked.

sourceA.title: 教学案例：a volunteer theatre committee：扩展论证
sourceA.text:
At a volunteer theatre committee, participants considered whether to use a plain summary beside an informal rehearsal discussion. The background was specific: a director said the opening scene was on thin ice, then asked for another rehearsal rather than cancelling the performance. However, two new volunteers understood the warning as an immediate withdrawal of permission. The proposed response was to explain that the metaphor signals vulnerability and invite the director to state the practical consequence.

A rehearsal room benefits from informal language: it allows people to express doubt without turning every comment into an official notice. The solution is therefore not to ban metaphors. It is to clarify the action whenever a phrase could reasonably be mistaken for a decision. The director might say that the scene needs more work and name the next rehearsal. Volunteers would then know both the concern and what they should do about it. This preserves the collaborative tone while preventing a figurative warning from becoming an accidental cancellation. The committee should also make formal changes through a separate, recognisable channel so that participants do not have to infer administrative consequences from colourful conversation. The opening scene is on thin ice, so another rehearsal would help. I took the warning figuratively rather than as a literal instruction. Before we pull the plug, let us establish what can still be repaired. She was testing the waters rather than committing the committee to a decision. The joke fell flat because its cultural reference was unfamiliar. An idiom can soften criticism while making its practical meaning less explicit. When you say the scene is shaky, which change are you requesting?

After the rehearsal, the committee discovers that one volunteer has already booked replacement scenery. She interpreted shaky as a judgement about the physical structure rather than the performance. This was not a failure to recognise an exotic expression; it was a plausible reading in a theatre where scenery and acting were discussed together. The director should clarify which object the evaluation concerns and what action is requested. The group agrees that figurative artistic comments will be followed by a concrete instruction whenever safety, expenditure or cancellation could be inferred. Informal speech remains useful, but consequential decisions will no longer depend on everyone selecting the same meaning from an ambiguous phrase.

sourceB.title: Moving the Goalposts
sourceB.text:
In a fictional craft competition, the organiser tells a disappointed entrant that the judges are not moving the goalposts. The entrant has never encountered the expression and asks why football has entered a discussion about ceramics. Another competitor explains that the organiser means the standards have not changed after the work was submitted. The explanation clarifies the idiom, but it does not establish that the organiser's substantive claim is true.

The entrant then points to a new requirement concerning written documentation. The original announcement asked for a finished object and a short description; the judges now expect a detailed record of development. The organiser says that process has always mattered and that the new form merely makes it visible. These positions need comparison with the actual instructions, rather than a decision based on who understands the metaphor.

An entrant can understand an expression perfectly and still challenge the claim expressed through it. Conversely, a request for clarification does not show that the person lacks a relevant objection. The distinction matters because the explanation of goalposts initially draws laughter from several experienced competitors. If that laughter becomes a judgement about competence, the committee may overlook the documentary issue the entrant subsequently raises.

The panel reviews the announcement and finds that development was mentioned among broad aims but not listed as material to submit. This leaves a genuine ambiguity. It does not prove that the judges intended to disadvantage newcomers. It does suggest that treating the missing record as a decisive fault would impose an expectation that entrants could not reliably recover from the submission list.

The committee agrees to assess the current entries on the specified materials and to publish a clearer requirement for the next competition. It also records how process will be evaluated. The idiom remains an efficient way to discuss shifting standards, but its efficiency must not replace examination of the standards themselves. The case illustrates two distinct tasks: explaining what a speaker means and investigating whether the claim is justified. Successful communication requires both when money, recognition or eligibility depends on the answer.

Clearer instructions would protect experienced entrants as well as newcomers.

listening.teaching:
At a planning meeting, our coordinator said we should keep the project on the back burner. I understood that as postponing detailed work while retaining the possibility of returning to it. A new colleague heard it as cancellation and removed the project from the shared calendar. The phrase had compressed a distinction that mattered to our next actions.

The coordinator was surprised because she thought the expression was familiar. Familiarity was not the only issue. We had never agreed what postponement involved: whether a small budget remained reserved, whether external partners should be informed or who would decide when work resumed. Even those who recognised the idiom could have acted differently.

We therefore translated the phrase into an explicit arrangement. No new spending would occur that month, existing notes would remain available, and the team would review the project after the funding meeting. One person would tell partners that no date had yet been fixed. The project was neither active on its previous schedule nor permanently abandoned.

This experience changed how I respond to compressed language. I can ask what a phrase means without pretending that its dictionary meaning settles the administrative decision. If an expression affects responsibilities, it is useful to confirm the action, duration and review point. That need not make every conversation formal. A short question can preserve the convenience of an idiom while preventing participants from attaching different consequences to the same apparently shared understanding. Our shared calendar now records the review date explicitly.
listening.test:
The chair told our group that the new booking proposal was a non starter. One member assumed that the idea could never be reconsidered. Another began revising it immediately, believing that only the current price made it impractical. Both interpretations were possible because the chair had given no explanation of the obstacle.

When asked, she said that the venue was unavailable on the proposed date. She did not object to the activity itself or its cost. A different date could therefore change the judgement. The idiom had conveyed strong rejection efficiently, but it had concealed the condition on which that rejection depended.

The minutes initially recorded that the committee rejected the event. We changed them to say that the proposed date was not feasible and that the organiser would investigate two alternatives. This was not a cosmetic revision. It restored a possibility that the broader wording would have closed and assigned a practical next step.

I would not infer bad faith from the chair's original expression. Informal meetings often use compressed judgements, particularly when time is short. But participants should not have to guess whether an obstacle is temporary, conditional or fundamental. Understanding that non starter means unworkable is only the beginning. The useful follow up asks what makes it unworkable and whether that condition can change. Our eventual clarification allowed the group to retain the concern about venue availability without converting it into opposition to an event that several members still wanted to organise.

sourceA.title: 教学案例：a university archive：扩展论证
sourceA.text:
At a university archive, participants considered whether to rewrite a request for missing catalogue records. The background was specific: the first message to an external donor read send the list today, whereas the revised message explained the deadline and asked whether delivery was feasible. However, a highly deferential rewrite could obscure the fact that the exhibition depended on those records. The proposed response was to state the consequence plainly while leaving the donor room to propose a workable time.

The archive depends on cooperation from somebody it cannot simply instruct as though they were a subordinate. Explaining the exhibition deadline gives the donor a reason to help and a basis for proposing an alternative. Yet politeness should not disguise the fact that missing records may affect the display. A useful message would identify the essential records, state the latest workable time and ask what can realistically be supplied. It might also offer a partial delivery if that would keep the exhibition moving. This approach treats courtesy as a means of making cooperation possible, rather than as an accumulation of apologies that leaves the recipient unsure what is actually being requested. Would it be feasible to send the records before Thursday afternoon? We need the list today, but please tell us if that deadline is impractical. The request sounds courteous without concealing its urgency. Familiarity permits brevity, but it does not excuse avoidable ambiguity. I would make the consequence explicit rather than bury it in apologies. The donor may welcome a clear explanation more than elaborate deference. Please let us know what timescale you could realistically accommodate.

The donor replies that the proposed deadline is possible only if the archive accepts an incomplete list first. A cooperative response should not interpret this condition as reluctance to help. It should establish which records are essential for the opening and which can follow. The exchange also reveals why an excessively apologetic first message would have been unhelpful: the donor needed to understand the dependency in order to suggest a partial solution. The archive can thank the donor sincerely while recording the arrangement precisely. Warmth, directness and clarity are not mutually exclusive styles from which only one may be chosen. They perform different functions within an effective request.

sourceB.title: The Unanswered Recommendation
sourceB.text:
A fictional researcher asks a former supervisor for a recommendation. Her draft begins with three paragraphs of apologies and praise before mentioning that the application closes in four days. A friend suggests replacing the entire message with a short command: upload my reference by Friday. Neither version handles the relationship and the task particularly well.

The supervisor is not an employee required to complete an assigned administrative duty. A request should acknowledge the time involved and allow an honest refusal. Yet excessive ceremony can bury information essential to making the decision. The closing date, the work required and the relevant documents matter more than a lengthy account of how uncomfortable the applicant feels about asking.

The researcher rewrites the message to explain the opportunity, name the deadline and ask whether the supervisor could provide a reference within that period. She attaches a summary of recent work and the submission instructions. She also says that she understands if the notice is too short. This gives the recipient a practical route to acceptance or refusal rather than requiring a response to emotional pressure.

The supervisor replies that a general recommendation is possible by Friday, but a detailed discussion of a new project is not. The researcher initially considers this unenthusiastic. On reflection, it is a clear statement of capacity. Treating it as a personal rejection would obscure the useful offer and make a simple decision unnecessarily difficult. The appropriate next question is whether the general recommendation meets the applications needs.

The final exchange is brief and cordial. The applicant accepts the general reference and supplies the information requested. The tone does not become less respectful because the arrangements are explicit. Nor would adding more deferential expressions improve an agreement whose terms are already clear. Appropriate register is therefore not a position on a single scale from friendly to formal. It involves matching explanation, directness and interpersonal care to the relationship, while preserving the substantive decision that the recipient is being asked to make.

Respect is visible in the realistic choice offered to the recipient, not simply in the number of polite expressions used.

listening.teaching:
I reviewed two notices about a temporary entrance closure. The first said that users must obey the diversion without exception. The second apologised repeatedly for any possible inconvenience but did not say which entrance remained open. Both were intended to help visitors, yet each neglected part of the task.

The strict version made the rule visible but supplied no reason or practical route. The apologetic version showed concern but left readers uncertain about what to do. We revised the notice to state that repairs required the east entrance to close, identify the accessible route through the courtyard and give the expected reopening time. A short apology followed the useful information.

We also considered the audience. Regular staff knew where the courtyard was; visitors attending their first appointment might not. A small map would therefore do more work than another polite phrase. The new notice explained how to ask for assistance if the diversion did not meet a person's needs.

I would not say that courtesy is unimportant. It helps people recognise that the institution has considered their situation. But courtesy should support the action rather than replace it. A reader should not need to infer an instruction from a series of expressions of regret. Equally, clarity does not require treating every visitor as disobedient. The best version gave the reason, the route and the time in a direct form, while preserving a respectful relationship with people whose day the closure might genuinely complicate.
listening.test:
Our project leader wrote to an external illustrator asking for a revised cover that afternoon. The message said, as discussed, please make the changes today. The difficulty was that only the broad design had been discussed; the deadline and the additional detail had not. The phrase suggested an agreement that the illustrator did not recognise.

She replied politely that she could provide a rough alternative by evening or a finished version two days later. One team member read this as resistance and proposed a firmer message. I disagreed. The reply identified two feasible options and made a capacity constraint explicit. Stronger wording would not create more working time.

We checked what the publication actually required. A rough image was enough for the internal meeting, while the printer needed the finished file later. The leader accepted the two stage arrangement and corrected the implication that the deadline had already been agreed. This preserved the urgency without treating an external collaborator as someone who had broken a promise.

The lesson concerns both accuracy and tone. As discussed can be useful shorthand when there is genuinely shared agreement. Here it concealed the difference between discussing a topic and accepting a specific obligation. A courteous but inaccurate framing could still exert unfair pressure. We now distinguish proposed deadlines from confirmed ones and supply the purpose of an urgent request. That gives collaborators information with which to negotiate rather than a rhetorical assumption they must first challenge before practical cooperation can begin.

sourceA.title: 教学案例：a public transport forum：扩展论证
sourceA.text:
At a public transport forum, participants considered whether to argue for late buses without dismissing other passengers. The background was specific: a speaker began it is the last connection that matters most to shift workers, then acknowledged that earlier services also needed repair. However, the emphasis could be heard as claiming that daytime journeys had no social value. The proposed response was to define the priority as a marginal funding decision rather than a ranking of passengers worth.

The forum is deciding how to allocate an additional service, not determining whose life matters most. That distinction should shape the argument. The speaker can show why the final connection has an unusually large effect on shift workers without implying that daytime passengers have trivial needs. An explicit comparison of the consequences would make the emphasis defensible. It would also allow opponents to challenge the cost or the predicted benefit rather than respond to a moral accusation nobody needs to make. The revised speech should retain its focus, because removing every emphatic construction would obscure the urgency. It should instead connect that focus to a limited decision and acknowledge the unmet needs outside it. It is the final connection that shift workers cannot afford to miss. That priority does not imply that earlier journeys are unimportant. Not once during the trial did the revised timetable require another vehicle. Compelling though the example is, it cannot settle the entire funding question. What matters here is the effect of the next small allocation. The emphasis is justified only if the qualification remains visible. Far from dismissing daytime users, the proposal addresses an additional gap.

A further difficulty arises when the forum prepares its public summary. The proposed headline says that the last bus is the only service that matters. Nobody used those words in the discussion. They convert a claim about the consequence of one additional allocation into a claim about the value of every other journey. The secretary suggests retaining the shift workers example but naming the limited funding decision explicitly. This would preserve urgency without manufacturing contempt for daytime users. The forum also agrees to publish the main cost objection beside the recommendation. Opponents may challenge the estimate, but they should not have to refute an argument the supporters never intended to make. Clear emphasis gives an audience a focus; distorted emphasis gives it a false choice.

sourceB.title: The Only Ward That Counts
sourceB.text:
At a fictional hospital consultation, a campaigner says that it is the children's rehabilitation room that should receive the next charitable grant. The current room is shared with deliveries, and some sessions are interrupted. Her argument concerns a specific grant whose conditions permit improvements to communal spaces but not the recruitment of clinical staff. A local headline later describes her position as children matter more than nurses.

This description changes the argument. The campaigner has not compared the moral worth of patients and staff; she has identified a use for money that cannot fund the suggested alternative. The headline also obscures the possibility that staff benefit when therapy occurs in a suitable space. Its force depends on presenting the consultation as a competition between groups whose interests may partly overlap.

There are nevertheless reasonable questions about the recommendation. Another department uses a crowded family room, and its representative asks whether the proposed benefit has been compared with that of improving their space. Pointing out the headlines distortion does not answer this comparison. The campaigner should provide the estimated number of sessions affected, the expected improvement and the limits of those estimates. The emotional power of an account involving children cannot replace that information.

During the consultation, a therapist says that not once in the past month has a complete week passed without an interruption. This construction emphasises a recurring problem, but the observation period remains one month. It does not establish the same frequency throughout the year. The statement can justify investigating the pattern and may support a modest immediate change; it should not be silently converted into a permanent average.

The final recommendation names the grant conditions, compares the two eligible spaces and explains why the rehabilitation room is preferred provisionally. It asks for a review after the renovation rather than promising that every interruption will disappear. The strongest public account would preserve these conditions alongside the compelling example. Readers can then disagree about priorities using the actual options. Removing every emotional detail would impoverish the argument, but leaving the detail without its limits would invite a conclusion stronger than the case can defend.

listening.teaching:
The council asked me to summarise a debate about a temporary reading room. A resident had said that what children needed was somewhere quiet after school. The sentence was an emphatic response to a proposal for more organised activities. It was not a claim that children never benefit from games, clubs or adult support.

My first summary nevertheless described quiet as the sole requirement. When I read it back, the resident objected. Her concern was that every available space already hosted a scheduled activity, leaving no option for a child who wanted to read independently. The missing alternative, rather than an absolute rejection of activities, explained her emphasis.

That clarification changed the decision we needed to examine. We could compare the cost of reserving one room for quiet use with the benefit lost by moving its existing club. We could not settle the issue merely by agreeing that reading was valuable. The club also served children, and some attended precisely because they needed a supervised social setting.

We eventually recorded both needs and proposed a short trial on two afternoons. The trial would measure use, ask pupils about practical access and record any disruption to the displaced activity. I retained the residents emphatic phrase as an introduction but followed it with her explanation. A summary can preserve persuasive force without turning a contextual contrast into an absolute doctrine. The distinction matters because the exaggerated version would have required her to defend a position she had not taken and would have hidden the feasible compromise the discussion eventually produced.
listening.test:
At the sports centre meeting, a speaker said that it was the changing rooms, not another publicity campaign, that should receive the next improvement fund. He described broken lockers and a shower that had been out of service for weeks. Afterwards, a leaflet claimed that he opposed attracting new members.

The claim does not follow. His contrast concerned the use of one restricted fund at that moment. He later said that promotion might be useful after the basic facilities worked reliably. That qualification was absent from the leaflet, which turned a sequence of priorities into a permanent opposition between maintenance and growth.

There was still a real budget dispute. A manager argued that more members could produce the income needed for repairs. The speaker replied that recruiting people into unreliable facilities risked losing them quickly. Neither consideration was self evidently decisive. The group needed cost estimates, information about available funding and a realistic assessment of how membership might respond.

The revised minutes therefore recorded the maintenance recommendation and the manager's objection. They did not replace the dispute with a vague statement that everyone supported improvement. Nor did they suggest that the speaker had abandoned publicity altogether. A later proposal could change the balance by bringing in a separate promotional grant. The correct account leaves room for that possibility because it reports what the original emphasis was doing: prioritising a particular action under particular conditions, rather than declaring an unchanging view about the centre's future.
