sourceA.title: 教学案例：a local food festival planning meeting：扩展论证
sourceA.text:
At a local food festival planning meeting, participants considered whether to choose between one large kitchen and several small stalls. The background was specific: Mira preferred a central kitchen for hygiene checks, Arun defended stalls for shorter queues, and Jo asked whether either option fitted the available electrical supply. However, rapid agreement about the event date was being treated as agreement about the kitchen design. The proposed response was to record each proposal separately and leave the power question open until an electrician checked the site.

The organiser needs a record of the changing discussion, not a transcript that merely captures every word. A useful summary would list the central kitchen, the separate stalls and the electrical constraint as distinct items. It would show which questions have been answered and which remain open. The group should not interpret momentum as consensus: people may agree that the event should happen while disagreeing about how it can operate safely. A brief confirmation round would cost little compared with redesigning the site later. It would also give quieter participants a clear chance to correct the summary. After the electrical check, the discussion can return to hygiene and queues with a more reliable account of what is feasible. Mira supported the kitchen plan, whereas Arun was still discussing queues. Was that agreement about the date or about the proposed layout? Jo has raised a condition that neither proposal yet satisfies. Let me separate the decisions we have made from those still outstanding. I lost the referent of that last yes during the overlap. We appear to agree on timing, but not necessarily on facilities.

A recording of the meeting later shows that Arun said yes immediately after Jo asked whether the electrician was available on Tuesday. In the minutes, the word had been attached to the central kitchen proposal. Correcting the record does not require accusing the secretary of dishonesty. Rapid conversation supplies acknowledgements, answers and proposals in overlapping sequences, and even a faithful transcript may not label their functions. The revised minutes name the question answered and leave Aruns preference about kitchen design open. The group also adopts a short confirmation round before closing consequential decisions. This turns a fragile inference from timing into an opportunity for participants to state their commitments explicitly.

sourceB.title: Three Versions of a Decision
sourceB.text:
At a fictional coastal museum, a committee discusses moving a collection upstairs during repairs. The curator supports moving the fragile objects first. The caretaker asks whether the upper floor can carry the loaded cabinets. The treasurer says that the existing budget can cover lifting equipment but not another storage rental. These contributions concern different parts of the decision, although all occur within a minute.

When the chair asks whether the committee can proceed, the caretaker begins to say yes if the surveyor confirms the floor loading. The curator interrupts to suggest a date. Someone then answers yes to a question about the availability of volunteers. In a draft summary, the chair records unanimous agreement to move every cabinet on that date. The summary preserves the momentum of the meeting but loses two conditions.

The caretaker objects that approval was conditional on a structural check. The curator adds that her initial proposal concerned fragile objects, not the whole collection. The treasurer confirms the budget statement but says it was not an endorsement of any particular moving method. These corrections do not reveal three people changing their minds. They reveal that their earlier contributions were attached to different propositions.

A transcript would help, but words alone would still require interpretation. Yes may acknowledge a date, accept an invitation to speak or endorse a proposal. If its referent is uncertain, counting affirmative words cannot establish consensus. Nor should silence after a rapid interruption automatically be treated as acceptance, especially when a participant was trying to state a qualification.

The committee produces a new record with separate headings for scope, safety, cost and timing. It confirms a provisional plan to move fragile objects after the floor assessment, with the final method to be reviewed. Volunteers remain available on the suggested date, but their availability is not itself a reason to bypass the check. The revised process takes longer at the end of the meeting, yet saves the institution from acting on an agreement that nobody had actually made in the form first recorded.

A later signature should confirm that actual record, rather than supply retrospective approval for a stronger version.

listening.teaching:
I chaired a discussion about borrowing a minibus. Sam wanted transport for a Saturday trip, Priya asked who could drive it and Ellis checked whether the insurance covered volunteers. These were related questions, but they were not interchangeable. I failed to maintain that distinction in my first summary.

Priya said yes when I asked whether she could contact a driver. A moment later I wrote that she had agreed to drive. She corrected me immediately. Her commitment was to make an enquiry, not to undertake the journey herself. The difference mattered because no driver had yet accepted, and the booking could incur a charge.

Ellis had also said that the insurance looked suitable, followed by a condition about approved drivers. An interruption prevented the condition from appearing in my notes. When I read the summary aloud, he restored it. The group had not withdrawn agreement; the summary had expanded tentative statements into completed arrangements.

We rewrote the action list using verbs that named each commitment: contact, check, confirm and book. Booking would occur only after the first two actions produced satisfactory answers. This made the sequence clear and prevented an available vehicle from being confused with an authorised journey. I now read consequential decisions back before ending a meeting, particularly when several people have spoken quickly. The point is not to demand formal votes on every remark. It is to give people a chance to correct the scope and conditions of an agreement before somebody relies on it.
listening.test:
The team discussing an exhibition heard three proposals in quick succession. One member wanted a later opening date. Another preferred a smaller display on the existing date. A third suggested opening one room first and adding the rest later. Each option addressed pressure on preparation time in a different way.

During the exchange, the technician said that Tuesday would work. The draft minutes attached this to the later opening. In fact, he had been answering a question about testing the lights, and he had expressed no preference about the public date. The exact word was recorded correctly; its function was not.

The problem grew when the chair treated the absence of further objections as consensus. Two members believed the options were still being compared, while another thought the staged opening had been accepted. None had been asked to confirm a final formulation. The apparent agreement therefore rested on incompatible understandings.

At the next meeting we separated the options, named the unresolved constraint and asked each person to respond to one complete proposal. The group selected a staged opening, conditional on completing the safety checks for the first room. The technician retained Tuesday for the lighting test. This outcome did not require choosing whose memory was morally superior. It required reconstructing which contribution concerned which proposition and creating a clearer decision point. A reliable record needs that structure as well as accurate words; otherwise, the same short acknowledgement can be used to support several decisions the speaker never endorsed.

sourceA.title: 教学案例：a regional oral history project：扩展论证
sourceA.text:
At a regional oral history project, participants considered whether to train interviewers to request clarification respectfully. The background was specific: an interviewer recognised every written word in a transcript but repeatedly missed the speakers place names when hearing them without context. However, familiar vocabulary on a page concealed a genuine difficulty with connected speech and regional vowel patterns. The proposed response was to practise with consented recordings from several speakers and check place names rather than guessing them.

The project should treat comprehension as an outcome to be checked, not a quality attributed to a listener on the basis of confidence. Interviewers can prepare local place names, but preparation should not be confused with performance on an unfamiliar recording. Training should include several consenting speakers and opportunities to compare an unaided first hearing with a checked transcript afterwards. Clarification requests belong in the training as well. They allow the interviewer to protect the historical record without pretending to understand a name. A printed script may help vocabulary learning, yet cannot reproduce reduced syllables, timing or regional pronunciation. Progress should consequently be documented through new audio tasks as well as written exercises. I recognised the place name on paper but missed it in connected speech. Could you repeat the street name and then spell the final word? An unfamiliar vowel pattern does not imply unfamiliar vocabulary. I should verify the name instead of selecting the nearest familiar one. The written transcript cannot establish how much I understood unaided. Please correct me if I have joined two separate names together. The difficulty emerged when the speaker reduced several unstressed syllables.

An interviewer later recognises a place name because she knows which village the speaker is likely to mention. This contextual success is useful, but the project should not confuse it with hearing every sound correctly. The distinction becomes visible when a similar name appears unexpectedly in a new recording. Training can use context while occasionally testing what happens when familiar predictions fail. The aim is not to remove context from communication; it is to prevent confidence from resting entirely on a guess. Interviewers should record uncertain names, request repetition where appropriate and verify the final transcription. Respect for speakers includes preserving what they said rather than replacing unfamiliar detail with a more comfortable expectation.

sourceB.title: The Confident Dispatcher
sourceB.text:
A fictional courier service asks dispatchers to confirm unfamiliar destination names. One experienced dispatcher completes calls quickly and rarely asks for repetition. A new colleague takes longer but produces fewer corrected bookings. The supervisor initially praises the experienced worker as the stronger listener because the calls sound smoother. A review of errors complicates that judgement.

The experienced dispatcher often substitutes a familiar place when a name resembles one on the usual route. Most substitutions happen to be right because the company serves the same district repeatedly. The method becomes unreliable when a caller requests a delivery outside that district. Context has supplied useful expectations, but confidence has concealed the distinction between recognising a name and selecting a likely one.

The new colleague repeats the complete destination and asks for spelling when two names remain possible. This can sound hesitant, yet it gives the caller a clear chance to correct the record. The review should therefore assess the final shared understanding rather than fluency alone. Asking a question is not automatically evidence of weaker language ability; refusing to ask is not proof of accurate comprehension.

The supervisor also notices that errors are commonly attributed to callers accents. Some do involve unfamiliar pronunciation, but others arise when a caller changes a house number halfway through an utterance or refers to a building by an old name. A general accent label combines several distinct problems and can unfairly place all responsibility on the caller. Better training separates pronunciation, correction structure, local knowledge and line quality.

The service introduces confirmation of complete addresses and uses recordings made with appropriate consent for training. It tests unfamiliar names as well as routine ones, while making clear that laboratory success cannot guarantee performance during every noisy call. The experienced dispatcher retains valuable local knowledge; the new colleague contributes a more reliable repair strategy. Neither must be reduced to the label good or bad listener. The practical goal is accurate coordination across variation, supported by procedures that reveal uncertainty before a parcel is sent to the wrong place.

That distinction allows training to target an observed difficulty rather than a convenient stereotype about another persons voice.

listening.teaching:
When I began transcribing interviews, I thought recognising the written transcript afterwards meant that I had nearly understood the recording. It often meant something narrower. Once I knew the intended words, I could connect the sounds with them. Without that support, my first interpretation sometimes remained quite different.

The distinction became clear with names. A speaker mentioned a small harbour, and I heard the name of a larger town I knew well. The sentence still made sense, so I did not mark uncertainty. Only a later reference to a ferry revealed the mistake. Familiarity had made the wrong interpretation comfortable rather than accurate.

My supervisor suggested keeping a first pass record before consulting the transcript. We then compared what I heard unaided, what I inferred from context and what I recognised only after checking. This did not make context illegitimate. Real listeners use it constantly. It helped us identify where predictions were doing most of the work.

We also practised respectful clarification with consenting speakers. Asking for a name again, or checking its spelling, protected the historical record. It did not require describing the speakers accent as defective. Written exercises helped vocabulary, but progress in listening required new audio from more than one voice. I now treat a familiar transcript as a learning aid, not a certificate that I would understand unfamiliar speech under different conditions. That more limited claim gives me a clearer direction for practice. The first hearing remains a separate source of evidence.
listening.test:
The travel desk received a complaint after a ticket was issued for the wrong island. The caller had named the destination correctly, then corrected the departure date. The clerk combined the familiar island name from an earlier booking with the newly corrected date. He remembered the conversation as clear because the resulting itinerary sounded plausible.

The recording showed that this was not simply an unfamiliar accent problem. The destination was audible, and the correction concerned another part of the request. The clerk needed to keep the slots in the booking separate while updating one of them. His confidence in the overall story had hidden a mistake in how information was assigned.

The manager proposed a pronunciation workshop, which might be useful for other reasons. It would not directly address this error. The more relevant change was to repeat the whole itinerary after any correction: destination, date, time and passenger details. The caller could then confirm the final version rather than assume that the changed element had been attached to the right journey.

I would also avoid concluding that the clerk was generally incapable. He had substantial route knowledge, and that knowledge helped on many calls. Here it supported an incorrect expectation. The review should preserve that distinction and test the revised procedure with unfamiliar combinations. A successful routine call does not establish that a listener can manage every correction, and a single failure does not explain itself merely because the speakers voices differ. The useful question is which part of understanding broke down and what would make it visible earlier.

finalModules.focus: Infer irony from context while distinguishing its target, effect and uncertain intention.

vocab.head: irony
vocab.example: The irony of the welcome ceremony became apparent when guests were asked to admire a newly installed ramp that ended at a locked door.
vocab.exampleZh: 当宾客被请去欣赏一条尽头却是锁门的新坡道时，欢迎仪式的反讽意味就显现了。

vocab.head: flawless
vocab.example: A visitor described the planning as flawless while pointing towards the inaccessible entrance, making the literal praise difficult to reconcile with the scene.
vocab.exampleZh: 一位来访者指着无法通行的入口称规划完美无缺，让字面赞扬难以与眼前情景一致。

vocab.head: target
vocab.example: The target of the criticism appeared to be the arrangement rather than the volunteer who happened to be standing beside the entrance.
vocab.exampleZh: 批评所针对的似乎是安排本身，而非恰好站在入口旁的志愿者。

vocab.head: delivery
vocab.example: Her measured delivery gave no exaggerated signal of amusement, although the contradiction between her words and her gesture remained available to the listeners.
vocab.exampleZh: 她平稳的说话方式并未夸张地表示幽默，不过言语与动作之间的矛盾仍可被听者察觉。

vocab.head: deadpan
vocab.example: A deadpan remark can depend on shared recognition, which cannot be assumed merely because two people speak the same language with confidence.
vocab.exampleZh: 不动声色的玩笑可能依赖共同认知，而不能仅因两个人都能自信使用同一语言就假定存在。

vocab.head: incongruity
vocab.example: Some guests noticed the incongruity immediately, while another asked whether a second entrance had actually been opened for the occasion elsewhere.
vocab.exampleZh: 一些客人马上注意到不协调，另一位却问是否已在别处为活动开放第二入口。

vocab.head: literal
vocab.example: That question was reasonable under a literal reading, reminding the organiser that understanding the information and recognising the joke were separate achievements.
vocab.exampleZh: 按字面理解那个问题合情合理，提醒组织者理解信息和识别玩笑是两种不同的表现。

vocab.head: reception
vocab.example: Audience reception also varied among those who understood the criticism: one laughed, whereas another considered public embarrassment an unhelpful response to an immediate problem.
vocab.exampleZh: 即使理解批评，受众反应也不同：有人笑了，有人觉得公开让人难堪无助于解决眼前问题。

vocab.head: attribute
vocab.example: We should therefore hesitate to attribute a single intention or a uniform emotional effect to the remark on the basis of its wording alone.
vocab.exampleZh: 因此，不能仅凭措辞就轻易认定这句话只有一种意图或统一的情感效果。

vocab.head: hostility
vocab.example: The volunteer initially heard hostility towards herself, but the visitor immediately asked who could find the key and offered to help redirect arrivals.
vocab.exampleZh: 志愿者起初觉得对方针对自己有敌意，但来访者随即问谁能找到钥匙，并主动帮忙引导来宾。

vocab.head: qualification
vocab.example: This action supplies an important qualification to a reading of deliberate humiliation, without proving that the wording had caused nobody any discomfort.
vocab.exampleZh: 这一行动为故意羞辱的解读提供重要限定，却不能证明措辞没有让任何人不舒服。

vocab.head: rapport
vocab.example: The visitor and the volunteer had not previously established rapport, so a style that worked among friends was carrying additional interpersonal risk.
vocab.exampleZh: 来访者与志愿者此前没有建立融洽关系，因此在朋友间有效的风格带来了额外的人际风险。

vocab.head: repair
vocab.example: A short conversational repair followed: the visitor explained that she meant the design, not the person, and acknowledged the unfortunate timing of the joke.
vocab.exampleZh: 随后出现了简短的沟通补救：来访者解释针对的是设计而非个人，并承认玩笑时机不佳。

vocab.head: uptake
vocab.example: Checking the uptake meant asking whether the practical concern was understood, rather than requiring the volunteer to declare that she now found the comment funny.
vocab.exampleZh: 检查理解与回应意味着询问实际问题是否明白，而非要求志愿者声称现在觉得评论好笑。

vocab.head: proportionate
vocab.example: A proportionate response would preserve the access complaint, clarify the misunderstanding and avoid turning either participant into a symbol of complete insensitivity.
vocab.exampleZh: 适度回应应保留无障碍方面的投诉、澄清误解，并避免将任一方视为完全不体贴的象征。

vocab.head: contextual
vocab.example: The case shows why contextual evidence can support an ironic reading while leaving important questions about intention, judgement and social effect open.
vocab.exampleZh: 这个案例说明语境证据可以支持反讽解读，同时让意图、判断和社会效果的重要问题保持开放。

sourceA.title: 反讽的对象与关系：原创教学叙事
sourceA.text: The irony of the welcome ceremony became apparent when guests were asked to admire a newly installed ramp that ended at a locked door. A visitor described the planning as flawless while pointing towards the inaccessible entrance, making the literal praise difficult to reconcile with the scene. The target of the criticism appeared to be the arrangement rather than the volunteer who happened to be standing beside the entrance. Her measured delivery gave no exaggerated signal of amusement, although the contradiction between her words and her gesture remained available to the listeners. A deadpan remark can depend on shared recognition, which cannot be assumed merely because two people speak the same language with confidence. Some guests noticed the incongruity immediately, while another asked whether a second entrance had actually been opened for the occasion elsewhere. That question was reasonable under a literal reading, reminding the organiser that understanding the information and recognising the joke were separate achievements. Audience reception also varied among those who understood the criticism: one laughed, whereas another considered public embarrassment an unhelpful response to an immediate problem. We should therefore hesitate to attribute a single intention or a uniform emotional effect to the remark on the basis of its wording alone. The volunteer initially heard hostility towards herself, but the visitor immediately asked who could find the key and offered to help redirect arrivals. This action supplies an important qualification to a reading of deliberate humiliation, without proving that the wording had caused nobody any discomfort. The visitor and the volunteer had not previously established rapport, so a style that worked among friends was carrying additional interpersonal risk. A short conversational repair followed: the visitor explained that she meant the design, not the person, and acknowledged the unfortunate timing of the joke. Checking the uptake meant asking whether the practical concern was understood, rather than requiring the volunteer to declare that she now found the comment funny. A proportionate response would preserve the access complaint, clarify the misunderstanding and avoid turning either participant into a symbol of complete insensitivity. The case shows why contextual evidence can support an ironic reading while leaving important questions about intention, judgement and social effect open.

sourceB.title: The Generous Deadline
sourceB.text:
During a fictional residents meeting, the chair announces that comments on a complicated redevelopment proposal must be submitted by nine the following morning. It is already eight in the evening. A resident replies, with no visible smile, that the committee is being exceptionally generous with people's time. Several people laugh. The chair responds that eleven hours is technically longer than one working day, and the exchange quickly becomes a dispute about arithmetic.

The arithmetic is not the residents principal point. Her description is difficult to read as genuine gratitude because the interval includes the night and follows the late release of a lengthy document. These circumstances support an ironic interpretation: the praise draws attention to an inadequate opportunity for participation. Yet the fact that other residents laugh does not prove they agree with every criticism she might hold about the committee. They could recognise the contrast while disagreeing about the appropriate extension.

A second resident then calls the chair a thief of public voices. This is a stronger accusation, not simply another wording of the first remark. It attributes a deliberate intention to exclude. The available facts establish an inconvenient and arguably unreasonable deadline, but they do not establish why it was chosen. The chair says that an external funding schedule is involved. This explanation needs checking; it should neither be accepted automatically nor discarded merely because the earlier response was defensive.

The meeting becomes more productive when someone asks which parts of the timetable are fixed and which can still change. The committee agrees to accept initial objections by morning and supporting detail three days later, while publishing the correspondence concerning the funding date. The arrangement does not erase the original difficulty, especially for residents unable to attend the meeting. It nevertheless addresses the practical concern more directly than a contest over whether generous was factually accurate.

A careful account would distinguish an ironic challenge to a procedure from an unsupported accusation about personal motives. It would also preserve the question of access for absent residents. Recognising humour is only the first step; understanding what follows from it requires attention to the problem, the evidence and the people who have not yet had an opportunity to respond.

listening.teaching:
I was the technician at the community cinema when the projector failed during the welcoming speech. The host looked at the blank screen and said that our commitment to minimalism had reached an impressive new level. Most of the audience laughed, and I understood why: everyone had expected a film, not an empty rectangle. I did not understand the line as a serious description of our artistic policy.

What interested me afterwards was the reaction of the new assistant. She thought the host was mocking her because she had checked the projector before the audience arrived. That interpretation was possible in the moment, but the host had not named her, and he later thanked the technical team while taking responsibility for starting before the backup test was complete. Those details matter when deciding whom the remark targeted.

They do not establish that the assistant was wrong to feel exposed. The joke occurred in front of an audience, and she knew she had performed the check. An intention to lighten the atmosphere and an uncomfortable effect on a particular person can coexist. Telling her simply to develop a sense of humour would avoid that distinction.

The useful response was to discuss both the equipment procedure and the public remark. We agreed that future hosts would announce a delay plainly before adding humour, and that technical faults would be reviewed privately without guessing at blame. The lesson is not that jokes are prohibited. It is that a shared laugh does not remove the need to identify the practical problem and to check how the people most closely involved understood the exchange.
listening.test:
Our workshop leader thanked us for our remarkably spacious storage system while stepping over boxes that blocked the exit. I understood the praise as ironic because the gesture and the obstruction contradicted a literal reading. However, a visiting participant thought she meant that we had been given too much space and offered to move our materials into a smaller room.

The misunderstanding showed that the remark depended on knowledge of what the room was supposed to look like. Regular members knew that a clear walkway had been part of the agreed plan. The visitor had not attended that discussion. His language knowledge was not necessarily the problem; the relevant shared background was missing.

The leader clarified that the boxes needed moving because they restricted access. She also said that she had made the joke before giving the visitor enough information. This was more useful than asking him why he had taken her literally. It turned an ambiguous criticism into an instruction everyone could follow.

Later, one member claimed that the leader had been furious with the entire group. The account does not establish that intensity of feeling. Her words, action and subsequent clarification support criticism of the storage arrangement. They leave her exact emotion uncertain. We should preserve the supported criticism without enlarging it into a complete psychological judgement. Equally, the eventual clarification does not make the original wording universally clear in retrospect. For this listener, it plainly was not, and the group learned something about the assumptions on which its everyday humour depended.

vocab.head: reservation
vocab.example: The compliment is followed by a reservation that changes its practical force.
vocab.exampleZh: 这句赞扬之后的保留意见改变了它的实际作用。

vocab.head: withheld

sourceA.title: 教学案例：a design grant selection panel：扩展论证
sourceA.text:
At a design grant selection panel, participants considered whether to interpret a cautious endorsement of an ambitious proposal. The background was specific: a reviewer praised the teams imagination and added that the timetable would certainly keep everyone occupied, while asking for a contingency plan. However, the sentence did not explicitly call the schedule unrealistic, but its placement after repeated deadline questions mattered. The proposed response was to report the reservation as an inference supported by context rather than as a direct quotation of rejection.

The panel can preserve a constructive relationship without treating praise as approval. Asking for a contingency plan gives the applicants something concrete to address, whereas debating whether the reviewer secretly disliked the team would achieve little. I would record the strength identified, the timetable concern inferred from the surrounding questions, and the revision needed before a decision. If the reviewer later clarified that no reservation was intended, the summary should change accordingly. That possibility does not make every inference equally speculative. Placement and practical consequence provide evidence, but they support a limited conclusion about the proposal rather than an account of the reviewers personality. The response should be equally specific. The compliment is followed by a reservation that changes its practical force. She did not reject the idea outright, but she withheld immediate approval. The timetable would keep everyone occupied may imply concern about feasibility. That interpretation is supported by the repeated requests for contingency plans. I would not attribute personal hostility on the basis of that sentence. Quoting the praise alone would misrepresent the reviewers overall stance. The hedge softens the judgement without necessarily weakening the reservation.

The applicants ask whether the panel liked their idea. The administrator could answer this narrowly, reporting the praise for imagination, but the answer would be incomplete if it omitted the unresolved timetable. A useful response distinguishes evaluation of the concept from readiness to fund it. The panel may welcome a proposal and still require revision before approval. The administrator should therefore identify what was praised, what remained uncertain and what action was requested. She should not translate courtesy into acceptance or caution into hostility. If the panel later clarifies its position explicitly, that new evidence takes precedence over an earlier inference; responsible interpretation remains open to correction.

sourceB.title: An Interesting First Attempt
sourceB.text:
A fictional design teacher describes a student's model as an interesting first attempt. She praises the arrangement of public space, then asks how emergency access would work and suggests another review before the final display. The student tells a friend that the teacher loved the project. Another student says that first attempt is a polite way of calling it hopeless. Both summaries enlarge one part of the exchange beyond what it establishes.

Interesting can express genuine engagement without indicating readiness for approval. First attempt can place the work within a continuing process rather than condemn it. The strongest evidence about the next decision lies in the request for another review and the question about emergency access. These details show that an issue remains to be resolved. They do not reveal whether the teacher privately doubts the student's ability.

The student might reasonably ask for clarification. A useful question would identify the required change or the standard for the next review. Asking whether the teacher really likes her would shift attention from the work to an emotional judgement the teacher may not have made. The difference matters because uncertainty about a practical requirement is answerable in a way that guessing another persons inner attitude is not.

Later, the teacher writes that the central layout should be retained while the service route is redesigned. This explicit instruction narrows the earlier ambiguity. It supports the view that one aspect was valued and another required revision. A reader should update the interpretation rather than cling to a dramatic initial reading simply because it was psychologically appealing.

The case also shows the limits of interpreting single phrases in isolation. A list of expressions labelled polite rejection would encourage students to hear every qualified compliment as hostility. A list labelled praise would lose the reservations. Competent interpretation tracks the sequence, the requested action and later clarification. It can report a supported inference while marking it as an inference, preserving a route to correction. The final account should therefore say that the teacher engaged positively with the layout but withheld final approval pending a practical redesign. Anything more personal needs additional evidence.

listening.teaching:
The committee told us that our event proposal was ambitious and that the volunteer schedule would certainly give us plenty to think about. I initially repeated ambitious as a positive verdict. My colleague noticed that the schedule had been questioned three times and that approval was postponed until we supplied a backup plan.

Her interpretation was not that the committee hated the idea. It was that the polite phrasing carried a reservation about whether our staffing assumptions were realistic. The surrounding sequence supported that reading more strongly than the adjective alone. The practical consequence, a request for another plan, was particularly important.

We wrote back asking which periods required additional cover. That question produced useful guidance. The committee identified the evening entrance and the final cleanup, while confirming that the main programme could remain. We revised those sections instead of rewriting the event from scratch or treating the whole proposal as accepted.

This taught me to separate approval of an idea from approval of its implementation. A speaker can express interest and caution at the same time. Summaries should preserve both when both affect the next action. They should also distinguish what was explicitly stated from what is inferred. If the committee had later said that our reading was mistaken, we would have needed to reconsider it. Context makes an inference defensible; it does not turn it into a quotation or provide unrestricted access to a speakers private feelings. The distinction keeps later correction possible without embarrassment.
listening.test:
The editor returned my article with a note calling the interviews vivid and suggesting that a careful reader might want to know where the figures came from. I felt relieved by vivid and almost missed the significance of the second clause. The article had not been accepted; the source of a central statistic remained unresolved.

A friend interpreted the note as sarcastic dismissal. I could not justify that conclusion. The editor had identified a specific issue and invited a revision. There was no evidence that the praise was insincere or that she wanted me to abandon the subject. Her restrained wording could simply preserve a working relationship while making further checking necessary.

I asked whether a link to the original report would be sufficient. She replied that the report used a narrower population than my article implied. This made the problem more precise: it concerned the scope of the claim as well as the presence of a citation. I rewrote the passage and explained the limitation.

The later exchange should change any interpretation of the first note. We now know what concern the indirect phrase introduced. It would be misleading to continue reporting either enthusiastic acceptance or total rejection. The strongest summary is that the editor valued the interviews but required a better supported statistical claim. Recognising that mixed position allowed me to act on the feedback without making unsupported assumptions about her attitude towards me. It also prevented a compliment from becoming a reason to ignore the reservation attached to it.

sourceA.title: 教学案例：a review of an exhibition about household objects：扩展论证
sourceA.text:
At a review of an exhibition about household objects, participants considered whether to evaluate whether limited scale necessarily meant limited insight. The background was specific: the reviewer complained that no national production figures appeared, although the exhibition explicitly explored how three families repaired inherited objects. However, a fair demand for context could become an unfair demand that a small exhibition turn into a different kind of project. The proposed response was to judge the stated purpose first and then explain what broader context would add.

A small exhibition can illuminate repair as a family practice precisely because it does not attempt to describe an entire national economy. That choice does not exempt it from criticism. The reviewer could ask whether the three families are introduced clearly, whether repaired objects support the claims made about them, or whether a little wider context would prevent misleading impressions. Those questions engage with the actual exhibition. Demanding a complete statistical account may instead replace its purpose. I would recommend a short contextual panel if it helped visitors locate the stories, while preserving the close attention that makes the project distinctive. Evaluation becomes more persuasive when it explains the relationship between an omission and a real limitation for the intended audience. The exhibition should first be judged against its stated purpose. Missing national statistics limit context without necessarily defeating the project. The reviewer appears to demand a different exhibition rather than a better version. That criticism identifies an omission but does not explain its significance. The domestic scale enables detail that a national survey might lose. I would distinguish restricted scope from inadequate execution.

The exhibition curator does not answer criticism by saying that every choice is merely personal. A stated purpose can be examined: do the objects actually support the claims made about repair, and are visitors told why these families were selected? These questions differ from demanding a national industrial history, yet they may still expose weaknesses. The reviewer should make the criterion visible and connect each objection with an effect on understanding. The curator, in turn, can accept useful context without abandoning the exhibitions intimate scale. Fair criticism respects the object of evaluation while retaining the right to ask whether its own chosen purpose has been achieved convincingly.

sourceB.title: A Map That Is Not an Atlas
sourceB.text:
A fictional publisher releases a pocket map of public drinking fountains. It shows locations, opening restrictions and whether a tap can be reached from a wheelchair. A reviewer criticises it for omitting restaurants, public toilets and a history of the citys water supply. The publisher replies that those subjects were never promised. This response identifies a problem in the review, but it does not settle the quality of the map.

The relevant question is whether the selected information serves the maps purpose. A pocket format can reasonably exclude extensive history. Excluding a warning that a fountain is seasonal would be harder to defend because it affects the very activity the map claims to support. Some omissions merely define scope; others undermine performance within that scope. A fair review should distinguish them.

The reviewer subsequently checks the entries and finds that two taps shown as continuously available are behind gates locked in the evening. This is a stronger criticism than the absence of restaurant listings. It identifies inaccurate practical information that a user could rely on. The map might still be useful overall, but its reliability requires correction and a visible update procedure.

The publisher initially says that no small map can contain everything. That principle is true but does not answer the specific objection. The complaint is not that the map lacks every possible detail; it is that the information it includes is misleading under relevant conditions. A defence of limited scope cannot become a universal shield against accountability.

The revised review recommends the map for its clear focus and accessibility information while warning that opening restrictions need checking. The publisher corrects the entries and prints the date of verification. Neither side must retreat into an absolute verdict of excellent or useless. The strongest evaluation explains what the object enables, for whom, under which conditions and with what remaining limitations. This gives readers a basis for action rather than requiring them to choose between an unfair demand for completeness and an equally unfair refusal to acknowledge errors inside the chosen task.

Readers can then judge whether the limitation affects their own intended use, instead of relying on an unexplained overall rating.

listening.teaching:
A reviewer described our short documentary as politically empty because it contained no interview with a national minister. The film followed a local repair worker through three days and asked how small businesses managed tools they could not easily replace. We had not promised a comprehensive account of industrial policy.

That did not mean the review had nothing to teach us. At one point the worker blamed an import rule for a delay, and we presented the statement without checking what the rule actually required. The reviewer was right to question that passage. Our limited observational purpose did not excuse a factual implication we had chosen to include.

We separated the two criticisms. Demanding a ministerial interview would turn the film into another project. Asking us to verify the explanation of the delay concerned the project we had made. We added a note clarifying the rule and retained the focus on daily work.

This distinction is useful whenever a small work receives a large demand. Scope should guide the criteria of judgement, but cannot immunise every choice from examination. A reviewer should explain how an omission affects the stated aim. A creator should answer the strongest relevant objection instead of using an irrelevant demand as a reason to dismiss the whole review. Both sides then remain accountable to the actual work, rather than debating a different film that could also have been worth making but was never the film offered to the audience.
listening.test:
Our beginner cooking booklet was criticised for containing no advanced knife techniques. Its purpose was to help students prepare five inexpensive meals in a shared kitchen. We thought that criticism missed the intended audience, and in that respect we had a reasonable defence.

The same review noted that two recipes used ingredients omitted from the shopping list. This was different. Beginners were especially likely to rely on that list, so the omission directly interfered with the booklets practical purpose. Saying that no booklet could include everything would not answer it.

We corrected the list and asked readers to test the recipes with only the equipment named in the introduction. That produced another useful discovery: one instruction assumed access to a lid, although the equipment list did not mention one. The issue was not sophisticated expertise but consistency between the promise and the resources supplied.

I would therefore describe the review as mixed rather than wholly fair or wholly unfair. Its demand for advanced techniques applied an inappropriate standard. Its comments about the lists exposed genuine weaknesses. Rejecting both together would protect us from useful criticism; accepting both would encourage us to abandon the simple purpose that readers valued. Evaluation becomes more productive when each objection is linked to a criterion and a consequence. The revised booklet remains introductory, but its introduction is now a more reliable guide to what a reader needs and what the recipes actually require. That is a meaningful improvement without a change in its chosen scale.

vocab.head: retrospect
vocab.example: In retrospect, Daniel described his last visit to the house as an errand, although his careful preparation suggested that more was at stake.
vocab.exampleZh: 回顾时，丹尼尔把最后一次拜访说成跑腿，但他精心准备的样子暗示事情并非如此简单。

vocab.head: pretext
vocab.example: Returning a borrowed atlas provided a convenient pretext for approaching a door he had avoided since the previous winter.
vocab.exampleZh: 归还借来的地图集为他接近那扇自去年冬天起一直回避的门提供了方便的借口。

vocab.head: withheld
vocab.example: He withheld any explanation of the winter quarrel, assuring the reader that its details would contribute nothing to an understanding of the visit.
vocab.exampleZh: 他没有解释冬天的争吵，并向读者保证那些细节无助于理解这次拜访。

vocab.head: conspicuous
vocab.example: That conspicuous omission mattered because the narrator otherwise remembered the colour of the envelope and the precise position of every chair.
vocab.exampleZh: 这一醒目的省略之所以重要，是因为叙述者对信封颜色及每张椅子的确切位置都记得清楚。

vocab.head: equivocal
vocab.example: His sister answered with an equivocal gesture, moving aside without either inviting him in or asking him to remain outside.
vocab.exampleZh: 姐姐作出了含义不明的动作，向旁边让开，却既未请他进去，也未叫他留在外面。

vocab.head: attribute
vocab.example: Daniel attributed significance to her silence immediately, presenting it as proof that she had expected him to return with an apology.
vocab.exampleZh: 丹尼尔立即赋予她的沉默特殊意义，将其视为她期待自己回来道歉的证明。

vocab.head: counterpart
vocab.example: Her actual words supplied no verbal counterpart to that interpretation; she merely asked whether the atlas still contained the loose coastal map.
vocab.exampleZh: 她实际说的话并未印证这种解读；她只是问地图集里是否还夹着那张散页海岸地图。

vocab.head: reassurance
vocab.example: He seemed to seek reassurance in the familiar objects, describing a repaired cup at greater length than the person holding it.
vocab.exampleZh: 他似乎在熟悉的物件中寻求安慰，对修补过的杯子的描写比对拿杯子的人更详尽。

vocab.head: focalisation
vocab.example: The restricted focalisation gives access to his expectations while leaving his sister's thoughts beyond the reader's direct knowledge throughout the encounter.
vocab.exampleZh: 受限制的叙事聚焦让读者了解他的期待，却始终无法直接得知姐姐的想法。

vocab.head: discrepancy
vocab.example: A revealing discrepancy appears when he says the conversation was effortless and then reports three unsuccessful attempts to change its subject.
vocab.exampleZh: 一个意味深长的不一致出现在他声称交谈轻松自如、却又报告三次转移话题均未成功之时。

vocab.head: deflection
vocab.example: Those attempts may be deliberate deflection, but the text does not identify the question he finds most difficult to answer honestly.
vocab.exampleZh: 这些尝试可能是有意回避，但文本并未指出哪个问题最令他难以坦诚回答。

vocab.head: tentative
vocab.example: A tentative reading would connect his attention to objects with his reluctance to acknowledge how the relationship has changed in his absence.
vocab.exampleZh: 一种试探性解读会把他对物件的关注与不愿承认离开后关系变化的态度联系起来。

vocab.head: plausibility
vocab.example: To test the plausibility of that reading, we must examine the final exchange rather than treating each earlier detail as independent confirmation.
vocab.exampleZh: 要检验这种解读的合理性，我们必须考察最后的对话，而不能把每个先前细节都当作独立印证。

vocab.head: undermine
vocab.example: His sisters offer to keep the atlas might undermine an interpretation of complete rejection, even though it does not establish reconciliation.
vocab.exampleZh: 姐姐提出留下地图集，可能削弱彻底拒绝的解读，尽管这也不能证明双方已经和解。

vocab.head: reconciliation
vocab.example: A claim of reconciliation therefore requires more than Daniel's closing statement that everything important had finally been returned to its proper place.
vocab.exampleZh: 因此，声称和解需要比丹尼尔结尾所说重要东西终于归位更多的依据。

vocab.head: restraint
vocab.example: Interpretive restraint preserves the narrator's emotional complexity without turning uncertainty into permission to invent a family history the story never supplies.
vocab.exampleZh: 解读上的克制保留了叙述者情感的复杂性，却不把不确定性当成编造故事未交代的家史的许可。

sourceA.title: 文学中的不可靠叙述：原创教学叙事
sourceA.text: In retrospect, Daniel described his last visit to the house as an errand, although his careful preparation suggested that more was at stake. Returning a borrowed atlas provided a convenient pretext for approaching a door he had avoided since the previous winter. He withheld any explanation of the winter quarrel, assuring the reader that its details would contribute nothing to an understanding of the visit. That conspicuous omission mattered because the narrator otherwise remembered the colour of the envelope and the precise position of every chair. His sister answered with an equivocal gesture, moving aside without either inviting him in or asking him to remain outside. Daniel attributed significance to her silence immediately, presenting it as proof that she had expected him to return with an apology. Her actual words supplied no verbal counterpart to that interpretation; she merely asked whether the atlas still contained the loose coastal map. He seemed to seek reassurance in the familiar objects, describing a repaired cup at greater length than the person holding it. The restricted focalisation gives access to his expectations while leaving his sister's thoughts beyond the reader's direct knowledge throughout the encounter. A revealing discrepancy appears when he says the conversation was effortless and then reports three unsuccessful attempts to change its subject. Those attempts may be deliberate deflection, but the text does not identify the question he finds most difficult to answer honestly. A tentative reading would connect his attention to objects with his reluctance to acknowledge how the relationship has changed in his absence. To test the plausibility of that reading, we must examine the final exchange rather than treating each earlier detail as independent confirmation. His sisters offer to keep the atlas might undermine an interpretation of complete rejection, even though it does not establish reconciliation. A claim of reconciliation therefore requires more than Daniel's closing statement that everything important had finally been returned to its proper place. Interpretive restraint preserves the narrator's emotional complexity without turning uncertainty into permission to invent a family history the story never supplies. The narrator supplies a persuasive ending without necessarily supplying reliable evidence for the settlement he wishes it to announce.

sourceB.title: The Photograph Behind the Counter
sourceB.text:
Leah, the narrator of this fictional story, insists that she entered the watchmaker's shop only because it was raining. The opening paragraph makes that explanation sound ordinary: she describes a broken umbrella, a narrow pavement and the shelter offered by the shop window. Yet she also knows that the proprietor closes early on Thursdays, and she notices immediately that a photograph has disappeared from behind the counter. These details suggest prior knowledge without establishing why she has it.

The proprietor recognises her but addresses her formally. Leah reports that his formality proves he has forgotten their friendship. A reader should hesitate before accepting this conclusion. Forgetting someone and choosing a formal manner with a recognised visitor are different possibilities. The story gives us the manner and Leah's judgement, not direct access to the proprietor's memory. When he asks whether she still has the blue watch, she describes the question as irrelevant and turns to the weather.

The missing photograph becomes a focus of her attention. She imagines that it has been thrown away, then notices a clean rectangular mark on the wall and treats it as confirmation. A mark establishes that something has been removed; it does not establish where the object went. Later, the proprietor mentions repairs to the ceiling, supplying a possible practical explanation that Leah does not discuss. This alternative does not settle the matter either. The timing of the repairs remains unclear, and practical explanations can coexist with emotional decisions.

At the end, he offers to mend her umbrella while she waits. Leah declines, saying that the rain has stopped, although the final image shows water running from the awning. One reading is that she wishes to leave before another personal question arises. Another is that she refuses an act of care she no longer feels entitled to accept. Both explain more than a simple claim that she came only for shelter. Neither permits a confident reconstruction of an unnamed betrayal. The most defensible interpretation identifies the gap between her declared purpose and her behaviour, then leaves the unresolved history unresolved. Her evasions reveal pressure; they do not provide a complete account of its cause.

listening.teaching:
At our reading group, someone argued that the station master in the story must be the speaker's father. The argument was appealing because both figures were associated with a silver whistle. But the whistle appears only twice, and nobody in the text states a family relationship. I asked whether the connection could be symbolic rather than genealogical. That suggestion did not prove the original reading wrong; it exposed an assumption that needed support.

We returned to the paragraph where the speaker remembers waiting beside an empty ticket window. One member read the waiting as evidence of abandonment. Another noticed that the speaker never says how long the station master has been away. A short absence and a permanent departure would create different histories, and the story leaves the duration unclear. We could still discuss the emotional effect of waiting without choosing one history as fact.

The strongest contribution came from a reader who initially supported the father interpretation. She identified a later sentence in which the whistle is described as belonging to the station rather than to a person. She revised her position without dismissing the earlier connection. The image might link the figures, she said, while leaving the kind of connection open.

That is the distinction I want us to practise. An interpretation can be worth considering before it is established. The task is to show which details it explains, what it assumes and what competing reading remains possible. If a new detail weakens our account, acknowledging it improves the discussion rather than ending it.
listening.test:
The passage we discussed yesterday describes a woman cleaning an empty classroom before returning its keys. Several readers concluded that she had been dismissed unfairly. They pointed to her repeated polishing of a desk nobody would use that evening. That is a possible account, but the passage never identifies her job or the reason she is leaving. She might be a teacher, a caretaker or someone helping to close the building for another purpose.

The empty room carries emotional weight regardless of that missing information. The woman checks each window, removes a drawing from the wall and places it carefully between two books. These actions suggest attachment. They do not establish whether the departure is unwanted. One reader noticed that the woman smiles when the last light goes out. Another observed that the smile is described only as brief, leaving its meaning open.

Our disagreement became more useful when we stopped trying to name a hidden administrative event. We compared the readings of loss and completion instead. Both could explain careful cleaning, but they placed different weight on the smile and the rescued drawing. The final sentence, in which she leaves the keys on the outside of the door, complicated both accounts because it suggested someone else would arrive soon.

I would therefore report attachment and transition as strongly supported, while treating dismissal as an unconfirmed reconstruction. That judgement could change if another passage supplied the missing context. For now, the absence of that context is part of the reading problem, not an invitation to fill it with the most dramatic available story.

questions.prompt: What most clearly challenges Daniel's description of an effortless conversation?
options: His repeated unsuccessful changes of subject.
His memory of furniture placement.
His return of the coastal map.
questions.answer: His repeated unsuccessful changes of subject.
questions.explanation: 叙述者的概括与具体行为不一致；改话题失败直接削弱轻松交谈的说法。

questions.prompt: What does the offer to keep the atlas establish?
options: Proof that the quarrel is resolved.
A detail that complicates complete rejection.
Confirmation that the sister expected an apology.
questions.answer: A detail that complicates complete rejection.
questions.explanation: 留下地图集削弱彻底拒绝，却不足以证明和解或读懂姐姐的期待。

questions.prompt: Why is the clean mark insufficient to establish the photographs fate?
options: The repairs prove it was stored safely.
The narrator cannot see the wall clearly.
It indicates removal without establishing a destination.
questions.answer: It indicates removal without establishing a destination.
questions.explanation: 痕迹支持移走，不支持丢弃；修缮也只是另一种可能。

questions.prompt: Which conclusion is most defensible about Leah?
options: Her account understates the personal pressure of the visit.
She does not recognise the proprietor.
She knows the photograph has been destroyed.

questions.explanation: 行为与自称避雨之间存在差距，但缺少完整历史。

questions.prompt: How does the later whistle description affect the discussion?
options: It establishes the station master as the father.
It weakens a particular family inference without removing the connection.
It makes the earlier image irrelevant.
questions.answer: It weakens a particular family inference without removing the connection.
questions.explanation: 物件属于车站使家族推断减弱，但意象联系仍可保留。

questions.prompt: What does the speaker recommend doing with a plausible reading?
options: Accept it until another reader disproves every element.
Avoid it whenever the author leaves anything unstated.
Test its assumptions against details and alternatives.
questions.answer: Test its assumptions against details and alternatives.
questions.explanation: 合理解读仍应检查假设、反证与竞争解释。

questions.prompt: What is the speakers reservation about the dismissal interpretation?

The smile proves she welcomed dismissal.

It introduces evidence of continuing use beyond her departure.

questions.explanation: 钥匙留外侧暗示有人将到来，但不确定离开的原因。

finalModules.title: 因果识别与选择偏差
finalModules.focus: Separate a credible mechanism from evidence that identifies a causal effect.

vocab.head: association
vocab.example: Higher marks among room users establish an association rather than a causal effect.
vocab.exampleZh: 使用自习室者分数更高，表明关联而非因果效应。

vocab.head: Prior attendance
vocab.example: Prior attendance may influence both room use and examination performance.
vocab.exampleZh: 先前的出勤情况可能同时影响自习室使用和考试表现。

vocab.head: selection bias
vocab.example: The proposed mechanism is credible but does not eliminate selection bias.
vocab.exampleZh: 提出的机制可信，却不能消除选择偏差。

vocab.head: comparison
vocab.example: We need a comparison that addresses differences already present before the change.
vocab.exampleZh: 我们需要一种能够处理变化前既有差异的比较。

vocab.head: compatible with
vocab.example: The result is compatible with several explanations the design cannot separate.
vocab.exampleZh: 这个结果与研究设计无法区分的多种解释相容。

vocab.head: narrow the conclusion
vocab.example: I would narrow the conclusion instead of dismissing the observation entirely.
vocab.exampleZh: 我会缩小结论范围，而不是完全否定观察结果。

vocab.head: precise estimate
vocab.example: Even a precise estimate can answer the wrong causal question.
vocab.exampleZh: 即使估计很精确，也可能回答了错误的因果问题。

vocab.head: inferred mechanisms
vocab.example: The report should distinguish measured outcomes from inferred mechanisms.
vocab.exampleZh: 报告应区分测量到的结果和推断的机制。

vocab.head: less plausible
vocab.example: What evidence would make the selection explanation less plausible?
vocab.exampleZh: 什么证据会让选择因素的解释不那么可信？

vocab.head: provided
vocab.example: Comparing changes may help, provided the groups had credible earlier trends.
vocab.exampleZh: 比较变化可能有帮助，前提是各组先前趋势可信。

vocab.head: identification
vocab.example: The limitation concerns identification, not merely the size of the sample.
vocab.exampleZh: 这个局限关乎因果识别，而不只是样本大小。

vocab.head: descriptive finding
vocab.example: Uncertainty about causation does not make the descriptive finding worthless.
vocab.exampleZh: 因果关系不确定，并不使描述性发现失去价值。

vocab.head: counterfactual
vocab.example: The causal question requires a credible counterfactual.
vocab.exampleZh: 因果问题需要可信的反事实比较。
vocab.register: neutral to formal; use according to context

vocab.head: selection
vocab.example: Selection into the programme may reflect prior motivation.
vocab.exampleZh: 加入项目的选择可能反映先前动机。
vocab.register: neutral to formal; use according to context

vocab.head: mechanism
vocab.example: A plausible mechanism does not identify its independent effect.
vocab.exampleZh: 合理机制不能识别其独立效应。
vocab.register: neutral to formal; use according to context

vocab.head: attrition
vocab.example: Uneven attrition weakened the final comparison.
vocab.exampleZh: 不均衡的样本流失削弱了最终比较。
vocab.register: neutral to formal; use according to context

sourceA.title: 教学案例：a fictional study of library study rooms：扩展论证
sourceA.text:
At a fictional study of library study rooms, participants considered whether to evaluate whether booking rooms improved examination results. The background was specific: students who reserved quiet rooms earned higher marks, but the report also noted that frequent users had stronger attendance before the rooms opened. However, the association could reflect prior motivation, and a plausible concentration mechanism did not remove that alternative explanation. The proposed response was to compare changes over time and seek a design that addresses selection rather than calling correlation proof.

The room users may genuinely benefit from a quiet environment, and that possibility deserves investigation. The problem is not that a concentration mechanism is absurd; it is that the observed comparison cannot isolate it. Stronger prior attendance suggests that users already differed from non users in a way relevant to examination marks. Collecting more detail about those differences could help, but it would not automatically make every adjustment credible. The evaluation should specify the causal question and explain why its comparison addresses selection. Meanwhile, the descriptive finding can still guide a modest decision about demand for rooms. It should not be advertised as a proven increase in grades caused by the booking system. Higher marks among room users establish an association rather than a causal effect. Prior attendance may influence both room use and examination performance. The proposed mechanism is credible but does not eliminate selection bias. We need a comparison that addresses differences already present before the change. The result is compatible with several explanations the design cannot separate. I would narrow the conclusion instead of dismissing the observation entirely.

The study team considers adding interviews in which room users describe improved concentration. These accounts would help explain experience and might suggest a mechanism. They would not remove the earlier difference in attendance between users and non users. The team should therefore decide whether its next question is how people use the rooms or how much the rooms independently change marks. Both questions matter, but they require different evidence. A more ambitious causal evaluation also raises practical issues: access cannot simply be withheld from students without considering fairness. The final report proposes a transparent allocation procedure for an oversubscribed period, with appropriate consent and review, rather than presenting a convenient comparison as though it had already answered the harder question.

sourceB.title: The Mentoring Badge
sourceB.text:
A fictional apprenticeship programme introduces a digital badge for learners who attend optional mentoring sessions. At the end of the year, badge holders are more likely to secure permanent jobs than other apprentices. The organisers announce that the badge has improved employment prospects and ask employers to recognise it as evidence of readiness for work.

The observed difference is genuine within the records, but its interpretation is uncertain. Attendance is optional. Learners with predictable schedules may find it easier to attend, and those schedules may also allow them to complete placements more consistently. Supervisors can recommend learners for sessions, and the recommendations may reflect expectations about future performance. Neither difference is captured by the badge itself.

The organisers respond that mentors teach useful interview techniques. This is a credible account of how mentoring might help, but it does not establish how much of the employment gap it caused. A mechanism and a causal estimate answer different questions. Interviews with successful participants may describe valuable support while leaving the comparison problem unresolved. Increasing the number of those interviews would deepen one kind of evidence without automatically producing the other.

There is a further complication. Several apprentices who left the programme do not appear in the final survey. If departure was related to difficulties that also affected attendance, the retained sample may be especially unrepresentative. The evaluators need to examine who is missing and why, rather than report a precise percentage as though completeness were assured.

None of these limitations proves that mentoring is ineffective. The responsible conclusion is narrower: badge holders in the available records had better employment outcomes, while the programme's independent contribution remains uncertain. The organisers could investigate allocation when demand exceeds capacity, collect relevant baseline information and seek an ethically reviewed comparison. They should also separate a badge documenting participation from a claim of demonstrated job readiness. Employers may value the former, but should know exactly what it records. The evaluation becomes stronger when it makes the unanswered question visible, not when it converts uncertainty into either an advertising guarantee or a declaration that the programme has no value.

listening.teaching:
The garden project asked whether its weekly sessions reduced loneliness. Participants completed a questionnaire before joining and again after six weeks. The average score improved, and the team wanted to announce that gardening had caused the improvement. I advised a more limited statement.

During the same period, participants met a regular group, received transport help and had access to a community lunch. Gardening might matter, but the design could not separate it from those other features. There was also no comparison with people whose scores might have changed over six weeks without the project. These are limitations of the causal question, not reasons to dismiss the participants' accounts.

The project leader suggested asking everyone whether the garden had helped. That would be worthwhile if we wanted to understand perceived benefits. It would not create a missing counterfactual. A person can sincerely credit one activity for a change that had several causes. We therefore planned interviews and a separate discussion about a stronger evaluation, rather than pretending that one method answered both questions.

The public summary now says that participants reported less loneliness after six weeks in the programme. It describes the transport and lunch as part of what was offered. It also notes that the design cannot isolate the contribution of gardening. This wording is less dramatic, but it lets supporters understand what the project has established. The next decision is whether the whole package is worth continuing while better evidence is collected, not whether a single questionnaire has proved a universal therapeutic effect.
listening.test:
A company tested a new flexible schedule with volunteers from one department. Their absence rate fell over three months, and managers proposed extending the policy because flexibility had apparently improved health. The volunteers were enthusiastic, and several described better sleep. Those accounts were relevant, but they did not settle the interpretation of the absence data.

The department had also changed supervisors and completed a demanding seasonal project. Either change might affect absence. Volunteers could differ from colleagues who preferred their existing hours. In addition, the trial began immediately after an unusually high absence month, making some decline possible even without a new policy. The report needed to consider these alternatives rather than use a plausible health story as a substitute for comparison.

I did not recommend abandoning flexibility. The trial showed that it could operate in that department and that some staff valued it. Those are useful findings for a practical decision. They are narrower than a demonstrated reduction in illness, especially because absence records do not directly measure health.

The company agreed to describe feasibility and reported experience separately from causal impact. A further rollout would collect comparable baseline data, record other workplace changes and define the outcome before examining results. Staff consultation would also address fairness in access to the policy. The revised plan may eventually support a stronger conclusion. For now, it preserves what the trial taught without claiming that every observed improvement arose from the schedule alone or that the same result is guaranteed elsewhere.

questions.prompt: What would concentration interviews add?
options: Removal of prior attendance differences.
Evidence about experience and possible mechanisms.
A direct estimate of the rooms independent effect.
questions.answer: Evidence about experience and possible mechanisms.
questions.explanation: 机制与体验信息不能自动解决选择问题。

questions.prompt: Why consider fairness in allocation?
options: A stronger design also has ethical and practical conditions.
Fairness makes causal comparisons unnecessary.
Existing differences prove the rooms ineffective.
questions.answer: A stronger design also has ethical and practical conditions.
questions.explanation: 方法改进并不免除伦理责任。

questions.prompt: Why is interview training not enough to explain the employment gap?
options: Interview skills cannot affect employment.
Badge holders did not attend mentoring.
A plausible mechanism does not isolate its causal contribution.
questions.answer: A plausible mechanism does not isolate its causal contribution.
questions.explanation: 可能机制与独立效应是不同问题。

questions.prompt: What does missing departure data threaten?
