sourceA.title: A visitor guide written together
sourceA.text: Our town’s first walking guide was written by a historian whose knowledge was impressive but whose sentences were extremely long. Although the information was accurate, visitors often stopped reading before they reached the description of the next building. The tourism office invited residents and language learners to help produce a version that would be easier to follow. Each volunteer was asked to explain one location in fewer than a hundred words without removing its main historical significance. This limit forced writers to decide which details were essential and which could be provided separately for interested readers. One contributor replaced an unfamiliar architectural term with a brief description of what visitors could actually see above the door. Another checked whether references such as this and it clearly pointed to the correct building rather than the previous one. The team read the draft aloud because a missing word or awkward connection was often easier to notice by listening. They also walked the route with first time visitors, who revealed that two directions depended on a shop sign that had disappeared. The final guide used permanent landmarks and included enough context for readers to understand why each stop had been selected. It was not simply shorter than the original; its organisation made the relationship between places and explanations much clearer for newcomers. The experience taught the volunteers that successful editing requires attention to grammar, meaning and the reader’s situation at the same time.

sourceB.title: Learning from an empty noticeboard
sourceB.text:
A university accommodation office placed all its announcements on an electronic noticeboard near the entrance. Staff believed the large screen would be more noticeable than paper messages. It displayed maintenance dates, social events and instructions for reporting faults. Yet students continued asking questions whose answers had already appeared there.
An investigation showed that each announcement remained visible for only eight seconds. A student carrying shopping bags could miss an entire message while opening the door. International students also needed more time to interpret unfamiliar terms. The problem was therefore not simply a lack of interest.
The office separated urgent notices from general news. Essential information stayed on screen, while a printed summary was available beside the lift. Every maintenance announcement included a date, an affected location and a contact person. Social events moved to a separate display inside the common room.
Questions about maintenance fell over the following month, although staff continued to offer help in person. They had learned that making information available was not the same as making it usable. The redesigned system gave residents enough time and context to act, instead of expecting them to adapt to the limitations of a fashionable display. Staff also scheduled regular checks to remove messages once they were no longer relevant.

writing.prompt: Write a report recommending improvements to a visitor guide. Consider language and directions.
writing.sample:
The current walking guide contains useful historical information, but visitors may find it difficult to follow. Two changes would make it more practical without removing its educational value.
First, the language should be revised. Several sentences contain too many ideas, and technical terms appear without explanation. Shorter sentences would help, but the aim should be clarity rather than a strict word limit. Essential unfamiliar terms could remain if a brief explanation followed them.
Second, the directions should rely on permanent landmarks. A reference to a temporary shop sign may become inaccurate within a few months. Street names and the visible features of buildings would be safer choices. Each instruction should also make clear whether visitors need to turn before or after a particular point.
I recommend testing the revised guide with people who do not know the town. Asking them to walk the route would reveal problems that experienced residents might overlook. Their experience should inform the final version.

speaking.prompt: Describe how to check whether written directions are clear.
followups: What evidence supports your view?
What would make you change your mind?
speaking.sample: I would first check that each instruction names a visible, permanent landmark. Then I would ask somebody unfamiliar with the area to follow the route without extra help. If they stopped or turned incorrectly, I would ask which words influenced their decision. This is better than simply asking whether the directions look clear. I would also check references such as it and this, because they can point to more than one place.

sourceA.title: The night train returns
sourceA.text: When the night train returned to our region, newspaper headlines described it as a complete solution to uncomfortable travel. My first journey suggested a more complicated picture, although I was pleased to reach the city without losing a working day. The compartment was quiet enough for reading, but the movement made deep sleep difficult for passengers unfamiliar with overnight trains. A fellow traveller explained that saving a hotel bill mattered more to her than arriving completely rested for a holiday. For a businessman preparing to give a presentation, however, the same trade off might be much less attractive or practical. Ticket prices were lower when booked early, so comparisons with flights needed to use equivalent dates and booking conditions. The operator advertised reduced environmental impact, but its short publicity leaflet did not explain how the figures had been calculated. This absence did not prove the claim false; it meant that a careful reader needed additional information before accepting it. At the destination, a convenient tram connection helped passengers avoid a costly taxi ride from an airport far outside town. That advantage depended on where travellers actually needed to go, rather than on the station’s central location in itself. I would choose the train again for a relaxed visit, while considering other options before an important morning meeting. The service expands our choices, yet its usefulness cannot be judged accurately without considering the priorities and circumstances of different passengers.

sourceB.title: What an audience survey missed
sourceB.text:
A regional theatre surveyed people who had attended at least one performance during the previous year. Most respondents praised its programme and said they were likely to return. The board initially interpreted this as evidence that the theatre was meeting the needs of the whole region.
One researcher pointed out that the survey excluded people who had never attended. Their reasons might include high prices, unsuitable times or a belief that the building was not welcoming. Positive responses from existing customers could reveal satisfaction, but they could not explain the absence of everyone else.
The theatre commissioned interviews in libraries, workplaces and a youth centre. These conversations produced mixed results. Some residents simply preferred other activities, while others were interested but had difficulty getting home after evening performances. A trial afternoon show attracted several new visitors, although the theatre could not tell whether they would become regular customers.
The board retained the original survey because it still provided useful information. It changed the conclusion rather than discarding the evidence. The revised report distinguished the opinions of current audiences from barriers faced by potential audiences. This narrower claim was less impressive as publicity, but more valuable when deciding how to spend a limited budget.

writing.prompt: Write an essay: Should travel choices be judged mainly by price? Discuss two other considerations.
writing.sample:
Price is an important part of a travel decision, especially for people with a limited budget. Nevertheless, comparing tickets alone can give a misleading picture of which option is best.
Time should also be considered. A cheap flight may require a long journey to an airport and an early arrival for security checks. A more expensive train could bring a passenger much closer to the final destination. The relevant comparison is therefore the whole journey rather than the advertised travelling time.
Comfort matters differently according to the purpose of the trip. Somebody going on holiday may enjoy an overnight train despite sleeping less well. A person preparing for an important meeting might reasonably prefer a different arrangement.
In my view, travellers should begin with their actual priorities and compare options under similar booking conditions. The cheapest ticket can be a good choice, but it is not automatically the most economical or suitable journey overall.

speaking.prompt: Explain why two people might judge the same journey differently.
followups: What evidence supports your view?

speaking.sample: Two people can have different priorities even when they take the same route. A student visiting friends may accept a long overnight journey to save money. A person attending a morning interview might care more about arriving rested and avoiding delays. Neither choice is automatically unreasonable. I would compare the whole cost, including local transport and accommodation, and then decide which disadvantages I could realistically accept for that particular trip.

sourceA.title: Restoring a woodland path
sourceA.text: At the first meeting about restoring a woodland path, volunteers disagreed about whether visitors needed more information or fewer signs. The discussion initially seemed to concern appearance, but it soon revealed different ideas about who would use the route. Regular walkers already recognised the turns, whereas families visiting for the first time wanted reassurance that they were not lost. This difference explained why an apparently unnecessary marker could still be valuable to somebody with less local knowledge. Rather than choose one group’s preference, the team walked the path with visitors who had never seen it before. At a fallen tree, everyone paused because the original route continued behind branches that concealed the next turning point. The team cleared those branches first, which solved a navigation problem without adding another object to the landscape. Further along, however, two equally visible paths led in different directions, so a small arrow remained necessary at that junction. Its wording referred to the destination rather than merely saying continue, allowing walkers to connect the instruction with their map. After the changes, visitors made fewer wrong turns, although heavy rain later created a separate problem with the muddy surface. The final maintenance plan therefore separated tasks concerned with understanding the route from tasks concerned with moving along it safely. This distinction helped volunteers agree on priorities, because solving a communication problem would not automatically repair a damaged physical path.

sourceB.title: Three approaches to learning a craft
sourceB.text:
Three adults described what helped them learn pottery. Mira preferred demonstrations followed immediately by practice. Watching a complete film at home had seemed convenient, but she repeatedly forgot the early steps by the time she reached her wheel. A short demonstration in the workshop allowed her to try each movement while it was still fresh. She did not mind working slowly, provided she understood why a step mattered.
Daniel valued written notes. His instructor’s quick hand movements were difficult to follow, especially when several actions happened together. A numbered checklist helped him identify where he had lost control of the clay. He still watched demonstrations, but the written sequence gave him something stable to return to afterwards.
Rosa learned most from comparing two imperfect objects. When a teacher placed a cracked bowl beside a successful one, she could see how uneven thickness affected drying. General praise was less helpful because it did not tell her what to change. She welcomed specific criticism when it included a practical next step.
All three appreciated patient teaching, yet their accounts suggest that patience alone was insufficient. Each person needed information in a form that helped them notice and correct a particular difficulty during practice.

writing.prompt: Write an article explaining how to make a walking route easier for newcomers to follow.
writing.sample:
People who know a walking route well often underestimate how confusing it can be for newcomers. Improving a route should therefore begin with observation rather than simply adding more signs.
First, invite someone unfamiliar with the area to follow the path. Notice where they hesitate and ask what information they expected to find. A hidden turning may become clear after a few branches are removed. In that case, an additional sign would create unnecessary clutter.
At a genuine choice between two paths, however, a clear marker is useful. It should name a destination that also appears on the map. An instruction such as continue may not help someone who cannot identify the intended direction.
Finally, organisers must distinguish clear navigation from physical safety. Excellent signs will not repair a muddy surface or a broken bridge. A good maintenance plan addresses both needs separately and checks the route again after changes in weather or vegetation.

speaking.prompt: Explain how signs and maps can work together.
followups: What evidence supports your view?

speaking.sample: Signs and maps are most useful when they use the same destination names. A sign saying continue may be unclear if two paths look equally likely. A named destination lets the walker connect the instruction with a wider route. However, more signs are not always the answer. Removing a visual obstruction might solve the problem more simply. I would test both the map and the signs with somebody unfamiliar with the area.

assessmentListening.text: I teach beginners to use sewing machines. One learner preferred watching my hands, while another understood better when I marked the sequence on paper. I originally thought I needed to choose the best method for the whole class. In fact, providing both helped everyone check different aspects of the task. The demonstration showed the movement, and the notes reminded them of the order. We then compared two short seams and discussed why one was uneven. The combination took a little longer at first, but learners needed less individual rescue later. It taught me to match information to the difficulty rather than label each person as one fixed kind of learner.

sourceA.title: A podcast volunteer reflects
sourceA.text: I agreed to help record our neighbourhood podcast because I thought speaking into a microphone would be the easy part. To be honest, I was far less comfortable when I heard my first recording and noticed how quickly I interrupted people. My colleague said the energy was promising, which sounded encouraging until she added that the guests hardly finished a sentence. She was not asking me to sound less interested; she wanted me to leave enough space for a worthwhile answer. At the next interview, I prepared fewer questions and listened for points that could lead naturally to a follow up. There were uncomfortable pauses, although the guest later told me that those moments had helped her collect her thoughts. I would not describe the result as polished, but the conversation was certainly more revealing than our first attempt together. One listener suggested background music, and I can see the attraction, especially when an episode begins with a long introduction. Still, music underneath every answer might make careful listening harder for some people, so we are testing it only between sections. What surprised me most was how much editing depended on understanding the speaker’s intention rather than removing every hesitation automatically. A small pause can signal uncertainty, and cutting it out may make a cautious statement sound stronger than the speaker intended. I am pleased we tried the project, but I now think of interviewing as a listening skill before considering it a performance.

sourceB.title: An organiser reviews a street festival
sourceB.text:
People keep asking whether I was delighted with the street festival. Well, seeing the square full of families was wonderful, and the volunteers did an extraordinary amount of work. I would certainly like another festival next year. That does not mean I would repeat every decision we made.
The main stage looked impressive, but it faced the market stalls. Traders told us they struggled to hear customers whenever a band played. We had checked the sound from the audience area and forgotten that people elsewhere were trying to hold conversations. Moving the stage would be more useful than simply asking musicians to be quieter.
I was initially doubtful about the children’s storytelling tent because it seemed rather modest beside the bigger attractions. In fact, it was busy all afternoon. Its success reminded me that an activity need not be spectacular to be worthwhile.
As for attendance, the crowd was larger than we expected. I would hesitate to promise the same result next year, though. The weather was unusually kind, and another local event had been cancelled. I am encouraged by the response, but our next budget should be based on a cautious estimate rather than our happiest memory of the day.

writing.prompt: Write a review of a community podcast. Mention a strength, a weakness and a practical recommendation.
writing.sample:
Our neighbourhood podcast offers a welcome opportunity to hear local people discuss experiences that rarely appear in the news. Its strongest feature is the range of guests, from shop owners to volunteers restoring public gardens.
The most recent episode was particularly interesting because the interviewer allowed the guest to explain why the work mattered personally. These details made the conversation more memorable than a simple list of achievements. Occasional pauses also sounded natural rather than unprofessional.
However, the introduction was too long, and background music sometimes made quieter answers difficult to hear. This could discourage listeners who use small speakers or have difficulty separating speech from other sounds.
I recommend shortening the opening and keeping music between sections instead of underneath the interview. A written summary with the guest’s main points would improve access as well. Overall, the programme is worth developing, provided that the team continues to put understandable conversation ahead of decorative effects.

speaking.sample: I enjoy interviews that let guests develop an answer instead of rushing through a list of questions. A natural pause can show that someone is thinking carefully. However, an interviewer still needs to keep the conversation focused. I am less enthusiastic about constant background music because it can hide quieter speech. I would use it briefly between sections and ask several listeners whether the final recording is comfortable to follow.

sourceA.title: A researcher explains urban shade
sourceA.text: When we began mapping shade in the city, our first task was to decide what we actually needed to measure. Air temperature alone was not enough, because standing in direct sunlight can feel very different from standing beneath a tree nearby. We therefore recorded surface temperature, shade coverage and the times when people were most likely to use each public space. At first, volunteers visited every location at noon, which made the timetable easy but missed changes later in the afternoon. After reviewing the early results, we introduced morning and late afternoon visits to capture the movement of shadows across important routes. One school entrance looked comfortable at lunchtime yet offered almost no protection when children were waiting to be collected after lessons. That observation changed our priorities more than the hottest single reading, since it connected a physical condition with a repeated daily need. We considered planting trees, installing shelters and changing where people waited, rather than assuming that one solution would suit every site. Trees offered additional benefits, but they required suitable soil, continued watering and enough time to develop a useful canopy over the pavement. Temporary shelters could work sooner, although their design had to account for wind, maintenance and access for people using wheelchairs. Our final recommendations combined immediate changes with longer term planting and made clear which proposals still needed detailed engineering advice. The study did not produce a single ranking of beautiful places; it identified when practical protection mattered most to the people using them.

sourceB.title: An interview about a swimming pool
sourceB.text:
Interviewer: Why did the town review the swimming pool timetable?
Manager: We received requests for more sessions, but they were not all asking for the same thing. Some swimmers wanted quiet exercise before work. Families wanted weekend lessons, and rehabilitation groups needed warm water with easy access to the shallow end.
Interviewer: Did you simply extend opening hours?
Manager: That was our first idea. However, heating and staffing costs would have risen considerably. We examined existing attendance before making that commitment. The early afternoon lane sessions were often half empty, while family lessons had waiting lists.
Interviewer: What changed?
Manager: We moved two lessons into those quieter periods and kept one lane available for individual swimmers. We also published the water temperature beside the timetable, since calling a session gentle did not tell rehabilitation users whether conditions would suit them.
Interviewer: Has the problem been solved?
Manager: Not entirely. Some parents cannot attend in the afternoon, and we still need more qualified instructors. The revised timetable uses the building better, but it does not remove every barrier. Our next review will include people who asked about lessons but never booked, because attendance figures alone cannot explain why somebody stayed away.

writing.prompt: Write a report recommending how to make a busy outdoor waiting area more comfortable in summer.
writing.sample:
This report considers how to improve the outdoor waiting area beside the community centre. The main problem is a lack of shade during the late afternoon, when many families collect children from activities.
An immediate improvement would be to move the waiting point closer to the existing covered entrance. Staff should first check that this would not block wheelchair access or emergency routes. Clear signs could then help families find the new location.
For the longer term, the centre should investigate planting suitable trees. They could improve comfort and the appearance of the area, but they would require space, watering and several years of growth. A temporary shelter may be necessary while they develop.
I recommend observing the area at different times before choosing a permanent design. A solution based only on conditions at noon might fail during the actual collection period. The final plan should therefore combine evidence about sunlight with information about how people use the space.

speaking.prompt: Summarise the main stages of an investigation into a public space.
followups: What evidence supports your view?

speaking.sample: First, I would identify who uses the space and when they need it most. Then I would collect observations at several times rather than rely on one visit. The findings should be connected to practical needs, such as waiting safely or moving through an entrance. Finally, I would compare short term and long term solutions, explaining costs and uncertainty. A follow up visit would show whether the change actually helped users.

assessmentListening.text: The archive project has three stages. First, volunteers photograph the old letters using a support that keeps the camera steady. Please do not flatten folded pages forcefully; ask the conservation officer if a page resists opening. sourceA.title: Two ways of learning outdoors
sourceA.text: Imagine one photograph showing teenagers beside a river with measuring equipment and another showing a family following signs through a nature reserve. Both groups appear to be learning outdoors, although the purpose of their activities and the support available may be rather different. The teenagers might be carrying out a school investigation, since one person is recording figures while another checks an instrument near the water. By contrast, the family seems to be choosing its own pace, with a child pointing towards an illustrated notice beside the path. I cannot tell whether either group is enjoying the experience, but both activities seem to encourage attention. Working with instruments could help the teenagers understand ideas that would remain abstract if they only read about them in a classroom. However, they may have less freedom to follow an unexpected interest because their group probably needs to complete a planned task together. The family’s visit is likely to be more flexible, although a clear explanation would still help them interpret unfamiliar plants or animal behaviour. Rather than describing every visible object, a useful comparison connects a few details with the question of how each group might learn. Words such as probably and perhaps make clear that these are reasonable possibilities rather than facts that the photographs can fully establish. If asked which activity would be more memorable, I would choose the investigation because making a measurement could create a strong personal connection. Someone who prefers exploring freely might choose the family visit, showing that several conclusions can be defensible.

sourceB.title: Photographs in a local history exhibition
sourceB.text:
A curator was selecting photographs for an exhibition about work in the town. One image showed a crowded workshop from the nineteen thirties. Another showed a recent employee working alone at a computer. Several visitors to an early preview concluded that modern work must be lonelier.
The curator thought the comparison was interesting but incomplete. The old photograph had been taken during a planned visit, when workers were asked to stand together. The recent image showed only one corner of a much larger office. Neither photograph revealed how people communicated throughout a normal day.
Instead of removing the pictures, she added short accounts from workers. A retired mechanic described the companionship of the workshop but also its noise and strict supervision. A current employee explained that she worked alone on some tasks and collaborated online with colleagues elsewhere on others.
The final display invited visitors to compare visible conditions while questioning what remained outside the frame. It did not claim that images were useless. Rather, it demonstrated that photographs are selected moments, and a confident interpretation can become misleading if the viewer forgets how the image was produced. Visitors were encouraged to distinguish observation from assumption before drawing broader conclusions about social change.

writing.prompt: Write an article explaining why photographs can tell powerful but incomplete stories.
writing.sample:
Photographs can communicate a situation immediately. A crowded room or an empty street may attract attention more quickly than a long written explanation. However, an image is a selected moment rather than a complete account.
The details inside the frame can support useful observations. We may notice how people are positioned or what equipment they are using. The difficulty begins when we treat an interpretation as a certain fact. A person sitting alone might be concentrating, waiting for a colleague or taking a break. The photograph cannot tell us which explanation is correct.
Context therefore matters. Knowing why and when an image was taken can change our understanding. Short accounts from the people involved may reveal circumstances that are invisible in the picture.
In my view, the best use of photographs combines close observation with cautious questions. Images remain powerful evidence, provided that viewers recognise their limits and seek additional information before making broad claims about other people’s lives.

sourceA.title: Choosing a welcome event
sourceA.text: Our student committee had to choose a welcome event for new arrivals, and the first suggestions included a concert and a sports afternoon. Instead of voting immediately, we agreed to discuss how each option would help people who had not yet made friends. I suggested a concert because music could give people a shared experience, but my partner wondered whether anyone would actually talk during it. That was a fair point, so I asked whether a short performance followed by small group activities might solve the problem. She thought it could, although she was concerned that the extra equipment would leave too little money for refreshments and accessible transport. We then considered the sports afternoon, distinguishing competitive matches from simple activities that did not require previous skill or expensive clothing. Neither of us wanted less confident students to feel watched or judged while they were still finding their place in the community. My partner proposed an indoor team challenge with practical puzzles, which seemed to combine cooperation with opportunities for informal conversation afterwards. I supported the idea on condition that teams were mixed carefully and instructions were available in clear language for everyone taking part. Before making our decision, we checked it against the same criteria we had used for the concert rather than favouring our newest suggestion automatically. The final proposal was neither person’s original choice, but both could explain why it addressed our main concern. Productive discussion meant using each other’s contributions to build a decision, rather than simply taking turns to speak.

sourceB.title: A residents’ meeting about a courtyard
sourceB.text:
Residents of an apartment building had a small budget to improve their shared courtyard. Three proposals were presented: more parking, a children’s play corner and a quiet garden. The meeting became tense when supporters described their own choice as the only practical one.
The chair asked each group to identify the problem it wanted to solve. Parking supporters were worried about deliveries rather than long term storage. Parents wanted a safe place to wait after school, not necessarily large climbing equipment. Older residents wanted seating away from the noisy entrance.
These explanations revealed that the proposals were not entirely incompatible. A short delivery bay could operate in the morning, while movable planters separated seating from a small open area later in the day. The design would still require clear rules, and nobody claimed it would satisfy every preference.
Before approving the plan, residents agreed on a three month trial. They would record access problems and complaints rather than judge success by the appearance of the courtyard alone. The chair’s main contribution was not inventing the final layout. It was helping people move from defending objects to explaining needs, which made a compromise possible without pretending that the original disagreement had never existed.

writing.prompt: Write a proposal for an event that helps newcomers meet people. Explain your criteria and recommendation.
writing.sample:
The purpose of this proposal is to recommend a welcome event that helps new students start conversations. The activity should be affordable, accessible and comfortable for people who arrive without friends.
A concert could create a shared experience, but it would offer limited opportunities to speak during the performance. A competitive sports afternoon might encourage teamwork, although students with little confidence in sport could feel excluded.
I recommend a short indoor team challenge using practical puzzles. Participants would have a reason to communicate without needing specialist knowledge or equipment. Organisers should mix the teams and explain that cooperation matters more than winning. A relaxed refreshment break afterwards would allow conversations to continue naturally.
Clear instructions and suitable access are essential. Before confirming the plan, the committee should ask several incoming students whether the activity sounds welcoming. The event should be judged by how comfortably people can participate, rather than by how impressive it looks in photographs.

Before deciding, I would ask my partner whether this arrangement might still exclude any group.

sourceA.title: Should schools set community projects?
sourceA.text: A school considering compulsory community projects should begin by asking what students are expected to learn rather than counting volunteer hours. Supporters argue that working with people outside school helps young learners understand needs that textbooks may describe only in general terms. For example, helping to design a clear visitor map could show why accessible communication matters to somebody unfamiliar with an area. This benefit is not automatic, however, because repeating a simple task without explanation may teach little about the community or its difficulties. Students need preparation, appropriate responsibility and time to reflect on what the experience has changed in their understanding of other people. Critics reasonably point out that compulsory service can create pressure for students who already care for relatives or work after lessons. A fair programme would therefore offer flexible schedules and several forms of participation rather than assume that everyone has the same free time. It should also avoid treating community organisations as places that must accept unprepared students simply because the school wants a useful activity. The strongest argument for these projects concerns meaningful cooperation, while the strongest objection concerns unfair demands on participants and their hosts. An effective essay develops both points with explanation instead of presenting a long list of benefits followed by an unrelated personal story. Its conclusion should answer the original question and acknowledge the conditions that determine whether the proposal is likely to work in practice. I would support a well supervised programme with genuine choice, but not a fixed requirement that rewards attendance while ignoring learning and fairness.

sourceB.title: An essay competition changes its rules
sourceB.text:
A youth magazine ran an essay competition asking whether cities should provide more space for cycling. In the first year, several entries used impressive vocabulary but barely addressed the question. Some described personal holidays, while others listed environmental problems without explaining how cycling space would help.
The editors revised their guidance. They asked writers to state a clear position, develop two relevant reasons and consider one practical objection. They also published an example showing how a simple observation could become an argument. A busy junction was not merely described as dangerous; the writer explained how separating traffic might reduce a particular conflict.
In the next competition, entries became more focused. However, a new problem appeared: several writers repeated the model’s structure so closely that their arguments sounded identical. The editors therefore clarified that organisation was a tool, not a script that every writer had to copy.
The winning essay supported safer cycling routes but questioned a proposal to remove all delivery access from shopping streets. It distinguished the goal from one possible method and recommended timed access as a compromise. Its success came from relevant reasoning and controlled language, rather than from a large number of unusual expressions. The judges praised its ability to recognise a difficulty without abandoning the central argument.

lessons.title: 反对意见

lessons.title: 展开

lessons.title: 承认

writing.prompt: Write an essay: Should community projects be a required part of school education? Discuss learning and fairness.
writing.sample:
Community projects can make education more meaningful by connecting classroom ideas with real situations. However, I believe that schools should require thoughtful participation rather than impose identical hours on every student.
The main advantage is the opportunity to understand other people’s needs. For example, helping a local organisation improve its information can show students why clear communication matters. This learning is more likely when teachers provide preparation and ask students to reflect afterwards. Repeating a task without understanding its purpose is less valuable.
Fairness is another important consideration. Some students already work or care for relatives after school. A rigid timetable could punish them for responsibilities they cannot avoid. Schools should therefore offer several suitable activities and flexible ways to complete them.
In conclusion, I support community learning when it is carefully supervised and accessible. The programme should be judged by the quality of cooperation and learning, rather than simply by a total of hours recorded on a form.

speaking.prompt: Give a reasoned opinion about compulsory community projects.
followups: What evidence supports your view?
What would make you change your mind?
speaking.sample: I support community projects if students understand their purpose and receive proper supervision. They can reveal needs that remain abstract in a textbook. However, a fixed number of hours may be unfair to students with jobs or caring responsibilities. I would offer several activities and flexible schedules. Students should explain what they learned afterwards, because attendance alone does not show that meaningful learning or useful cooperation actually took place.

assessmentListening.text: When I read students’ essays, I look first for an answer to the actual question. A paragraph can contain accurate grammar and still contribute little if its example is unrelated. I ask writers to underline the sentence that states each paragraph’s main point, then explain how the next details support it. If they cannot explain the connection, they may need a different example or a clearer reason. This is not a demand that every essay look identical. Different structures can work, provided the reader can follow the argument and see why the conclusion is justified by what came before.

sourceA.title: One event, four different texts
sourceA.text: After organising a weekend book exchange, Elena discovered that writing about the event required different choices for different readers and purposes. Her email to a volunteer began with thanks and asked politely whether the borrowed tables could remain until Monday morning. Because the recipient already knew the event, she did not waste space explaining its history or describing every activity in detail. The article for a community magazine needed a more inviting opening, so she began with a child finding a favourite story unexpectedly. She used that moment to introduce the wider question of how sharing books might bring neighbours together beyond a single weekend. Her review of the venue was more evaluative, comparing the convenient location with the difficulty of hearing announcements inside the crowded hall. A useful recommendation followed from those observations: the hall suited informal exchanges, but organisers would need a better system for spoken instructions. The report for the council used clear sections on attendance, access and costs, with a short summary of the changes proposed for next time. Although all four texts concerned the same event, copying identical paragraphs into each would have ignored what their readers actually needed to know. Elena checked whether every request was explicit, every judgement had support and every important piece of information appeared in an appropriate place. She also replaced exaggerated praise with specific details, recognising that a credible recommendation can include a weakness without becoming an entirely negative review. Her final revisions helped each intended reader understand, decide or respond, rather than merely making the language impressive.

sourceB.title: A complaint that received a useful reply
sourceB.text:
Tariq bought a weekend photography workshop as a birthday gift for his sister. The website described a small outdoor group with individual feedback. On the day, heavy rain forced the class indoors, and the instructor taught eighteen participants in a single room. Tariq understood the weather problem but felt that the promised feedback had disappeared.
His first draft of a complaint called the whole experience terrible. Before sending it, he replaced that judgement with specific facts: the advertised group size, the number who attended and the absence of individual discussion. He acknowledged that rain was outside the company’s control and explained that his concern was the difference between the advertised teaching and what was delivered.
The company replied with an apology and offered his sister a place on a smaller feedback session. It did not refund the entire workshop because instruction had still been provided. Tariq accepted the offer after confirming that the new session would involve no extra payment.
The exchange did not prove that polite language always produces a satisfactory result. It showed how a clear account of a problem, supported by relevant details and a reasonable requested remedy, can make it easier for another person to respond constructively rather than defend against a vague accusation.

writing.prompt: Write a polite email to a venue manager. Explain a specific problem at an event, acknowledge a positive feature and request a reasonable solution.
writing.sample:
Dear Ms Chen,
Thank you for allowing our reading group to use the community hall last Saturday. The central location was convenient, and your staff helped us arrange the tables before visitors arrived.
I am writing about the sound system. We had booked the hall on the understanding that announcements would be audible throughout the room. Unfortunately, the microphone stopped working after the first announcement, and several visitors missed the explanation of how to exchange books. We informed the duty assistant, but no replacement was available.
We would like to hold another event next month. Would you please confirm whether the equipment can be checked in advance and whether a backup microphone could be provided? As part of the agreed service was unavailable, we would also appreciate a modest reduction in the next booking fee.
We hope to continue using the hall and would welcome a practical arrangement. Thank you for considering these requests.
Kind regards,
Elena Morris

sourceA.title: Planning a quieter neighbourhood
sourceA.text: Our project group received a residents’ survey and a short interview with a transport planner about noise on a busy shopping street. The survey showed that evening deliveries disturbed several households, while the interview explained why shops depended on flexible access for vehicles. At first, one student wanted to choose whichever source seemed more convincing, but this would have treated different questions as direct contradictions. The residents described their experience, whereas the planner discussed practical constraints that a proposed change would need to address before being introduced. We therefore made separate notes on the problem, the people affected and the conditions under which each possible solution might be workable. A complete ban on deliveries sounded simple, yet it might force businesses to close or transfer journeys to nearby streets with similar problems. Restricting the noisiest activities during late hours appeared more balanced, although the available evidence did not specify which vehicles caused the greatest disturbance. Our recommendation was to collect that missing information during a short trial rather than pretend the existing sources already answered every relevant question. When writing the summary, we identified whose view each claim represented and avoided presenting a small survey as the opinion of every resident. We also paraphrased the main ideas instead of copying striking phrases that sounded impressive but did not fit the purpose of our proposal. The presentation acknowledged disagreement, while showing that protecting rest and supporting shops were not necessarily incompatible goals. Integrating information meant building a reasoned response, not attaching summaries without explaining their relationship.

sourceB.title: A school chooses its lunch policy
sourceB.text:
A school board reviewed a proposal to introduce one vegetarian lunch day each week. A supplier estimated that several suitable dishes would cost less than the current meat options. A student survey showed interest in environmental issues, but it did not ask whether pupils would actually choose the proposed meals.
The catering manager recommended a tasting session before a permanent change. She was concerned that a cheaper meal would not save resources if much of it was discarded. Parents also raised questions about allergies and portion sizes. These concerns did not directly challenge the environmental aim; they identified conditions the menu would need to satisfy.
During a four week trial, staff recorded how many portions were selected and weighed the leftovers. Two dishes were popular, while a third produced considerably more waste. Students said its unfamiliar name had not explained what ingredients it contained.
The board approved a revised menu and clearer descriptions, but postponed claims about long term savings until a full term of records was available. It used the supplier’s estimate, the survey and the trial for different purposes. The decision was stronger because no single piece of evidence was expected to answer every question about cost, acceptance and environmental impact.

writing.prompt: Write a proposal for reducing street noise while maintaining access for local shops. Identify missing information.
writing.sample:
This proposal aims to reduce late evening noise without preventing shops from receiving essential deliveries. Residents’ accounts show that disturbance is a genuine concern, while the transport interview explains why unrestricted closure could create difficulties for businesses.
I recommend a short trial limiting the noisiest deliveries during late hours. Before setting exact times, the council should identify which vehicles cause the most disturbance and consult shops about realistic alternatives. Otherwise, the policy might simply move the problem to a neighbouring street.
During the trial, residents could record the timing of significant noise, and businesses could report delays or additional costs. These records would help distinguish an effective change from one that only appears successful.
The current evidence supports further action, but it does not justify promising that one restriction will solve every problem. A carefully monitored trial would allow the council to protect rest while adjusting the arrangements in response to practical difficulties.

speaking.prompt: Explain how you would combine a survey with an expert interview.
followups: What evidence supports your view?
What would make you change your mind?
speaking.sample: I would first identify what each source can actually tell me. A residents’ survey may describe experiences, while an expert interview may explain constraints or possible methods. They do not have to disagree simply because they emphasise different issues. I would note where the sources support each other and where information is missing. My recommendation would then acknowledge uncertainty and explain what additional evidence would help choose between the remaining options.

assessmentListening.text: We compared a bus company’s timetable with interviews from hospital patients. The timetable showed a direct service every hour, so at first the route appeared convenient. Patients pointed out that appointments often finished just after a departure, leaving a long wait with no sheltered seating. The two sources were not contradictory: one described the service, and the other described how it fitted actual journeys. We recommended checking appointment patterns before changing bus frequency. A small adjustment to departure times might help, but we needed information from other passengers too. Improving one group’s connection should not accidentally create a larger problem elsewhere on the route.

sourceA.title: What a course completion badge means
sourceA.text: When I finished a long language course, the completion badge felt satisfying, but an unexpected conversation soon revealed gaps that the familiar lessons had hidden. A visitor asked me to compare two travel options, and I understood the individual words without immediately seeing which details mattered to the decision. Instead of repeating my strongest memorised sentence, I asked about her priorities and discovered that arriving rested mattered more than paying the lowest fare. Useful assessment includes unfamiliar situations where learners decide what to say instead of recognising a rehearsed answer. I began keeping a record of misunderstandings, separating missing vocabulary from problems with following an argument or organising my response under pressure. This made revision more focused, because another list of words would not necessarily solve a difficulty caused by weak connections between ideas. For listening practice, I chose new speakers and topics, then checked whether I could explain the main point without seeing a transcript first. For writing, I completed a timed task and asked another reader to identify places where my intended meaning was unclear or insufficiently supported. Speaking with a partner was especially revealing, since an unexpected question required me to clarify a view rather than deliver a prepared performance unchanged. I repeated checks after a delay, because immediate success could reflect temporary familiarity with particular material. The resulting profile showed stronger reading than spontaneous speaking, which was more useful for planning practice than a single flattering score without explanation. The badge marked an achievement, yet independent evidence about understanding and communication guided my next learning goals.

sourceB.title: A tour guide’s practice plan
sourceB.text:
Nora wanted to become a volunteer guide at a science centre. She already knew the exhibition facts and could deliver a prepared introduction smoothly. During a practice visit, however, a child asked why one experiment produced a different result when repeated. Nora repeated the official explanation without addressing the question.
Her supervisor suggested a new practice plan. Instead of memorising longer scripts, Nora would explain the same process to three different audiences: a young child, an interested adult and a visitor with limited scientific vocabulary. A partner would interrupt with questions that were not supplied in advance.
The first sessions were uncomfortable. Nora sometimes lost her place, but she began noticing when a listener needed an example rather than another technical term. She also practised saying that she needed to check an answer instead of inventing a confident explanation.
After a month, the supervisor repeated the exercise using an unfamiliar exhibit. Nora was less fluent than with her rehearsed material, but she asked useful questions, checked understanding and explained her uncertainty clearly. The supervisor judged this a meaningful improvement. The aim was not flawless performance on a familiar script, but dependable communication when the situation changed and the visitor’s needs could not be predicted beforehand.

writing.prompt: Write a learning plan based on stronger reading and weaker spontaneous speaking. Include ways to verify improvement.
writing.sample:
My recent practice suggests that I understand written arguments more confidently than I respond to unexpected spoken questions. My next plan will therefore focus on spontaneous communication while maintaining regular reading.
Twice a week, I will discuss an unfamiliar topic with a partner. We will exchange short materials beforehand, but we will not prepare exact questions. During the conversation, I will practise asking for clarification, explaining reasons and checking whether my meaning is clear.
After each session, I will identify one recurring difficulty rather than attempt to correct everything immediately. If I lack a useful phrase, I will practise it in several new situations. If my ideas are disorganised, I will work on clearer connections instead of simply learning more vocabulary.
To verify improvement, I will repeat a similar task with different material after two weeks and ask an independent listener for feedback. Progress will mean communicating more reliably across new situations, not merely delivering a familiar answer more smoothly.

speaking.prompt: Explain how you would check whether course learning transfers to real communication.
followups: What evidence supports your view?
What would make you change your mind?
speaking.sample: I would use unfamiliar materials and questions rather than repeat the lesson exactly. For speaking, a partner should ask follow up questions without warning. A useful result should identify strengths and weaknesses separately, because a high reading score does not automatically mean that spontaneous conversation is equally strong.

sourceA.title: An evening service with conditions
sourceA.text:
A fictional town library is considering two additional evening openings each week. Its manager wants a proposal that distinguishes a useful idea from an affordable commitment. Staff have collected comments, but a popular suggestion is not automatically a workable timetable. The following briefing explains how the team should discuss its evidence and responsibilities. The service is intended for residents who cannot visit during normal working hours, including carers and people on rotating shifts.

The pilot could begin on one evening rather than two, allowing the rota to be checked under ordinary conditions. Comments from visitors should be considered alongside attendance records. Otherwise, a busy first night might be mistaken for evidence that the same level of demand will continue throughout the year.

We must allocate funds before advertising additional opening hours. The survey provides an indication of demand, not a complete forecast. The manager should make a firm commitment only after checking staffing. We need to take account of staff working consecutive evenings. Extended hours could meet the needs of people on rotating shifts. A limited trial would provide evidence without creating an indefinite obligation.

We should draw a distinction between attendance and satisfaction. The council must bear the cost of additional security staff. Early results may shed light on which evening is busiest. A written rota would reduce uncertainty about individual responsibilities. We cannot rule out lower attendance during winter storms. The final report should set out the conditions for continuing.

sourceB.title: A workshop changes its booking policy
sourceB.text:
The Cedar bicycle workshop used to promise same-day repairs whenever a customer arrived before noon. That phrase sounded reassuring, but it concealed an important condition: specialist parts were not always available. Customers planned their journeys around an expectation that the mechanics could not consistently meet. The owner therefore replaced the promise with a diagnosis appointment and a written estimate of completion time. Diagnosis is now offered on the day of arrival; completion depends on the fault and the supply of parts.

A customer group welcomed the clearer distinction, although some members feared that the new wording would excuse unnecessary delays. In response, the workshop began recording the time between diagnosis and completion, separating delays within its control from those caused by unavailable parts. It publishes the median waiting time for each category, rather than combining every repair into one attractive average. This does not eliminate disappointment, but it makes explanations more specific.

The mechanics also changed their telephone language. Instead of saying that a repair was almost finished, they describe the remaining task and the next agreed update. The policy has a cost: estimates take time, and unexpected faults still require negotiation. Nevertheless, the owner considers a qualified commitment more useful than confident language that cannot be supported. The customer group will review the records after three months before deciding whether the new approach has improved reliability.

writing.prompt: Write a recommendation to the library manager. Distinguish a trial from a permanent commitment, specify evidence to collect, and explain one staffing safeguard.
writing.sample:
I recommend a bounded evening-opening trial, with staffing and security confirmed before publicity. The purpose is to test a service residents can use, rather than announce a promise that the library cannot sustain. The pilot could begin on one evening rather than two, allowing the rota to be checked under ordinary conditions. Comments from visitors should be considered alongside attendance records. Otherwise, a busy first night might be mistaken for evidence that the same level of demand will continue throughout the year.

We must allocate funds before advertising additional opening hours. The survey provides an indication of demand, not a complete forecast. The manager should make a firm commitment only after checking staffing. We need to take account of staff working consecutive evenings. Extended hours could meet the needs of people on rotating shifts. A limited trial would provide evidence without creating an indefinite obligation.

We should draw a distinction between attendance and satisfaction. The council must bear the cost of additional security staff. Early results may shed light on which evening is busiest. A written rota would reduce uncertainty about individual responsibilities. We cannot rule out lower attendance during winter storms. The final report should set out the conditions for continuing.

After the trial, the manager should publish the findings and explain whether continuing is justified. A clear stopping point protects staff while leaving open the possibility of a useful long-term service.

sourceA.title: What a shorter queue really means
sourceA.text:
The fictional Brookside advice centre has reorganised its reception system. Managers want to explain the early figures without exaggerating what they establish. Queue length, waiting time and the quality of advice are related, but they are not identical measures. Some appointments now take place by telephone, which changes who appears in the reception data. The centre has prepared language for a cautious progress briefing rather than a celebratory announcement.

A person receiving detailed advice may need a longer appointment, so faster service is not always better service. The centre should examine whether clients understand their next step. It should also check whether telephone users and people visiting in person face different barriers before describing the system as an improvement for everyone.

A shorter queue does not necessarily imply faster individual service. The figures suggest improvement but do not prove its cause. Telephone appointments may account for part of the apparent decline. The reduction was modest rather than dramatic. We should distinguish an accurate count from a representative sample. Some clients described the new reception process as convenient.

Convenience alone does not establish that the advice was appropriate. The manager acknowledged limitations without dismissing the positive results. A plausible explanation still needs independent checking. The evidence is consistent with a benefit, although alternatives remain. We need comparable figures from a similar period. The final statement should reflect the uncertainty in the findings.

sourceB.title: A quiet carriage experiment
sourceB.text:
A regional train operator reserved one carriage on six weekday services for passengers who preferred a quieter journey. The signs asked people to keep conversations brief and use headphones. They did not require complete silence. After four weeks, complaints about telephone conversations fell on those services, while the total number of complaints across the route remained broadly unchanged.

The operator's first internal summary described the policy as effective. A passenger representative asked for a more precise statement. Fewer complaints on selected trains might reflect improved behaviour, but passengers might also have moved to other carriages or stopped reporting incidents. Moreover, the trial services were chosen because they had unusually frequent complaints in the preceding month. A subsequent decline could partly reflect a return to more typical conditions.

The revised summary says that the results are encouraging and consistent with a useful local effect. It does not claim that the policy has reduced noise across the whole network. The next trial will include comparable services without a designated quiet carriage, and observers will record noise at fixed points in the journey. Observers cannot measure whether a passenger feels relaxed merely by counting conversations. The operator therefore plans a short anonymous survey as well. The passenger representative supports continuing the experiment, provided that the distinction between reduced complaints and reduced disturbance remains explicit.

writing.prompt: Write a cautious briefing about the advice centre. Explain why queue length is insufficient, propose two additional measures, and distinguish a finding from an explanation.
writing.sample:
The reception changes are encouraging, but the evidence does not yet justify a broad claim about service quality. The centre should explain what has improved and what remains uncertain. A person receiving detailed advice may need a longer appointment, so faster service is not always better service. The centre should examine whether clients understand their next step. It should also check whether telephone users and people visiting in person face different barriers before describing the system as an improvement for everyone.

A shorter queue does not necessarily imply faster individual service. The figures suggest improvement but do not prove its cause. Telephone appointments may account for part of the apparent decline. The reduction was modest rather than dramatic. We should distinguish an accurate count from a representative sample. Some clients described the new reception process as convenient.

Convenience alone does not establish that the advice was appropriate. The manager acknowledged limitations without dismissing the positive results. A plausible explanation still needs independent checking. The evidence is consistent with a benefit, although alternatives remain. We need comparable figures from a similar period. The final statement should reflect the uncertainty in the findings.

The next review should combine comparable waiting figures with evidence of whether clients understood the advice. That would support a more informative judgement than treating a shorter visible queue as success in itself.

sourceA.title: Rewriting a housing notice
sourceA.text:
A fictional housing cooperative needs access to residents' kitchens to inspect shared water pipes. Its first notice sounded abrupt and gave no way to discuss individual circumstances. A revised version must remain clear about the inspection while respecting privacy and making the required action easy to identify. The team is preparing both a formal letter and a short reminder message. Each version must preserve the same deadline and contact arrangements.

Privacy is central to residents' response. The letter should explain what staff will inspect, how identity will be checked and how a different appointment can be requested. A shorter reminder can omit background discussion, but it must not drop the action that residents are expected to take.

We would appreciate access to your kitchen during the inspection window. Please contact the office if the proposed time is unsuitable. The inspection is required, but alternative appointments are available. Residents are requested to reply by Thursday afternoon. For clarity, the visit does not involve opening personal cupboards. A member of staff will show identification before entering.

Could you let us know whether anyone requires additional support? The reminder should retain the deadline stated in the formal letter. Friendly wording must not obscure what residents need to do. We apologise for the inconvenience caused by the inspection. If you have already replied, no further action is needed. A firm request can remain respectful and specific.

sourceB.title: A theatre explains a cancellation
sourceB.text:
A small theatre cancelled a Sunday matinee when an electrical inspection identified a fault affecting the stage lighting. The fault did not affect the building's emergency exits, but repairing it while preparing the performance would have created an unacceptable risk. The first message to ticket holders contained a long technical description and placed the refund instructions at the bottom. Several readers thought that they were being asked to return to the venue before receiving their money.

The communications manager rewrote the notice in a simpler order. It opens with the cancellation and an apology, then explains that refunds will be made automatically to the original payment method within ten working days. People who paid in cash should telephone the box office to arrange a refund. Tickets cannot be transferred to the following weekend because that performance is already fully booked.

A separate message to the visiting production company contains the technical details and the revised maintenance schedule. The public notice does not include them, since they do not help ticket holders decide what to do. Nevertheless, both messages identify the same reason for cancellation. The manager rejected a suggestion to describe it merely as an operational issue, considering that phrase unnecessarily evasive. A brief follow-up will be sent once performances resume. The theatre wants to sound considerate without implying that an alternative seat can be offered when none is available.

sourceA.title: Editing a volunteer handbook
sourceA.text:
An environmental charity is updating its fictional volunteer handbook. Earlier versions were assembled from messages written by several coordinators. The information is useful, but inconsistent terms, unclear pronouns and mixed time references make some instructions hard to follow. The editor wants volunteers to understand the revised text without needing to guess the writer's intention. Corrections should preserve the policy rather than silently change it.

Volunteers may read the handbook while preparing equipment, with little time to resolve ambiguous instructions. A correction therefore needs to be checked against the actual procedure by someone familiar with it. The editor should record any uncertainty and ask the coordinator, rather than substitute a fluent sentence with a different meaning.

Each volunteer is responsible for checking the equipment before departure. The guide explains how to collect, label and store samples. When Maya returned, she gave the keys to the coordinator. Last month the team recorded faults; this month it is testing repairs. The equipment has been checked, but the route has not been approved. Fewer volunteers attended than the coordinator had expected.

The revised instructions distinguish advice from compulsory requirements. Changing a word can unintentionally change the scope of a rule. A clear correction should preserve the original factual meaning. The editor queried the figure instead of inventing a replacement. A consistent term helps readers recognise the same procedure. We should explain why a revision improves accuracy or clarity.

sourceB.title: A food cooperative corrects its report
sourceB.text:
The annual report of the Meadow food cooperative stated that deliveries had increased by a quarter. During proofreading, an employee noticed that the calculation referred to the number of delivery days, not the number of orders. The cooperative had added a Friday service, while the total number of orders had risen only slightly. The error was therefore more than an awkward choice of words: it changed the apparent scale of growth.

The editor asked the accounts team to verify both figures before making a correction. She also found a sentence saying that drivers had discussed complaints with customers after they returned. Since the pronoun could refer to either group, the report now states that drivers discussed complaints after returning to the depot. That edit clarified timing without claiming that complaints had been resolved.

The revised report includes a short correction note explaining the delivery-day measure. The chair initially worried that drawing attention to the mistake would damage confidence. Other members argued that a visible correction would be less damaging than leaving a misleading claim in circulation. They agreed to retain the original publication date and add the date of the correction, so that readers can distinguish the two versions. For future reports, each numerical claim will have a named source and a second checker. The editor emphasised that fluent prose is not a substitute for checking what a sentence actually asserts.

writing.prompt: Write an editing policy for the charity. Explain how to handle unclear references, inconsistent terminology and doubtful facts, using examples from the handbook briefing.
writing.sample:
The charity should adopt an editing process that checks meaning before polishing style. The handbook's purpose is to guide volunteers accurately, so each change must be checked against the actual procedure. Volunteers may read the handbook while preparing equipment, with little time to resolve ambiguous instructions. A correction therefore needs to be checked against the actual procedure by someone familiar with it. The editor should record any uncertainty and ask the coordinator, rather than substitute a fluent sentence with a different meaning.

Each volunteer is responsible for checking the equipment before departure. The guide explains how to collect, label and store samples. When Maya returned, she gave the keys to the coordinator. Last month the team recorded faults; this month it is testing repairs. The equipment has been checked, but the route has not been approved. Fewer volunteers attended than the coordinator had expected.

The revised instructions distinguish advice from compulsory requirements. Changing a word can unintentionally change the scope of a rule. A clear correction should preserve the original factual meaning. The editor queried the figure instead of inventing a replacement. A consistent term helps readers recognise the same procedure. We should explain why a revision improves accuracy or clarity.

The coordinator should approve any change that might alter a requirement. Keeping a record of factual queries will help future editors distinguish a verified correction from a stylistic preference.

sourceA.title: A lecture on urban shade
sourceA.text:
In a fictional public lecture, landscape researcher Elena explains why a city should not judge its tree programme by planting totals alone. A young tree offers little shade immediately, and survival depends on soil, watering and protection. Her lecture moves from the problem of summer heat to the practical choices a maintenance team must make. The briefing below preserves that sequence so that listeners can reconstruct the argument rather than merely remember isolated statistics.

For a school route, the location of shade can matter more than a distant increase in canopy cover. Elena therefore asks the audience to connect measurement with the intended benefit. Her practical conclusion is to care for existing trees while choosing new sites in relation to people's daily movements.

The speaker first establishes why planting totals can be misleading. She then turns to the conditions required for young trees to survive. The shaded playground is an illustration, not the entire argument. Although mature trees provide shade, benefits develop over many years. Maintenance should be treated as part of the investment. The proposal depends on reliable summer watering.

A survival rate tells us more than an initial planting count. The lecturer qualifies her recommendation rather than withdrawing it. In this context, shade distribution matters as much as total cover. The conclusion returns to the neighbourhoods with the least protection. My notes separate the central claim from supporting examples. A useful summary preserves the conditions attached to the recommendation.

sourceB.title: Why a wetland lecture changed direction
sourceB.text:
At a college lecture on flood management, the speaker began with a photograph of a restored wetland. Several students expected a simple argument that natural landscapes should replace engineered defences. Instead, the lecturer described the wetland as one component of a wider system. Its shallow basins could hold runoff after ordinary rainfall, but during an exceptional storm their capacity would be exceeded. Walls and drainage channels remained necessary near the hospital downstream.

The speaker then compared two possible measures of success: the amount of water stored and the number of properties protected. These measures were connected, yet neither could stand alone. A large storage volume in the wrong location might do little for the neighbourhood at greatest risk. Conversely, protecting a small number of critical buildings could be especially valuable. The lecturer used the hospital to illustrate this second point, rather than to claim that every town should prioritise the same type of building.

A student asked whether the restored habitat justified the project even without a flood benefit. The lecturer regarded that as a legitimate separate question. Bird counts could inform an ecological assessment, but they could not establish the reliability of flood protection. Her conclusion was deliberately conditional: restoration deserved consideration where its capacity, position and maintenance fitted the wider plan. She asked students to retain those conditions when summarising the talk.

writing.prompt: Write a structured summary of Elena’s lecture for a council member. Explain the problem, the proposed response, the example and the conditions for success.
writing.sample:
Elena's lecture recommends evaluating an urban tree programme through survival, location and maintenance, rather than through planting totals alone. The proposal connects the physical benefits of trees with the way people use neighbourhood space. For a school route, the location of shade can matter more than a distant increase in canopy cover. Elena therefore asks the audience to connect measurement with the intended benefit. Her practical conclusion is to care for existing trees while choosing new sites in relation to people's daily movements.

The speaker first establishes why planting totals can be misleading. She then turns to the conditions required for young trees to survive. The shaded playground is an illustration, not the entire argument. Although mature trees provide shade, benefits develop over many years. Maintenance should be treated as part of the investment. The proposal depends on reliable summer watering.

A survival rate tells us more than an initial planting count. The lecturer qualifies her recommendation rather than withdrawing it. In this context, shade distribution matters as much as total cover. The conclusion returns to the neighbourhoods with the least protection. My notes separate the central claim from supporting examples. A useful summary preserves the conditions attached to the recommendation.

The council should therefore connect funding to a maintenance plan and meaningful measures. This preserves the lecture's conditional recommendation while allowing practical action in neighbourhoods that currently have little shade.
