sourceA.title: Who should decide local learning priorities?
sourceA.text:
This original practice topic asks whether local authorities should determine all publicly funded adult-learning priorities or give residents a stronger role. It is designed for argument development, not for memorising a universal essay. A convincing answer should address the extent of agreement, explain why its reasons matter and use a plausible example without presenting invented figures as research. Related speaking practice asks learners to move from a personal experience to a broader social question.

A strong essay should explain how resident participation could improve decisions and how its limitations would be managed. The writer can then connect that balance to an explicit position. In speech, the same reasoning should develop naturally from a familiar example into a broader discussion rather than emerge as a memorised essay.

Residents should influence priorities without being expected to design every course. Local knowledge can reveal needs that a standard survey overlooks. However, vocal participants may not represent the whole community. Authorities remain responsible for access, quality and public spending. A combined approach would use consultation within transparent criteria. For example, carers may need shorter sessions at predictable times.

The example illustrates a mechanism rather than proving a national trend. I agree to a considerable extent, but not without safeguards. My experience is relevant, although it cannot represent every learner. At a broader level, the issue is whose needs become visible. I would develop fewer reasons fully rather than list many briefly. A clear position should remain consistent throughout the answer.

sourceB.title: An essay workshop on public spaces
sourceB.text:
An examination-preparation class discussed whether cities should devote more land to parks even when housing is scarce. The tutor did not ask learners to reproduce a model opinion. Instead, she asked each writer to define the decision being considered. Protecting an existing park, converting unused land and replacing occupied housing were different proposals with different consequences.

One draft claimed that parks always improved public health. The tutor suggested narrowing the claim and explaining the mechanism: accessible green space may support exercise and relaxation, but design, safety and maintenance affect whether residents use it. Another draft argued that housing should take priority because everyone needed somewhere to live. That reason was relevant, yet it did not answer whether a particular parcel of land was suitable for housing or whether the district already lacked recreation space.

The revised essays were expected to state a position and develop it through linked reasoning. Acknowledging the competing need did not require dividing the essay into two equally enthusiastic halves. Writers could favour one priority while specifying the circumstances under which the other deserved greater weight. The tutor also warned against invented statistics and memorised openings that added no meaning. In oral follow-up, learners compared a local place they knew with the wider planning problem. Effective preparation involved adapting language to the question and responding to challenge, rather than delivering the same polished answer regardless of the prompt.

writing.prompt: Some people believe local authorities should decide all priorities for publicly funded adult learning. Others think residents should have a stronger role. Discuss both views and give your own opinion. Write at least 250 words, developing reasons rather than listing slogans.
writing.sample:
Local authorities must be accountable for publicly funded adult education, but this does not mean that they should make every decision without residents. I favour a system in which public bodies set transparent standards and budgets while communities help identify needs and evaluate whether provision is useful.

The argument for central responsibility is substantial. Authorities can compare needs across neighbourhoods, maintain quality requirements and protect courses whose value is not immediately popular. If decisions were made only by whoever attended a public meeting, confident participants could secure resources while people with less time or influence remained unheard. Financial responsibility also requires someone to explain why one service has been funded instead of another.

Nevertheless, residents possess practical knowledge that a general plan may overlook. A course advertised as accessible may be impossible for carers to attend if it runs at unpredictable times. Workers may need short evening sessions rather than a full daytime programme. Consultation can expose these barriers before money is committed, provided that it reaches beyond existing students and organised groups.

A combined approach would ask residents about problems and preferences, then assess proposals against published criteria such as access, demand, cost and educational value. A small trial could test an uncertain proposal before expansion. Feedback should influence subsequent decisions, but enthusiasm should not be mistaken for proof of learning.

In conclusion, authorities should retain responsibility for fairness and public expenditure while giving residents a meaningful role. The aim is not to transfer every technical decision to a public vote, but to ensure that professional planning remains informed by the people it is intended to serve.

sourceA.title: Building a defensible language portfolio
sourceA.text:
The final original briefing concerns a fictional learner preparing an independent review. A portfolio can show completed tasks and responses to feedback, but familiar work alone does not establish how the learner handles new material. The review therefore includes unseen listening and reading, independent writing and interaction with another person. It reports strengths and limitations separately. Neither course completion nor a local transcription score is treated as an official CEFR or IELTS result.

A reviewer needs enough information to distinguish a stable ability from a successful rehearsed performance. The learner should therefore label assistance, revisions and repeated tasks honestly. The resulting profile can guide further practice even when the evidence is too limited to support a single confident level for all four skills.

My portfolio distinguishes first attempts from revised work. Familiar material can show learning without proving general transfer. I need evidence from tasks that I have not rehearsed. Listening, reading, writing and interaction should be reviewed separately. A transcript cannot establish every aspect of spoken performance. An external reviewer should know what help was permitted.

A disagreement between reviewers calls for examination of the evidence. I would treat an uneven profile as information for planning. The next plan should target recurring weaknesses rather than every possible error. A delayed task with new material helps check retention and transfer. Course completion is not an official proficiency certificate. Any score estimate should state its evidence and uncertainty.

sourceB.title: A review separates three kinds of progress
sourceB.text:
An adult-learning programme evaluated its graduates through a portfolio and unfamiliar tasks. One learner had completed every lesson and produced polished revised essays, but struggled to respond when an interviewer changed the question. Another had gaps in the completion record yet handled unfamiliar reading confidently. These cases showed why participation, supported practice and independent performance should not be collapsed into one number.

The reviewers recorded separate evidence for listening, reading, writing and spoken interaction. They noted when a task had been repeated or prepared with assistance. A strong revised essay remained useful evidence of learning and editing, but it was not labelled an unaided first attempt. Reviewers also avoided judging speaking solely from a transcript, since timing, intelligibility and interaction were not fully represented in the written words.

Where two reviewers disagreed substantially, they discussed the criteria and requested another independent sample rather than averaging away the uncertainty. Learners received a practical follow-up plan: maintain strengths, practise identified weak areas and repeat selected tasks later using new material. No conversion from course points to a guaranteed examination band was offered. The programme could describe progress toward its internal objectives, while an external examination remained a separate assessment. Its final report was more informative because it acknowledged uneven profiles and missing evidence, rather than forcing every learner into a confident single-level declaration.

sourceA.title: 教学案例：a neighbourhood water laboratory
sourceA.text:
At a neighbourhood water laboratory, participants considered whether to describe its new filter as effective under the conditions tested. The background was specific: twelve household samples became clearer after filtration, although the trial did not measure dissolved contaminants or long term maintenance. However, clear water was being mistaken for safe water in the public demonstration. The proposed response was to publish the measured outcomes beside the unmeasured risks and remove the unqualified word safe.

The public demonstration creates a particular responsibility. Spectators can see a change in appearance immediately, whereas the untested chemical properties remain invisible. The institution should not rely on a small disclaimer to undo a striking visual suggestion of safety. I would place the measured outcome beside the demonstration itself and explain which tests were not conducted. The laboratory could then decide whether additional testing is feasible. If it is not, the narrower claim can still be useful. People may value a filter that removes visible particles, provided they do not confuse that benefit with protection from every contaminant. Responsible communication makes the boundary part of the main message rather than an inconvenient technical footnote. A plausible account is not necessarily the most probable one. The filter reduced visible particles without establishing that the water was safe. We should qualify the claim before it acquires a life of its own. The result holds under the conditions specified in the report. Absence of detected harm does not amount to evidence of harmlessness. Her wording conveys confidence without implying that the question is settled. The observation substantiates a narrower claim than the advertisement makes.

sourceB.title: 独立测验：a community seed library
sourceB.text:
This independent fictional case introduces a different setting. Its purpose is to test transfer, so the conclusion must be recovered from the new details rather than carried over from an earlier example. The participants have a practical decision to make, and an attractive first impression is not enough.

At a community seed library, the discussion concerned whether to label a tomato variety resilient rather than drought proof. There was a reason the idea initially appeared attractive: plants survived two unusually dry weeks in sheltered gardens, but almost every gardener watered them during the hottest afternoons. That account nevertheless contained an important reservation: survival under assisted conditions did not establish independence from irrigation. The suggested response was to retain the survival record while explicitly naming the assistance and the narrow observation period.

The label matters because a gardener buying seed may treat a description as advice about future care. A plant that survives with afternoon watering has demonstrated something useful, but not the ability to thrive without that support. Removing all mention of resilience would throw away the observation; retaining an absolute promise would turn assistance into an invisible condition. The library can give gardeners a more informative record by naming the weather, the shelter and the watering. That record would also make later comparisons possible. A subsequent trial in an exposed bed might produce a different result without showing that the first gardeners had lied. Different conditions would simply answer a different question.

The conclusion remains specific to the conditions described. Another interpretation should account for the same details, identify any additional assumptions, and explain what evidence would change the judgement.

writing.prompt: Write an advisory commentary about the teaching case, using Source A only. Evaluate the initial proposal, explain the most important qualification, recommend a proportionate response, and identify what could change your judgement. Do not copy the model. Use an appropriate register for the people responsible at a neighbourhood water laboratory.
writing.sample:
The immediate objective should be to publish the measured outcomes beside the unmeasured risks and remove the unqualified word safe. At a neighbourhood water laboratory, the initial suggestion was to describe its new filter as effective under the conditions tested. The relevant background is that twelve household samples became clearer after filtration, although the trial did not measure dissolved contaminants or long term maintenance. Nevertheless, clear water was being mistaken for safe water in the public demonstration. A defensible response must preserve the distinction this creates rather than resolve the difficulty by ignoring part of the account.

The public demonstration creates a particular responsibility. Spectators can see a change in appearance immediately, whereas the untested chemical properties remain invisible. The institution should not rely on a small disclaimer to undo a striking visual suggestion of safety. I would place the measured outcome beside the demonstration itself and explain which tests were not conducted. The laboratory could then decide whether additional testing is feasible. If it is not, the narrower claim can still be useful. People may value a filter that removes visible particles, provided they do not confuse that benefit with protection from every contaminant. Responsible communication makes the boundary part of the main message rather than an inconvenient technical footnote.

I would record the recommendation together with its conditions and the information that could make it necessary to reconsider. The strongest objection should be answered in its actual form, not replaced by a more convenient one. If later evidence changes the position, the revision should be explained openly. The point is to make a proportionate decision that remains accountable to the details, rather than adopt a more impressive conclusion whose certainty the case cannot support.

speaking.sample: I would separate the original idea from the qualification that changes its meaning. The proposal was to describe its new filter as effective under the conditions tested. The relevant detail is that twelve household samples became clearer after filtration, although the trial did not measure dissolved contaminants or long term maintenance. For that reason, I would publish the measured outcomes beside the unmeasured risks and remove the unqualified word safe. This does not dismiss every contribution; it makes the decision more precise. If challenged, I would distinguish the stated details from my interpretation. I would also explain what information could change my mind, rather than defend the same conclusion regardless of the evidence.

assessmentListening.text: I want to explain a decision we reached during a neighbourhood insulation trial. It would be easy to report only the most memorable phrase and miss why the group changed its approach. The relevant background was that six households reported warmer bedrooms. However, the trial recorded perceptions but did not log room temperatures. We therefore needed to describe the improvement as reported rather than measured. That distinction mattered more than making the final summary sound confident. After discussing the alternatives, the group decided to install temperature loggers before the next winter comparison. The decision was not a claim that the initial observation had no value. It was a way to preserve what remained useful without carrying forward an implication the available detail could not justify. If someone later summarises our discussion, I would want both the reason for the concern and the agreed action to remain visible. Otherwise, a listener might reasonably understand a much stronger conclusion than we intended.

sourceA.title: 教学案例：a volunteer theatre committee
sourceA.text:
At a volunteer theatre committee, participants considered whether to use a plain summary beside an informal rehearsal discussion. The background was specific: a director said the opening scene was on thin ice, then asked for another rehearsal rather than cancelling the performance. However, two new volunteers understood the warning as an immediate withdrawal of permission. The proposed response was to explain that the metaphor signals vulnerability and invite the director to state the practical consequence.

A rehearsal room benefits from informal language: it allows people to express doubt without turning every comment into an official notice. The solution is therefore not to ban metaphors. It is to clarify the action whenever a phrase could reasonably be mistaken for a decision. The director might say that the scene needs more work and name the next rehearsal. Volunteers would then know both the concern and what they should do about it. This preserves the collaborative tone while preventing a figurative warning from becoming an accidental cancellation. The committee should also make formal changes through a separate, recognisable channel so that participants do not have to infer administrative consequences from colourful conversation. The opening scene is on thin ice, so another rehearsal would help. I took the warning figuratively rather than as a literal instruction. Before we pull the plug, let us establish what can still be repaired. She was testing the waters rather than committing the committee to a decision. The joke fell flat because its cultural reference was unfamiliar. An idiom can soften criticism while making its practical meaning less explicit. When you say the scene is shaky, which change are you requesting?

sourceB.title: 独立测验：a bicycle repair cooperative
sourceB.text:
The next original fictional account presents a decision that looks straightforward until the relevant qualification is considered. There is no hidden correct opinion about the institution. The reading task is to establish what the account supports, what it leaves open, and what the proposed response actually changes.

At a bicycle repair cooperative, the discussion concerned whether to clarify an idiomatic budget warning before approving new equipment. There was a reason the idea initially appeared attractive: the treasurer said the group was robbing Peter to pay Paul when it delayed rent to replace worn tools. That account nevertheless contained an important reservation: one member interpreted the remark as an accusation of theft rather than criticism of cash flow. The suggested response was to separate the figurative criticism from the accounting decision and record the actual transfers.

The accounting issue survives even when the metaphor is removed. Money needed for one obligation has been diverted to another, leaving a gap that will eventually require an answer. Yet a financial gap is not the same as an allegation that an individual has stolen funds. The members need to know the amount, the repayment date and the consequence of delaying rent. Discussing the implied offence instead would divert attention from that practical problem. A written record should therefore use the actual transactions rather than the colourful phrase. Members may still disagree about whether the purchase was justified, but they would at least be disagreeing about the same decision.

The conclusion remains specific to the conditions described. Another interpretation should account for the same details, identify any additional assumptions, and explain what evidence would change the judgement.

sourceA.title: 教学案例：a university archive
sourceA.text:
At a university archive, participants considered whether to rewrite a request for missing catalogue records. The background was specific: the first message to an external donor read send the list today, whereas the revised message explained the deadline and asked whether delivery was feasible. However, a highly deferential rewrite could obscure the fact that the exhibition depended on those records. The proposed response was to state the consequence plainly while leaving the donor room to propose a workable time.

The archive depends on cooperation from somebody it cannot simply instruct as though they were a subordinate. Explaining the exhibition deadline gives the donor a reason to help and a basis for proposing an alternative. Yet politeness should not disguise the fact that missing records may affect the display. A useful message would identify the essential records, state the latest workable time and ask what can realistically be supplied. It might also offer a partial delivery if that would keep the exhibition moving. This approach treats courtesy as a means of making cooperation possible, rather than as an accumulation of apologies that leaves the recipient unsure what is actually being requested. Would it be feasible to send the records before Thursday afternoon? We need the list today, but please tell us if that deadline is impractical. The request sounds courteous without concealing its urgency. Familiarity permits brevity, but it does not excuse avoidable ambiguity. I would make the consequence explicit rather than bury it in apologies. The donor may welcome a clear explanation more than elaborate deference. Please let us know what timescale you could realistically accommodate.

sourceB.title: 独立测验：an apartment residents association
sourceB.text:
A separate fictional case offers another opportunity to distinguish an observation from its interpretation. The people involved share enough common ground to continue working, but their initial description risks implying more than they have established. The difference becomes visible when the suggested action is compared with the available detail.

At an apartment residents association, the discussion concerned whether to adapt a reminder about shared storage to its audience. There was a reason the idea initially appeared attractive: a familiar neighbour welcomed a brief informal note, while a newly arrived tenant needed the rule and the reason spelled out. That account nevertheless contained an important reservation: using identical friendly jokes with both readers assumed a relationship that did not yet exist. The suggested response was to keep the rule consistent but adjust the greeting, explanation and degree of familiarity.

Equal treatment does not require identical sentences. The established neighbour already knows where the storage room is and why access matters; the newcomer may know neither. A joke can create warmth when a relationship supports it, but can suggest exclusion when it presumes knowledge the reader lacks. Conversely, an unnecessarily legalistic notice might make a minor reminder sound like a threat. The association should preserve the same requirement while changing the amount of context and the interpersonal framing. The test is whether each reader can understand the obligation and respond without having to guess what kind of relationship the writer assumes. That purpose is more useful than a universal preference for either formality or friendliness.

The conclusion remains specific to the conditions described. Another interpretation should account for the same details, identify any additional assumptions, and explain what evidence would change the judgement.

writing.sample:

At a university archive, the initial suggestion was to rewrite a request for missing catalogue records. The relevant background is that the first message to an external donor read send the list today, whereas the revised message explained the deadline and asked whether delivery was feasible. A defensible response must preserve the distinction this creates rather than resolve the difficulty by ignoring part of the account.

The archive depends on cooperation from somebody it cannot simply instruct as though they were a subordinate. It might also offer a partial delivery if that would keep the exhibition moving. This approach treats courtesy as a means of making cooperation possible, rather than as an accumulation of apologies that leaves the recipient unsure what is actually being requested.

I would record the recommendation together with its conditions and the information that could make it necessary to reconsider. The strongest objection should be answered in its actual form, not replaced by a more convenient one. If later evidence changes the position, the revision should be explained openly. The point is to make a proportionate decision that remains accountable to the details, rather than adopt a more impressive conclusion whose certainty the case cannot support.

sourceA.title: 教学案例：a public transport forum
sourceA.text:
At a public transport forum, participants considered whether to argue for late buses without dismissing other passengers. The background was specific: a speaker began it is the last connection that matters most to shift workers, then acknowledged that earlier services also needed repair. However, the emphasis could be heard as claiming that daytime journeys had no social value. The proposed response was to define the priority as a marginal funding decision rather than a ranking of passengers worth.

The forum is deciding how to allocate an additional service, not determining whose life matters most. That distinction should shape the argument. The speaker can show why the final connection has an unusually large effect on shift workers without implying that daytime passengers have trivial needs. An explicit comparison of the consequences would make the emphasis defensible. It would also allow opponents to challenge the cost or the predicted benefit rather than respond to a moral accusation nobody needs to make. The revised speech should retain its focus, because removing every emphatic construction would obscure the urgency. It should instead connect that focus to a limited decision and acknowledge the unmet needs outside it. It is the final connection that shift workers cannot afford to miss. That priority does not imply that earlier journeys are unimportant. Not once during the trial did the revised timetable require another vehicle. Compelling though the example is, it cannot settle the entire funding question. What matters here is the effect of the next small allocation. The emphasis is justified only if the qualification remains visible. Far from dismissing daytime users, the proposal addresses an additional gap.

sourceB.title: 独立测验：a small museum board
sourceB.text:
In this newly invented case, readers should attend to the relationship between a stated aim and the evidence used to defend it. The account does not invite a judgement about personalities. Instead, it supplies a limited situation in which a careful summary can preserve something that a confident headline loses.

At a small museum board, the discussion concerned whether to defend a quiet visiting hour while recognising staffing limits. There was a reason the idea initially appeared attractive: a curator said not once had the trial required additional security, but the attendance log covered only three sessions. That account nevertheless contained an important reservation: a striking negative construction made a small observation sound like a universal guarantee. The suggested response was to preserve the useful observation and restrict the conclusion to the short trial.

The curator can reasonably use the trial to answer a claim that extra security was needed on every occasion. It cannot answer every possible staffing question across a full year. Attendance, exhibitions and visitor needs may change. The board should therefore ask whether the proposed expansion resembles the circumstances already observed. If it does, the small trial is relevant; if not, more checking is necessary. The impressive rhythm of the negative construction should not obscure that comparison. Nor should caution become a reason to pretend that the three sessions tell the board nothing. A limited observation can justify a limited next step, provided the next step includes a way to notice when its assumptions fail.

The conclusion remains specific to the conditions described. Another interpretation should account for the same details, identify any additional assumptions, and explain what evidence would change the judgement.

writing.prompt: Write an advisory commentary about the teaching case, using Source A only. Evaluate the initial proposal, explain the most important qualification, recommend a proportionate response, and identify what could change your judgement. Do not copy the model. Use an appropriate register for the people responsible at a public transport forum.
writing.sample:
The immediate objective should be to define the priority as a marginal funding decision rather than a ranking of passengers worth. At a public transport forum, the initial suggestion was to argue for late buses without dismissing other passengers. The relevant background is that a speaker began it is the last connection that matters most to shift workers, then acknowledged that earlier services also needed repair. Nevertheless, the emphasis could be heard as claiming that daytime journeys had no social value. A defensible response must preserve the distinction this creates rather than resolve the difficulty by ignoring part of the account.

The forum is deciding how to allocate an additional service, not determining whose life matters most. That distinction should shape the argument. The speaker can show why the final connection has an unusually large effect on shift workers without implying that daytime passengers have trivial needs. An explicit comparison of the consequences would make the emphasis defensible. It would also allow opponents to challenge the cost or the predicted benefit rather than respond to a moral accusation nobody needs to make. The revised speech should retain its focus, because removing every emphatic construction would obscure the urgency. It should instead connect that focus to a limited decision and acknowledge the unmet needs outside it.

I would record the recommendation together with its conditions and the information that could make it necessary to reconsider. The strongest objection should be answered in its actual form, not replaced by a more convenient one. If later evidence changes the position, the revision should be explained openly. The point is to make a proportionate decision that remains accountable to the details, rather than adopt a more impressive conclusion whose certainty the case cannot support.

The relevant detail is that a speaker began it is the last connection that matters most to shift workers, then acknowledged that earlier services also needed repair. However, the emphasis could be heard as claiming that daytime journeys had no social value. For that reason, I would define the priority as a marginal funding decision rather than a ranking of passengers worth. This does not dismiss every contribution; it makes the decision more precise. If challenged, I would distinguish the stated details from my interpretation. I would also explain what information could change my mind, rather than defend the same conclusion regardless of the evidence.

assessmentListening.text: I want to explain a decision we reached during a discussion about a village footbridge. It would be easy to report only the most memorable phrase and miss why the group changed its approach. The relevant background was that the chair stressed that it was the handrail that required immediate repair. However, the deck had also been inspected but was not judged urgently unsafe. We therefore needed to distinguish immediate priority from a claim that other work was unnecessary. That distinction mattered more than making the final summary sound confident. After discussing the alternatives, the group decided to repair the handrail first and schedule routine deck maintenance. The decision was not a claim that the initial observation had no value. It was a way to preserve what remained useful without carrying forward an implication the available detail could not justify. If someone later summarises our discussion, I would want both the reason for the concern and the agreed action to remain visible. Otherwise, a listener might reasonably understand a much stronger conclusion than we intended.
assessmentListening.delivery: Original fictional script. TTS or printed text does not substitute for independent assessment with unfamiliar human speech.

sourceA.title: 教学案例：a local food festival planning meeting
sourceA.text:
At a local food festival planning meeting, participants considered whether to choose between one large kitchen and several small stalls. The background was specific: Mira preferred a central kitchen for hygiene checks, Arun defended stalls for shorter queues, and Jo asked whether either option fitted the available electrical supply. However, rapid agreement about the event date was being treated as agreement about the kitchen design. The proposed response was to record each proposal separately and leave the power question open until an electrician checked the site.

The organiser needs a record of the changing discussion, not a transcript that merely captures every word. A useful summary would list the central kitchen, the separate stalls and the electrical constraint as distinct items. It would show which questions have been answered and which remain open. The group should not interpret momentum as consensus: people may agree that the event should happen while disagreeing about how it can operate safely. A brief confirmation round would cost little compared with redesigning the site later. It would also give quieter participants a clear chance to correct the summary. After the electrical check, the discussion can return to hygiene and queues with a more reliable account of what is feasible. Mira supported the kitchen plan, whereas Arun was still discussing queues. Was that agreement about the date or about the proposed layout? Jo has raised a condition that neither proposal yet satisfies. Let me separate the decisions we have made from those still outstanding. I lost the referent of that last yes during the overlap. We appear to agree on timing, but not necessarily on facilities.

sourceB.title: 独立测验：a community orchestra rehearsal committee
sourceB.text:
This independent fictional case introduces a different setting. Its purpose is to test transfer, so the conclusion must be recovered from the new details rather than carried over from an earlier example. The participants have a practical decision to make, and an attractive first impression is not enough.

At a community orchestra rehearsal committee, the discussion concerned whether to settle how to share a restricted practice hall. There was a reason the idea initially appeared attractive: the conductor wanted full ensemble sessions, the percussion leader requested sectional work, and the librarian suggested alternating weeks. That account nevertheless contained an important reservation: a brief yes followed a question about keys, but a later summary attributed it to the whole timetable. The suggested response was to ask each speaker to confirm the proposal they supported rather than counting isolated agreement words.

Conversation does not arrive as a sequence of neatly labelled votes. Speakers answer the most recent question they heard, return to an earlier objection, or acknowledge a detail without accepting the proposal around it. The librarian therefore needs a summary that identifies both the plan and the person endorsing it. A head count of affirmative words would be unreliable even if every word were transcribed perfectly. The group can resolve the ambiguity by reading back the proposed timetable and inviting corrections. Silence should not automatically be counted as agreement, especially after a rapid exchange in which some members have not had a clear opportunity to speak. The final record should preserve any remaining objection.

The conclusion remains specific to the conditions described. Another interpretation should account for the same details, identify any additional assumptions, and explain what evidence would change the judgement.

sourceA.title: 教学案例：a regional oral history project
sourceA.text:
At a regional oral history project, participants considered whether to train interviewers to request clarification respectfully. The background was specific: an interviewer recognised every written word in a transcript but repeatedly missed the speakers place names when hearing them without context. However, familiar vocabulary on a page concealed a genuine difficulty with connected speech and regional vowel patterns. The proposed response was to practise with consented recordings from several speakers and check place names rather than guessing them.

The project should treat comprehension as an outcome to be checked, not a quality attributed to a listener on the basis of confidence. Interviewers can prepare local place names, but preparation should not be confused with performance on an unfamiliar recording. Training should include several consenting speakers and opportunities to compare an unaided first hearing with a checked transcript afterwards. Clarification requests belong in the training as well. They allow the interviewer to protect the historical record without pretending to understand a name. A printed script may help vocabulary learning, yet cannot reproduce reduced syllables, timing or regional pronunciation. Progress should consequently be documented through new audio tasks as well as written exercises. I recognised the place name on paper but missed it in connected speech. Could you repeat the street name and then spell the final word? An unfamiliar vowel pattern does not imply unfamiliar vocabulary. I should verify the name instead of selecting the nearest familiar one. The written transcript cannot establish how much I understood unaided. Please correct me if I have joined two separate names together. The difficulty emerged when the speaker reduced several unstressed syllables.

sourceB.title: 独立测验：a telephone repair booking service
sourceB.text:
The next original fictional account presents a decision that looks straightforward until the relevant qualification is considered. There is no hidden correct opinion about the institution. The reading task is to establish what the account supports, what it leaves open, and what the proposed response actually changes.

At a telephone repair booking service, the discussion concerned whether to improve confirmation of addresses across diverse accents. There was a reason the idea initially appeared attractive: staff correctly repeated most street names after a second hearing, yet house numbers were sometimes lost when callers corrected themselves mid sentence. That account nevertheless contained an important reservation: the errors reflected correction structure as well as pronunciation, so an accent label alone explained little. The suggested response was to repeat the final address in full and invite correction before closing the booking.

The service cannot infer comprehension merely because an operator sounds confident. The crucial outcome is whether the delivery reaches the intended address. Corrections are especially demanding because a speaker may repeat one part, replace another and leave the rest understood. Staff need to reconstruct the final version, not combine every number they heard into a plausible sequence. Repeating that final version gives the caller a chance to reject it. Written confirmation may provide additional protection where available, but should not be presented as proof that the earlier call was fully understood. Nor should training imply that one accent is inherently defective. The practical aim is shared understanding across variation and noise.

The conclusion remains specific to the conditions described. Another interpretation should account for the same details, identify any additional assumptions, and explain what evidence would change the judgement.

writing.prompt: Write an advisory commentary about the teaching case, using Source A only. Evaluate the initial proposal, explain the most important qualification, recommend a proportionate response, and identify what could change your judgement. Do not copy the model. writing.sample:
The immediate objective should be to practise with consented recordings from several speakers and check place names rather than guessing them. At a regional oral history project, the initial suggestion was to train interviewers to request clarification respectfully. The relevant background is that an interviewer recognised every written word in a transcript but repeatedly missed the speakers place names when hearing them without context. Nevertheless, familiar vocabulary on a page concealed a genuine difficulty with connected speech and regional vowel patterns. A defensible response must preserve the distinction this creates rather than resolve the difficulty by ignoring part of the account.

The project should treat comprehension as an outcome to be checked, not a quality attributed to a listener on the basis of confidence. Interviewers can prepare local place names, but preparation should not be confused with performance on an unfamiliar recording. Training should include several consenting speakers and opportunities to compare an unaided first hearing with a checked transcript afterwards. Clarification requests belong in the training as well. They allow the interviewer to protect the historical record without pretending to understand a name. A printed script may help vocabulary learning, yet cannot reproduce reduced syllables, timing or regional pronunciation. Progress should consequently be documented through new audio tasks as well as written exercises.

I would record the recommendation together with its conditions and the information that could make it necessary to reconsider. The strongest objection should be answered in its actual form, not replaced by a more convenient one. If later evidence changes the position, the revision should be explained openly. The point is to make a proportionate decision that remains accountable to the details, rather than adopt a more impressive conclusion whose certainty the case cannot support.

For that reason, I would practise with consented recordings from several speakers and check place names rather than guessing them. This does not dismiss every contribution; it makes the decision more precise. If challenged, I would distinguish the stated details from my interpretation. assessmentListening.text: I want to explain a decision we reached during a call arranging a furniture delivery. It would be easy to report only the most memorable phrase and miss why the group changed its approach. The relevant background was that the customer corrected the building name twice during a noisy connection. However, the operator recognised the written name later but had guessed during the call. We therefore needed to separate guessing from successful unaided comprehension. That distinction mattered more than making the final summary sound confident. After discussing the alternatives, the group decided to repeat the entire address and ask the customer to confirm it. The decision was not a claim that the initial observation had no value. It was a way to preserve what remained useful without carrying forward an implication the available detail could not justify. If someone later summarises our discussion, I would want both the reason for the concern and the agreed action to remain visible. Otherwise, a listener might reasonably understand a much stronger conclusion than we intended.

sourceA.title: 教学案例：a rain soaked outdoor concert
sourceA.text:
At a rain soaked outdoor concert, participants considered whether to interpret a stage managers remark about perfect weather. The background was specific: she called the downpour ideal for our paper programmes, immediately moved the programmes under cover, and thanked the audience for waiting. However, the literal praise conflicted with both the practical action and the damaged materials. The proposed response was to read the remark as rueful humour while avoiding assumptions about how every audience member received it.

The immediate practical context supports a humorous reading: rain is damaging precisely the material praised as suited to the weather. The stage manager also acts to protect it, so the literal statement is not a reliable account of her judgement. Nevertheless, a reader should avoid claiming to know how every audience member felt. Some may recognise the joke, others may miss it, and others may understand it without enjoying it. In a live discussion, tone and shared expectations would add evidence. Since the case provides text, the commentary should explain the contradiction and leave those additional features unresolved. That is a stronger interpretation than confidently attaching a single emotional label to the speaker. Perfect weather for paper programmes, she said, as the rain intensified. The action following the remark makes a literal reading implausible. The humour appears directed at the situation rather than at the audience. I hear possible irony, but I would need the recording to judge delivery. Her deadpan expression may leave an unfamiliar listener uncertain. We should distinguish a supported interpretation from a claim about intention. The contrast between the words and the soaked programmes carries the joke.

sourceB.title: 独立测验：a crowded office equipment room
sourceB.text:
A separate fictional case offers another opportunity to distinguish an observation from its interpretation. The people involved share enough common ground to continue working, but their initial description risks implying more than they have established. The difference becomes visible when the suggested action is compared with the available detail.

At a crowded office equipment room, the discussion concerned whether to interpret a colleague praising an unreliable printer. There was a reason the idea initially appeared attractive: after the fourth paper jam he announced that the machine clearly enjoyed a challenge, then quietly fetched the maintenance form. That account nevertheless contained an important reservation: the playful personification could signal frustration without directing hostility at the colleague who had loaded the paper. The suggested response was to distinguish the target of the joke from the person present and ask about the fault if the relationship is uncertain.

The remark attributes enjoyment to a machine that cannot experience it. That mismatch helps explain the humour, but the preceding breakdowns supply its emotional context. The speaker may be frustrated and still be making a friendly joke. Nothing in the account establishes that the person loading the paper is being blamed. A colleague uncertain about the relationship could respond to the repair problem rather than repeat the joke at someone elses expense. Hearing the original delivery might strengthen or weaken a judgement about tone; the printed account cannot reproduce it. The defensible conclusion concerns the contrast and the immediate situation, not a complete diagnosis of the speakers attitude towards every person in the room.

The conclusion remains specific to the conditions described. Another interpretation should account for the same details, identify any additional assumptions, and explain what evidence would change the judgement.

writing.prompt: Write an advisory commentary about the teaching case, using Source A only. Evaluate the initial proposal, explain the most important qualification, recommend a proportionate response, and identify what could change your judgement. Do not copy the model. Use an appropriate register for the people responsible at a rain soaked outdoor concert.
writing.sample:
The immediate objective should be to read the remark as rueful humour while avoiding assumptions about how every audience member received it. At a rain soaked outdoor concert, the initial suggestion was to interpret a stage managers remark about perfect weather. The relevant background is that she called the downpour ideal for our paper programmes, immediately moved the programmes under cover, and thanked the audience for waiting. Nevertheless, the literal praise conflicted with both the practical action and the damaged materials. A defensible response must preserve the distinction this creates rather than resolve the difficulty by ignoring part of the account.

The immediate practical context supports a humorous reading: rain is damaging precisely the material praised as suited to the weather. The stage manager also acts to protect it, so the literal statement is not a reliable account of her judgement. Nevertheless, a reader should avoid claiming to know how every audience member felt. Some may recognise the joke, others may miss it, and others may understand it without enjoying it. In a live discussion, tone and shared expectations would add evidence. Since the case provides text, the commentary should explain the contradiction and leave those additional features unresolved. That is a stronger interpretation than confidently attaching a single emotional label to the speaker.

I would record the recommendation together with its conditions and the information that could make it necessary to reconsider. The strongest objection should be answered in its actual form, not replaced by a more convenient one. If later evidence changes the position, the revision should be explained openly. The point is to make a proportionate decision that remains accountable to the details, rather than adopt a more impressive conclusion whose certainty the case cannot support.

speaking.prompt: Without reading a script, explain your response to the teaching case at a rain soaked outdoor concert. Speak for two to three minutes, distinguish evidence from inference, and respond to a partner who disagrees.
followups: Which detail would most strongly justify changing your recommendation to read the remark as rueful humour while avoiding assumptions about how every audience member received it?
Restate the opposing view in its strongest reasonable form, then explain the remaining disagreement.
speaking.sample: I would separate the original idea from the qualification that changes its meaning. The proposal was to interpret a stage managers remark about perfect weather. The relevant detail is that she called the downpour ideal for our paper programmes, immediately moved the programmes under cover, and thanked the audience for waiting. However, the literal praise conflicted with both the practical action and the damaged materials. For that reason, I would read the remark as rueful humour while avoiding assumptions about how every audience member received it. This does not dismiss every contribution; it makes the decision more precise. If challenged, I would distinguish the stated details from my interpretation. I would also explain what information could change my mind, rather than defend the same conclusion regardless of the evidence.

assessmentListening.text: I want to explain a decision we reached during a rehearsal interrupted by a leaking roof. It would be easy to report only the most memorable phrase and miss why the group changed its approach. The relevant background was that a musician called the bucket solo the highlight of the afternoon. However, the remark followed several drops landing in an empty metal container. We therefore needed to interpret the praise as humour about an unwelcome interruption. That distinction mattered more than making the final summary sound confident. After discussing the alternatives, the group decided to move the instruments before continuing the rehearsal. The decision was not a claim that the initial observation had no value. It was a way to preserve what remained useful without carrying forward an implication the available detail could not justify. If someone later summarises our discussion, I would want both the reason for the concern and the agreed action to remain visible. Otherwise, a listener might reasonably understand a much stronger conclusion than we intended.
assessmentListening.delivery: Original fictional script. TTS or printed text does not substitute for independent assessment with unfamiliar human speech.

sourceA.title: 教学案例：a design grant selection panel
sourceA.text:
At a design grant selection panel, participants considered whether to interpret a cautious endorsement of an ambitious proposal. The background was specific: a reviewer praised the teams imagination and added that the timetable would certainly keep everyone occupied, while asking for a contingency plan. However, the sentence did not explicitly call the schedule unrealistic, but its placement after repeated deadline questions mattered. The proposed response was to report the reservation as an inference supported by context rather than as a direct quotation of rejection.

The panel can preserve a constructive relationship without treating praise as approval. Asking for a contingency plan gives the applicants something concrete to address, whereas debating whether the reviewer secretly disliked the team would achieve little. I would record the strength identified, the timetable concern inferred from the surrounding questions, and the revision needed before a decision. If the reviewer later clarified that no reservation was intended, the summary should change accordingly. That possibility does not make every inference equally speculative. Placement and practical consequence provide evidence, but they support a limited conclusion about the proposal rather than an account of the reviewers personality. The response should be equally specific. The compliment is followed by a reservation that changes its practical force. She did not reject the idea outright, but she withheld immediate approval. The timetable would keep everyone occupied may imply concern about feasibility. That interpretation is supported by the repeated requests for contingency plans. I would not attribute personal hostility on the basis of that sentence. Quoting the praise alone would misrepresent the reviewers overall stance. The hedge softens the judgement without necessarily weakening the reservation.

sourceB.title: 独立测验：a local newspaper editorial meeting
sourceB.text:
In this newly invented case, readers should attend to the relationship between a stated aim and the evidence used to defend it. The account does not invite a judgement about personalities. Instead, it supplies a limited situation in which a careful summary can preserve something that a confident headline loses.

At a local newspaper editorial meeting, the discussion concerned whether to decide whether a feature was ready for publication. There was a reason the idea initially appeared attractive: the editor described the interviews as lively and said the fact checking would make an excellent project for another week. That account nevertheless contained an important reservation: the compliment accompanied a postponement, so quoting only the positive adjective reversed the practical message. The suggested response was to state both the praise and the implied need for further verification while leaving personal motives unknown.

A summary that reports only lively interviews would leave readers expecting publication. A summary that says the editor hated the feature would invent a judgement absent from the exchange. The postponement and the reference to fact checking are more informative about readiness than either extreme. They show that further work is expected, even though the editor has chosen a courteous formulation. The writer can act on that information by asking which facts need checking and when the work can be reviewed. Asking whether the editor really meant the compliment would not settle those practical questions. A careful interpretation therefore preserves both a positive judgement about one quality and a reservation about another.

The conclusion remains specific to the conditions described. Another interpretation should account for the same details, identify any additional assumptions, and explain what evidence would change the judgement.

sourceA.title: 教学案例：a review of an exhibition about household objects
sourceA.text:
At a review of an exhibition about household objects, participants considered whether to evaluate whether limited scale necessarily meant limited insight. The background was specific: the reviewer complained that no national production figures appeared, although the exhibition explicitly explored how three families repaired inherited objects. However, a fair demand for context could become an unfair demand that a small exhibition turn into a different kind of project. The proposed response was to judge the stated purpose first and then explain what broader context would add.

A small exhibition can illuminate repair as a family practice precisely because it does not attempt to describe an entire national economy. That choice does not exempt it from criticism. The reviewer could ask whether the three families are introduced clearly, whether repaired objects support the claims made about them, or whether a little wider context would prevent misleading impressions. Those questions engage with the actual exhibition. Demanding a complete statistical account may instead replace its purpose. I would recommend a short contextual panel if it helped visitors locate the stories, while preserving the close attention that makes the project distinctive. Evaluation becomes more persuasive when it explains the relationship between an omission and a real limitation for the intended audience. The exhibition should first be judged against its stated purpose. Missing national statistics limit context without necessarily defeating the project. The reviewer appears to demand a different exhibition rather than a better version. That criticism identifies an omission but does not explain its significance. The domestic scale enables detail that a national survey might lose. I would distinguish restricted scope from inadequate execution.

sourceB.title: 独立测验：a review of a documentary about a village ferry
sourceB.text:
This independent fictional case introduces a different setting. Its purpose is to test transfer, so the conclusion must be recovered from the new details rather than carried over from an earlier example. The participants have a practical decision to make, and an attractive first impression is not enough.

At a review of a documentary about a village ferry, the discussion concerned whether to assess the relation between close observation and public relevance. There was a reason the idea initially appeared attractive: the film followed one operator through winter and included no interviews with transport ministers, which one critic treated as evidence of political innocence. That account nevertheless contained an important reservation: a missing interview could limit policy explanation without erasing the films attention to work and dependence. The suggested response was to identify the specific unanswered policy question instead of substituting a general label for analysis.

The absence of ministers may matter to a viewer seeking a national policy explanation. It does not prevent the film from showing how one operators labour connects a village to essential services. The reviewer needs to specify which claim the documentary makes and whether its evidence is adequate for that claim. If the film offers a comprehensive explanation of transport policy, the omission becomes more serious. If it offers close observation of a working life, another standard is appropriate. Calling it innocent bypasses this distinction. The criticism would gain force by identifying a moment where the narrative itself requires a policy explanation that the film fails to provide, rather than demanding a different film altogether.

The conclusion remains specific to the conditions described. Another interpretation should account for the same details, identify any additional assumptions, and explain what evidence would change the judgement.

writing.prompt: Write an advisory commentary about the teaching case, using Source A only. writing.sample:
The immediate objective should be to judge the stated purpose first and then explain what broader context would add. At a review of an exhibition about household objects, the initial suggestion was to evaluate whether limited scale necessarily meant limited insight. The relevant background is that the reviewer complained that no national production figures appeared, although the exhibition explicitly explored how three families repaired inherited objects. Nevertheless, a fair demand for context could become an unfair demand that a small exhibition turn into a different kind of project. A defensible response must preserve the distinction this creates rather than resolve the difficulty by ignoring part of the account.

A small exhibition can illuminate repair as a family practice precisely because it does not attempt to describe an entire national economy. That choice does not exempt it from criticism. The reviewer could ask whether the three families are introduced clearly, whether repaired objects support the claims made about them, or whether a little wider context would prevent misleading impressions. Those questions engage with the actual exhibition. Demanding a complete statistical account may instead replace its purpose. I would recommend a short contextual panel if it helped visitors locate the stories, while preserving the close attention that makes the project distinctive. Evaluation becomes more persuasive when it explains the relationship between an omission and a real limitation for the intended audience.

I would record the recommendation together with its conditions and the information that could make it necessary to reconsider. The strongest objection should be answered in its actual form, not replaced by a more convenient one. If later evidence changes the position, the revision should be explained openly. The point is to make a proportionate decision that remains accountable to the details, rather than adopt a more impressive conclusion whose certainty the case cannot support.

assessmentListening.text: I want to explain a decision we reached during a review of a small portrait exhibition. It would be easy to report only the most memorable phrase and miss why the group changed its approach. The relevant background was that the critic demanded a complete history of national painting. However, the exhibition had promised a close study of one artists family portraits. We therefore needed to judge the criticism against the stated scope. That distinction mattered more than making the final summary sound confident. After discussing the alternatives, the group decided to explain which limited historical context would improve the existing exhibition. The decision was not a claim that the initial observation had no value. It was a way to preserve what remained useful without carrying forward an implication the available detail could not justify. If someone later summarises our discussion, I would want both the reason for the concern and the agreed action to remain visible. Otherwise, a listener might reasonably understand a much stronger conclusion than we intended.

sourceA.title: 教学案例：a fictional story about a woman returning a borrowed key
sourceA.text:
At a fictional story about a woman returning a borrowed key, participants considered whether to interpret the narrators repeated attention to a quiet hallway. The background was specific: the key was described as warm in her hand, the door remained closed, and a final sentence said that nobody had asked her to hurry. However, these details could suggest relief, hesitation or an altered relationship, but none established a complete history of the household. The proposed response was to offer a principal interpretation and test it against an alternative supported by the same details.

The key and the closed door establish a pattern of contact and separation, but their emotional meaning is not fixed. The final reference to nobody asking the woman to hurry may suggest a new freedom, a painful absence of expectation, or both at once. A strong interpretation should explain why the chosen reading fits that sentence as well as the physical details. I would resist supplying an unseen argument or death merely to make the story unambiguous. Instead, I would compare two plausible readings and identify the phrase that each finds hardest to accommodate. Such a comparison treats uncertainty as a property of the narrative rather than a defect the reader must repair by inventing information. The warm key suggests attachment, although it does not establish affection. The closed door permits several readings rather than a single fixed symbolism. My interpretation depends on the final sentence as well as the repeated image. Relief and hesitation need not be mutually exclusive responses. We should not invent a family history to resolve the narratives ambiguity.

sourceB.title: 独立测验：a fictional poem about an abandoned railway platform
sourceB.text:
The next original fictional account presents a decision that looks straightforward until the relevant qualification is considered. There is no hidden correct opinion about the institution. The reading task is to establish what the account supports, what it leaves open, and what the proposed response actually changes.

At a fictional poem about an abandoned railway platform, the discussion concerned whether to interpret the contrast between a timetable and growing grass. There was a reason the idea initially appeared attractive: the timetable still promised departures while weeds covered the track, and the speaker addressed a traveller who never appeared. That account nevertheless contained an important reservation: the contrast supported a reading about failed promises but did not prove that the absent traveller had died. The suggested response was to keep emotional possibilities open and distinguish the speakers language from biographical claims about the writer.

The promised departures and unusable track create a tension between an official statement and the physical scene. That tension can support several emotional readings: abandonment, delayed hope, institutional forgetfulness or a refusal to accept change. The missing traveller intensifies the uncertainty without settling its cause. A reader who concludes that the traveller died needs a detail beyond absence alone, since many kinds of absence are possible. A reader who sees only scenery must still explain why the poem addresses someone who never arrives. Strong interpretation does not require eliminating ambiguity. It requires showing how a proposed reading accounts for the language while acknowledging the detail that leaves another reading available.

The conclusion remains specific to the conditions described. Another interpretation should account for the same details, identify any additional assumptions, and explain what evidence would change the judgement.

writing.prompt: Write an advisory commentary about the teaching case, using Source A only. Evaluate the initial proposal, explain the most important qualification, recommend a proportionate response, and identify what could change your judgement. Do not copy the model. Use an appropriate register for the people responsible at a fictional story about a woman returning a borrowed key.
writing.sample:
The immediate objective should be to offer a principal interpretation and test it against an alternative supported by the same details. At a fictional story about a woman returning a borrowed key, the initial suggestion was to interpret the narrators repeated attention to a quiet hallway. The relevant background is that the key was described as warm in her hand, the door remained closed, and a final sentence said that nobody had asked her to hurry. Nevertheless, these details could suggest relief, hesitation or an altered relationship, but none established a complete history of the household. A defensible response must preserve the distinction this creates rather than resolve the difficulty by ignoring part of the account.

The key and the closed door establish a pattern of contact and separation, but their emotional meaning is not fixed. The final reference to nobody asking the woman to hurry may suggest a new freedom, a painful absence of expectation, or both at once. A strong interpretation should explain why the chosen reading fits that sentence as well as the physical details. I would resist supplying an unseen argument or death merely to make the story unambiguous. Instead, I would compare two plausible readings and identify the phrase that each finds hardest to accommodate. Such a comparison treats uncertainty as a property of the narrative rather than a defect the reader must repair by inventing information.

I would record the recommendation together with its conditions and the information that could make it necessary to reconsider. The strongest objection should be answered in its actual form, not replaced by a more convenient one. If later evidence changes the position, the revision should be explained openly. The point is to make a proportionate decision that remains accountable to the details, rather than adopt a more impressive conclusion whose certainty the case cannot support.

speaking.prompt: Without reading a script, explain your response to the teaching case at a fictional story about a woman returning a borrowed key. Speak for two to three minutes, distinguish evidence from inference, and respond to a partner who disagrees.
followups: Which detail would most strongly justify changing your recommendation to offer a principal interpretation and test it against an alternative supported by the same details?
Restate the opposing view in its strongest reasonable form, then explain the remaining disagreement.
speaking.sample: I would separate the original idea from the qualification that changes its meaning. The proposal was to interpret the narrators repeated attention to a quiet hallway. The relevant detail is that the key was described as warm in her hand, the door remained closed, and a final sentence said that nobody had asked her to hurry. However, these details could suggest relief, hesitation or an altered relationship, but none established a complete history of the household. For that reason, I would offer a principal interpretation and test it against an alternative supported by the same details. This does not dismiss every contribution; it makes the decision more precise. If challenged, I would distinguish the stated details from my interpretation. I would also explain what information could change my mind, rather than defend the same conclusion regardless of the evidence.

assessmentListening.text: I want to explain a decision we reached during a reading group discussing a fictional letter. It would be easy to report only the most memorable phrase and miss why the group changed its approach. The relevant background was that the writer folded an empty page and placed it in a drawer. However, the passage supplied no reason why the message remained unwritten. We therefore needed to offer competing interpretations without inventing a definitive backstory. That distinction mattered more than making the final summary sound confident. After discussing the alternatives, the group decided to support each reading with the gestures actually described. The decision was not a claim that the initial observation had no value. It was a way to preserve what remained useful without carrying forward an implication the available detail could not justify. If someone later summarises our discussion, I would want both the reason for the concern and the agreed action to remain visible. Otherwise, a listener might reasonably understand a much stronger conclusion than we intended.
assessmentListening.delivery: Original fictional script. TTS or printed text does not substitute for independent assessment with unfamiliar human speech.

sourceA.title: 教学案例：a fictional study of library study rooms
sourceA.text:
At a fictional study of library study rooms, participants considered whether to evaluate whether booking rooms improved examination results. The background was specific: students who reserved quiet rooms earned higher marks, but the report also noted that frequent users had stronger attendance before the rooms opened. However, the association could reflect prior motivation, and a plausible concentration mechanism did not remove that alternative explanation. The proposed response was to compare changes over time and seek a design that addresses selection rather than calling correlation proof.

The room users may genuinely benefit from a quiet environment, and that possibility deserves investigation. The problem is not that a concentration mechanism is absurd; it is that the observed comparison cannot isolate it. Stronger prior attendance suggests that users already differed from non users in a way relevant to examination marks. Collecting more detail about those differences could help, but it would not automatically make every adjustment credible. The evaluation should specify the causal question and explain why its comparison addresses selection. Meanwhile, the descriptive finding can still guide a modest decision about demand for rooms. It should not be advertised as a proven increase in grades caused by the booking system. Higher marks among room users establish an association rather than a causal effect. Prior attendance may influence both room use and examination performance. The proposed mechanism is credible but does not eliminate selection bias. We need a comparison that addresses differences already present before the change. The result is compatible with several explanations the design cannot separate. I would narrow the conclusion instead of dismissing the observation entirely.

sourceB.title: 独立测验：a fictional evaluation of workplace mentoring
sourceB.text:
A separate fictional case offers another opportunity to distinguish an observation from its interpretation. The people involved share enough common ground to continue working, but their initial description risks implying more than they have established. The difference becomes visible when the suggested action is compared with the available detail.

At a fictional evaluation of workplace mentoring, the discussion concerned whether to assess a claim that mentoring prevented staff departures. There was a reason the idea initially appeared attractive: participants stayed longer than non participants, although supervisors had invited employees they already expected to promote. That account nevertheless contained an important reservation: promotion prospects could influence both selection and retention, leaving the programmes independent effect uncertain. The suggested response was to separate the descriptive retention difference from the causal claim and propose a fair comparison group.

A comparison between participants and non participants would be informative about observed retention. The difficulty begins when the report treats those groups as though participation were their only relevant difference. Supervisors expectations may already predict who is likely to stay. The programme might still help, but the observed gap cannot tell the evaluator how much help it provided. A better design would address the selection process before estimating the effect. That might require comparing otherwise similar employees under a defensible allocation procedure. Simply interviewing more participants about how much they enjoyed the mentoring would answer another useful question, not remove the causal uncertainty. The report should name both the finding and its boundary.

The conclusion remains specific to the conditions described. Another interpretation should account for the same details, identify any additional assumptions, and explain what evidence would change the judgement.
