sourceA.title: 教学案例：two fictional reports about an urban river path
sourceA.text:
At two fictional reports about an urban river path, participants considered whether to combine access benefits with observations of uneven use. The background was specific: a transport survey counted more weekday cyclists after resurfacing, while interviews with older pedestrians described difficulty at two shared corners. However, the counts and interviews addressed different questions, so treating one as a refutation of the other discarded useful evidence. The proposed response was to retain the overall increase and specify where design changes might improve access for particular users.

The river path is not experienced by an average user who simultaneously rides a bicycle and walks cautiously around every corner. Different people can gain and lose from the same design. The two reports should therefore be combined in a way that preserves their units of observation. Counting cyclists answers one question; listening to older pedestrians answers another. The authority could inspect the identified corners, test clearer separation or reduced speeds, and monitor whether the improvement creates new barriers elsewhere. It need not reject resurfacing to acknowledge a design problem. Equally, a positive traffic count cannot settle the question of access for everyone. The recommendation should state whose experience each proposed measure is intended to improve. More cyclists and less comfortable corners can both be genuine findings. The reports address different outcomes rather than necessarily contradicting each other. Aggregating the results would conceal which users encountered the difficulty. We should preserve the disagreement about priorities instead of averaging it away. The interviews explain experiences that the traffic counts cannot capture. Neither source alone supports a conclusion about universal accessibility. The synthesis needs to identify where the evidence converges and where it diverges.

sourceB.title: 独立测验：two fictional accounts of a school meal change
sourceB.text:
In this newly invented case, readers should attend to the relationship between a stated aim and the evidence used to defend it. The account does not invite a judgement about personalities. Instead, it supplies a limited situation in which a careful summary can preserve something that a confident headline loses.

At two fictional accounts of a school meal change, the discussion concerned whether to integrate reduced waste with complaints about choice. There was a reason the idea initially appeared attractive: kitchen records showed fewer discarded portions, whereas pupil discussions revealed that some children brought food from home instead. That account nevertheless contained an important reservation: the apparently positive waste result did not reveal whether children ate more of the meal or avoided it. The suggested response was to join the operational and participation evidence before recommending expansion.

Fewer discarded portions could reflect better acceptance, smaller servings or lower participation. The kitchen record alone cannot distinguish these possibilities. The pupil discussions make one alternative visible, although they do not establish how many children chose it. Together the sources suggest a need to count participation as well as waste and to understand why some pupils opt out. They do not justify dismissing the operational improvement, because less discarded food remains relevant. They also do not justify treating it as evidence that all pupils prefer the new meals. A recommendation to expand should explain which outcome it prioritises and how it will detect a gain in efficiency that conceals a loss in access.

The conclusion remains specific to the conditions described. Another interpretation should account for the same details, identify any additional assumptions, and explain what evidence would change the judgement.

writing.prompt: Write an advisory commentary about the teaching case, using Source A only. Evaluate the initial proposal, explain the most important qualification, recommend a proportionate response, and identify what could change your judgement. Do not copy the model. Use an appropriate register for the people responsible at two fictional reports about an urban river path.
writing.sample:
The immediate objective should be to retain the overall increase and specify where design changes might improve access for particular users. At two fictional reports about an urban river path, the initial suggestion was to combine access benefits with observations of uneven use. The relevant background is that a transport survey counted more weekday cyclists after resurfacing, while interviews with older pedestrians described difficulty at two shared corners. Nevertheless, the counts and interviews addressed different questions, so treating one as a refutation of the other discarded useful evidence. A defensible response must preserve the distinction this creates rather than resolve the difficulty by ignoring part of the account.

The river path is not experienced by an average user who simultaneously rides a bicycle and walks cautiously around every corner. Different people can gain and lose from the same design. The two reports should therefore be combined in a way that preserves their units of observation. Counting cyclists answers one question; listening to older pedestrians answers another. The authority could inspect the identified corners, test clearer separation or reduced speeds, and monitor whether the improvement creates new barriers elsewhere. It need not reject resurfacing to acknowledge a design problem. Equally, a positive traffic count cannot settle the question of access for everyone. The recommendation should state whose experience each proposed measure is intended to improve.

I would record the recommendation together with its conditions and the information that could make it necessary to reconsider. The strongest objection should be answered in its actual form, not replaced by a more convenient one. If later evidence changes the position, the revision should be explained openly. The point is to make a proportionate decision that remains accountable to the details, rather than adopt a more impressive conclusion whose certainty the case cannot support.

speaking.sample: I would separate the original idea from the qualification that changes its meaning. The proposal was to combine access benefits with observations of uneven use. The relevant detail is that a transport survey counted more weekday cyclists after resurfacing, while interviews with older pedestrians described difficulty at two shared corners. However, the counts and interviews addressed different questions, so treating one as a refutation of the other discarded useful evidence. For that reason, I would retain the overall increase and specify where design changes might improve access for particular users. This does not dismiss every contribution; it makes the decision more precise. If challenged, I would distinguish the stated details from my interpretation. I would also explain what information could change my mind, rather than defend the same conclusion regardless of the evidence.

assessmentListening.text: I want to explain a decision we reached during two accounts of a new market timetable. It would be easy to report only the most memorable phrase and miss why the group changed its approach. The relevant background was that stallholders reported higher morning sales while cleaners described later finishing times. However, the accounts measured different consequences of the same change. We therefore needed to retain both results rather than treating one as a refutation. That distinction mattered more than making the final summary sound confident. After discussing the alternatives, the group decided to compare financial benefits with the additional staffing burden. The decision was not a claim that the initial observation had no value. It was a way to preserve what remained useful without carrying forward an implication the available detail could not justify. If someone later summarises our discussion, I would want both the reason for the concern and the agreed action to remain visible. Otherwise, a listener might reasonably understand a much stronger conclusion than we intended.
assessmentListening.delivery: Original fictional script. TTS or printed text does not substitute for independent assessment with unfamiliar human speech.

sourceA.title: 教学案例：a public hearing on a community workshop
sourceA.text:
At a public hearing on a community workshop, participants considered whether to respond to a demand for an absolute safety guarantee. The background was specific: a resident asked whether an accident could ever happen, and the coordinator described inspections, training and the remaining limits of supervision. However, reciting procedures without answering the guarantee question sounded evasive even though the procedures were relevant. The proposed response was to say plainly that zero risk cannot be promised, then explain the controls and the conditions for stopping an activity.

A promise that no accident could ever occur would offer reassurance unsupported by any realistic supervision arrangement. The coordinator should answer that point before describing training and inspections. Otherwise, even accurate procedural information may sound like an attempt to avoid the question. The next step is to explain who checks equipment, who can stop an activity and what happens when a control fails. Residents then have criteria they can question rather than a general invitation to trust the organisers. The coordinator should also distinguish a documented hazard from an unknown frequency. Such distinctions make the remaining risk visible without presenting uncertainty as either a reason for panic or permission to ignore a preventable problem. No, we cannot guarantee that an accident will never happen. What we can explain is how risks are reduced and who can stop the activity. The question deserves a direct answer before a list of procedures. I do not have evidence for that precise figure, so I will not invent one. Let me distinguish the risk we have measured from the risk we have not.

sourceB.title: 独立测验：a charity funding interview
sourceB.text:
This independent fictional case introduces a different setting. Its purpose is to test transfer, so the conclusion must be recovered from the new details rather than carried over from an earlier example. The participants have a practical decision to make, and an attractive first impression is not enough.

At a charity funding interview, the discussion concerned whether to answer criticism of an uncertain impact estimate. There was a reason the idea initially appeared attractive: a panel member demanded an exact number of people whose lives had changed, but the charity held attendance records and follow up interviews rather than a causal evaluation. That account nevertheless contained an important reservation: inventing a precise impact total would turn incomplete evidence into false certainty. The suggested response was to state what can be counted, what remains an estimate, and what further evaluation would resolve.

Attendance is a count of participation, while a life changed is an interpretation requiring a definition and stronger evidence. Follow up interviews may reveal valuable experiences, but a striking story cannot establish how every participant would have fared without the charity. The funding panel deserves this distinction before it evaluates the proposal. The organisation can still describe its activities, the needs it addresses and the experiences reported by participants. It should also say whether it can track outcomes over time. Refusing an invented total is not an admission that the work is useless. It is a commitment to make claims whose strength matches the evaluation actually undertaken, while planning how to answer the harder question.

The conclusion remains specific to the conditions described. Another interpretation should account for the same details, identify any additional assumptions, and explain what evidence would change the judgement.

writing.prompt: Write an advisory commentary about the teaching case, using Source A only. Evaluate the initial proposal, explain the most important qualification, recommend a proportionate response, and identify what could change your judgement. Do not copy the model. Use an appropriate register for the people responsible at a public hearing on a community workshop.
writing.sample:
The immediate objective should be to say plainly that zero risk cannot be promised, then explain the controls and the conditions for stopping an activity. At a public hearing on a community workshop, the initial suggestion was to respond to a demand for an absolute safety guarantee. The relevant background is that a resident asked whether an accident could ever happen, and the coordinator described inspections, training and the remaining limits of supervision. Nevertheless, reciting procedures without answering the guarantee question sounded evasive even though the procedures were relevant. A defensible response must preserve the distinction this creates rather than resolve the difficulty by ignoring part of the account.

A promise that no accident could ever occur would offer reassurance unsupported by any realistic supervision arrangement. The coordinator should answer that point before describing training and inspections. Otherwise, even accurate procedural information may sound like an attempt to avoid the question. The next step is to explain who checks equipment, who can stop an activity and what happens when a control fails. Residents then have criteria they can question rather than a general invitation to trust the organisers. The coordinator should also distinguish a documented hazard from an unknown frequency. Such distinctions make the remaining risk visible without presenting uncertainty as either a reason for panic or permission to ignore a preventable problem.

I would record the recommendation together with its conditions and the information that could make it necessary to reconsider. The strongest objection should be answered in its actual form, not replaced by a more convenient one. If later evidence changes the position, the revision should be explained openly. The point is to make a proportionate decision that remains accountable to the details, rather than adopt a more impressive conclusion whose certainty the case cannot support.

speaking.prompt: Without reading a script, explain your response to the teaching case at a public hearing on a community workshop. Speak for two to three minutes, distinguish evidence from inference, and respond to a partner who disagrees.
followups: Which detail would most strongly justify changing your recommendation to say plainly that zero risk cannot be promised, then explain the controls and the conditions for stopping an activity?
Restate the opposing view in its strongest reasonable form, then explain the remaining disagreement.
speaking.sample: I would separate the original idea from the qualification that changes its meaning. The proposal was to respond to a demand for an absolute safety guarantee. The relevant detail is that a resident asked whether an accident could ever happen, and the coordinator described inspections, training and the remaining limits of supervision. However, reciting procedures without answering the guarantee question sounded evasive even though the procedures were relevant. For that reason, I would say plainly that zero risk cannot be promised, then explain the controls and the conditions for stopping an activity. This does not dismiss every contribution; it makes the decision more precise. If challenged, I would distinguish the stated details from my interpretation. I would also explain what information could change my mind, rather than defend the same conclusion regardless of the evidence.

assessmentListening.text: I want to explain a decision we reached during a school board question about a new climbing wall. It would be easy to report only the most memorable phrase and miss why the group changed its approach. The relevant background was that a parent asked whether injuries could be completely ruled out. However, the organiser had inspection records but could not eliminate every risk. We therefore needed to answer the guarantee question directly before describing safeguards. That distinction mattered more than making the final summary sound confident. After discussing the alternatives, the group decided to explain supervision rules and the conditions that would stop a session. The decision was not a claim that the initial observation had no value. It was a way to preserve what remained useful without carrying forward an implication the available detail could not justify. If someone later summarises our discussion, I would want both the reason for the concern and the agreed action to remain visible. Otherwise, a listener might reasonably understand a much stronger conclusion than we intended.

sourceA.title: 教学案例：a debate about keeping a public swimming pool open later
sourceA.text:
At a debate about keeping a public swimming pool open later, participants considered whether to weigh access for shift workers against staffing costs. The background was specific: supporters argued that current hours excluded people with irregular jobs, while opponents cited the cost of lifeguards rather than hostility to those users. However, portraying opponents as indifferent to health avoided the actual resource objection. The proposed response was to acknowledge the strongest cost argument and compare a limited trial with the present schedule.

The staffing objection deserves an answer in financial and operational terms. Accusing opponents of indifference would leave that objection intact while making cooperation harder. A limited late opening trial could provide demand information and a realistic record of staffing needs, provided its costs and review criteria were agreed in advance. Supporters would then need to accept the possibility that demand was lower than expected; opponents would need to accept evidence of substantial unmet need. This creates a disagreement that experience can inform. The argument should compare the trial with the current arrangement rather than contrast perfect access with unlimited expense. Both sides can care about public health while assigning different weights to the available options. The strongest objection concerns staffing costs, not indifference to swimmers. I accept that concern but question whether it rules out a limited trial. Could we state the opposing argument in terms its supporters would recognise? The example challenges a universal claim without settling the whole policy. Your conclusion follows only if no cheaper staffing arrangement is feasible. We agree on the access problem but differ over the proportional response.

sourceB.title: 独立测验：a debate over pedestrianising a market street
sourceB.text:
The next original fictional account presents a decision that looks straightforward until the relevant qualification is considered. There is no hidden correct opinion about the institution. The reading task is to establish what the account supports, what it leaves open, and what the proposed response actually changes.

At a debate over pedestrianising a market street, the discussion concerned whether to distinguish accessibility objections from opposition to cleaner air. There was a reason the idea initially appeared attractive: shopkeepers worried about deliveries and residents with limited mobility, even though most accepted that through traffic made the street unpleasant. That account nevertheless contained an important reservation: responding only with pollution statistics left the specific access problem unanswered. The suggested response was to test timed deliveries and accessible pickup points while examining whether traffic would move elsewhere.

Cleaner air is relevant, but it does not tell a person with limited mobility how to reach a shop. Equally, an access concern does not establish that the present traffic pattern is the only possible arrangement. The debate becomes productive when these interests are separated from the initial positions. Timed delivery windows and accessible collection points may address some objections, though their practicality needs testing. Traffic displacement also matters because a cleaner market street could shift burdens to neighbouring roads. An honest comparison should therefore consider the whole arrangement rather than its most appealing photograph. Participants can agree on the harm caused by traffic while disagreeing about whether this design distributes the benefits and costs fairly.

The conclusion remains specific to the conditions described. Another interpretation should account for the same details, identify any additional assumptions, and explain what evidence would change the judgement.

sourceA.title: 教学案例：a negotiation over rehearsal space in a school hall
sourceA.text:
At a negotiation over rehearsal space in a school hall, participants considered whether to agree a schedule between a drama group and a youth club. The background was specific: the drama group needed uninterrupted evenings before its performance, while the youth club needed predictable access rather than a particular weekday. However, splitting every evening equally would satisfy neither need and create repeated setup costs. The proposed response was to offer a short performance preparation block in exchange for a longer guaranteed youth club booking afterwards.

The groups initial positions make the room look impossible to share, but the reasons behind those positions reveal an exchange. Continuous preparation is especially valuable before a performance, while predictability may matter more than a particular weekday to the youth club. A negotiated block can therefore be fair without dividing each evening in half. The arrangement should specify dates, setup responsibilities and what happens if the performance moves. Confirmation matters because each group is being asked to rely on a later benefit. I would also schedule a short review after the first exchange. That gives both parties a way to correct practical problems without treating every request for adjustment as a breach of goodwill. Our priority is uninterrupted rehearsal time rather than any particular weekday. Would a guaranteed later booking compensate for the temporary loss of access? We can concede those evenings provided the later arrangement is confirmed. That is a conditional offer, not an agreement to surrender the slot. Let us compare the costs of setup before dividing the hours equally. The positions conflict, but the underlying interests may be compatible.

sourceB.title: 独立测验：a negotiation between a bakery and a community cafe
sourceB.text:
A separate fictional case offers another opportunity to distinguish an observation from its interpretation. The people involved share enough common ground to continue working, but their initial description risks implying more than they have established. The difference becomes visible when the suggested action is compared with the available detail.

At a negotiation between a bakery and a community cafe, the discussion concerned whether to revise a supply arrangement after a price increase. There was a reason the idea initially appeared attractive: the bakery needed orders earlier to reduce waste, while the cafe needed predictable weekly spending rather than the cheapest possible loaf. That account nevertheless contained an important reservation: an immediate demand for a price cut concealed an opportunity to exchange reliable volume for a stable rate. The suggested response was to link the price concession to a minimum order and set a review date both sides can meet.

The price discussion initially appears to be a contest over how much each side pays. Looking at waste and ordering reveals another dimension. Predictable volume helps the bakery plan production, and a stable rate helps the cafe plan its budget. A concession can therefore be tied to an action the other party values rather than offered without a return. The resulting agreement should define the minimum order, the notice required for changes and what happens when demand falls unexpectedly. A vague promise to be reasonable would leave the central risks untouched. Neither side needs to disclose every internal cost, but each needs enough information to judge whether the proposed exchange is reliable and acceptable.

The conclusion remains specific to the conditions described. Another interpretation should account for the same details, identify any additional assumptions, and explain what evidence would change the judgement.

writing.prompt: Write an advisory commentary about the teaching case, using Source A only. Evaluate the initial proposal, explain the most important qualification, recommend a proportionate response, and identify what could change your judgement. Do not copy the model. Use an appropriate register for the people responsible at a negotiation over rehearsal space in a school hall.
writing.sample:
The immediate objective should be to offer a short performance preparation block in exchange for a longer guaranteed youth club booking afterwards. At a negotiation over rehearsal space in a school hall, the initial suggestion was to agree a schedule between a drama group and a youth club. The relevant background is that the drama group needed uninterrupted evenings before its performance, while the youth club needed predictable access rather than a particular weekday. Nevertheless, splitting every evening equally would satisfy neither need and create repeated setup costs. A defensible response must preserve the distinction this creates rather than resolve the difficulty by ignoring part of the account.

The groups initial positions make the room look impossible to share, but the reasons behind those positions reveal an exchange. Continuous preparation is especially valuable before a performance, while predictability may matter more than a particular weekday to the youth club. A negotiated block can therefore be fair without dividing each evening in half. The arrangement should specify dates, setup responsibilities and what happens if the performance moves. Confirmation matters because each group is being asked to rely on a later benefit. I would also schedule a short review after the first exchange. That gives both parties a way to correct practical problems without treating every request for adjustment as a breach of goodwill.

I would record the recommendation together with its conditions and the information that could make it necessary to reconsider. The strongest objection should be answered in its actual form, not replaced by a more convenient one. If later evidence changes the position, the revision should be explained openly. The point is to make a proportionate decision that remains accountable to the details, rather than adopt a more impressive conclusion whose certainty the case cannot support.

speaking.sample: I would separate the original idea from the qualification that changes its meaning. The proposal was to agree a schedule between a drama group and a youth club. The relevant detail is that the drama group needed uninterrupted evenings before its performance, while the youth club needed predictable access rather than a particular weekday. However, splitting every evening equally would satisfy neither need and create repeated setup costs. For that reason, I would offer a short performance preparation block in exchange for a longer guaranteed youth club booking afterwards. This does not dismiss every contribution; it makes the decision more precise. If challenged, I would distinguish the stated details from my interpretation. I would also explain what information could change my mind, rather than defend the same conclusion regardless of the evidence.

assessmentListening.text: I want to explain a decision we reached during a negotiation about a shared exhibition room. It would be easy to report only the most memorable phrase and miss why the group changed its approach. The relevant background was that one group needed a full installation week while another needed fixed weekend access. However, an equal daily split would create repeated setup work for both. We therefore needed to exchange blocks of time according to underlying needs. That distinction mattered more than making the final summary sound confident. After discussing the alternatives, the group decided to confirm one installation week in return for guaranteed later weekends. The decision was not a claim that the initial observation had no value. It was a way to preserve what remained useful without carrying forward an implication the available detail could not justify. If someone later summarises our discussion, I would want both the reason for the concern and the agreed action to remain visible. Otherwise, a listener might reasonably understand a much stronger conclusion than we intended.

sourceA.title: 教学案例：a workshop explaining digital privacy to older residents
sourceA.text:
At a workshop explaining digital privacy to older residents, participants considered whether to explain metadata without treating it as the content of a message. The background was specific: the instructor compared a messages content with the outside of an envelope, then explained that digital records can reveal repeated contact patterns. However, the envelope analogy made the concept accessible but could conceal how detailed modern tracking becomes when records are combined. The proposed response was to use the analogy as a starting point and explicitly name where it stops being accurate.

The envelope analogy offers a useful entry point because it separates message content from information surrounding the message. It becomes misleading if listeners assume that digital metadata is limited to one sender and one address on one object. Combined records can reveal contact patterns at a scale the ordinary envelope does not suggest. The instructor should therefore name that limit immediately and show a second example involving several records over time. Asking participants to explain a new case would reveal more than asking whether the analogy was clear. The aim is not to make a technical term memorable at any cost. It is to leave listeners with a distinction they can use accurately after the convenient comparison has been set aside. Think of metadata as information about a message rather than its contents. The envelope analogy helps initially, but it understates the scale of tracking. Let me put that another way without changing the central distinction. Several harmless looking records can reveal a pattern when combined. The analogy stops being accurate at precisely that point.

sourceB.title: 独立测验：a science volunteer explaining an uncertainty interval
sourceB.text:
In this newly invented case, readers should attend to the relationship between a stated aim and the evidence used to defend it. The account does not invite a judgement about personalities. Instead, it supplies a limited situation in which a careful summary can preserve something that a confident headline loses.

At a science volunteer explaining an uncertainty interval, the discussion concerned whether to clarify what a range around an estimate does and does not mean. There was a reason the idea initially appeared attractive: the volunteer first called it a margin of doubt, then distinguished uncertainty in the estimate from differences between individual people. That account nevertheless contained an important reservation: a vivid phrase helped listeners begin but could make all forms of variation sound interchangeable. The suggested response was to restate the idea using the actual question and check the listeners understanding with a fresh example.

Uncertainty about an estimated average does not describe the range within which every individual observation must fall. The convenient phrase margin of doubt risks blurring these concepts. An example using repeated samples can reveal why the estimate changes, while a separate example can show differences between people. The volunteer should check understanding by asking listeners to apply the distinction, rather than asking whether the explanation sounded clear. If listeners confuse the two again, the reformulation has not yet achieved its purpose. A successful analogy is not one the audience remembers as a slogan; it is one that helps them reason accurately when the same idea appears in an unfamiliar form.

The conclusion remains specific to the conditions described. Another interpretation should account for the same details, identify any additional assumptions, and explain what evidence would change the judgement.

writing.prompt: Write an advisory commentary about the teaching case, using Source A only. Evaluate the initial proposal, explain the most important qualification, recommend a proportionate response, and identify what could change your judgement. Do not copy the model. Use an appropriate register for the people responsible at a workshop explaining digital privacy to older residents.
writing.sample:
The immediate objective should be to use the analogy as a starting point and explicitly name where it stops being accurate. At a workshop explaining digital privacy to older residents, the initial suggestion was to explain metadata without treating it as the content of a message. The relevant background is that the instructor compared a messages content with the outside of an envelope, then explained that digital records can reveal repeated contact patterns. Nevertheless, the envelope analogy made the concept accessible but could conceal how detailed modern tracking becomes when records are combined. A defensible response must preserve the distinction this creates rather than resolve the difficulty by ignoring part of the account.

The envelope analogy offers a useful entry point because it separates message content from information surrounding the message. It becomes misleading if listeners assume that digital metadata is limited to one sender and one address on one object. Combined records can reveal contact patterns at a scale the ordinary envelope does not suggest. The instructor should therefore name that limit immediately and show a second example involving several records over time. Asking participants to explain a new case would reveal more than asking whether the analogy was clear. The aim is not to make a technical term memorable at any cost. It is to leave listeners with a distinction they can use accurately after the convenient comparison has been set aside.

I would record the recommendation together with its conditions and the information that could make it necessary to reconsider. The strongest objection should be answered in its actual form, not replaced by a more convenient one. If later evidence changes the position, the revision should be explained openly. The point is to make a proportionate decision that remains accountable to the details, rather than adopt a more impressive conclusion whose certainty the case cannot support.

speaking.sample: I would separate the original idea from the qualification that changes its meaning. The proposal was to explain metadata without treating it as the content of a message. The relevant detail is that the instructor compared a messages content with the outside of an envelope, then explained that digital records can reveal repeated contact patterns. However, the envelope analogy made the concept accessible but could conceal how detailed modern tracking becomes when records are combined. For that reason, I would use the analogy as a starting point and explicitly name where it stops being accurate. This does not dismiss every contribution; it makes the decision more precise. If challenged, I would distinguish the stated details from my interpretation. I would also explain what information could change my mind, rather than defend the same conclusion regardless of the evidence.

assessmentListening.text: I want to explain a decision we reached during a workshop explaining a computer backup. It would be easy to report only the most memorable phrase and miss why the group changed its approach. The relevant background was that the instructor compared a backup with a spare key. However, the analogy omitted the fact that a backup must be updated when files change. We therefore needed to keep the useful comparison while stating where it fails. That distinction mattered more than making the final summary sound confident. After discussing the alternatives, the group decided to show how an old backup can restore an outdated version of a document. The decision was not a claim that the initial observation had no value. It was a way to preserve what remained useful without carrying forward an implication the available detail could not justify. If someone later summarises our discussion, I would want both the reason for the concern and the agreed action to remain visible. Otherwise, a listener might reasonably understand a much stronger conclusion than we intended.
assessmentListening.delivery: Original fictional script. TTS or printed text does not substitute for independent assessment with unfamiliar human speech.

sourceA.title: 教学案例：a review of a practical guide to repairing furniture
sourceA.text:
At a review of a practical guide to repairing furniture, participants considered whether to assess usefulness without demanding specialist completeness. The background was specific: the guide explained loose joints clearly and showed inexpensive tools, but its section on antique finishes offered only a brief caution. However, a beginner could benefit greatly while still needing expert help with valuable or fragile objects. The proposed response was to recommend the book to its intended readers and identify the specific tasks that exceed its scope.

A useful review helps readers decide whether a book suits their likely tasks. Here, ordinary furniture repairs and valuable antique finishes involve different levels of risk. The reviewer can praise the clear sequence and inexpensive tools while advising readers to seek specialist help in the latter case. That boundary should be specific enough to guide a purchase and a practical decision. A vague statement that the book is not comprehensive would add little, because no introductory guide can be comprehensive. Nor would an unqualified recommendation protect beginners who cannot recognise when a finish is fragile. The fairest verdict identifies what the guide enables, which audience benefits, and which jobs require support beyond its pages. The guide succeeds as an introduction without replacing specialist advice. Its clearest strength is the sequence of repairs a beginner can follow. The brief treatment of antique finishes limits its suitability for valuable objects. That limitation warrants a qualification rather than an outright dismissal. I would recommend it to beginners working on ordinary furniture. The review should explain whom the recommendation is intended to help. The illustrations carry practical information rather than merely decorating the page.

sourceB.title: 独立测验：a review of a public history podcast
sourceB.text:
This independent fictional case introduces a different setting. Its purpose is to test transfer, so the conclusion must be recovered from the new details rather than carried over from an earlier example. The participants have a practical decision to make, and an attractive first impression is not enough.

At a review of a public history podcast, the discussion concerned whether to balance compelling storytelling with transparent sourcing. There was a reason the idea initially appeared attractive: the episodes used vivid reconstructions and a separate source list, yet listeners could not always tell which spoken lines came from documents. That account nevertheless contained an important reservation: the programme could be engaging and well researched while still blurring evidence and dramatic invention in particular moments. The suggested response was to praise the accessible narrative and request clearer signals around reconstructed speech.

A separate source list is valuable, but it does not tell a listener at each moment whether an actor is reading documented speech or an invented reconstruction. That distinction affects how a vivid line should be remembered and repeated. The reviewer can acknowledge the programme makers research while identifying a weakness in the presentation of evidence. A short introduction or change in delivery might make the boundary clearer without destroying narrative momentum. The recommendation should not imply that dramatic reconstruction is automatically dishonest. Its fairness depends on what the audience is led to believe. The issue is therefore the transparency of the transition, not whether a history programme is permitted to be engaging.

The conclusion remains specific to the conditions described. Another interpretation should account for the same details, identify any additional assumptions, and explain what evidence would change the judgement.

sourceA.title: 教学案例：a draft proposal for a weekend bus route
sourceA.text:
At a draft proposal for a weekend bus route, participants considered whether to revise an argument that jumped from one example to a universal conclusion. The background was specific: the draft cited one crowded Saturday bus and declared that every weekend service would pay for itself, although no cost calculation appeared. However, stronger adjectives would not repair the missing link between observed demand and financial viability. The proposed response was to narrow the demand claim and add information about operating costs, frequency and variation across weekends.

The crowded journey is a reason to investigate demand, not a financial forecast. To reach the latter, the proposal needs an estimate of how often similar demand occurs, what the service would cost and how fares or subsidy would meet that cost. A holiday trip might be unusual, so the next observations should include ordinary weekends. The revised paragraph can retain the vivid example as an introduction while changing the conclusion to a case for testing. This is a more important improvement than replacing everyday words with impressive alternatives. Readers should be able to see the missing link and judge the information supplied to bridge it. A polished leap remains a leap even when its vocabulary sounds authoritative. One crowded bus does not establish that every weekend service will be viable. The missing warrant links observed demand to the financial conclusion. Replacing weak adjectives will not repair that gap in reasoning. The claim should be narrowed to what the observation actually supports. We need operating costs as well as an estimate of passenger demand. The revised paragraph separates an encouraging example from a general forecast.

sourceB.title: 独立测验：a draft article opposing a new school timetable
sourceB.text:
The next original fictional account presents a decision that looks straightforward until the relevant qualification is considered. There is no hidden correct opinion about the institution. The reading task is to establish what the account supports, what it leaves open, and what the proposed response actually changes.

At a draft article opposing a new school timetable, the discussion concerned whether to remove a false choice between tradition and complete disruption. There was a reason the idea initially appeared attractive: the writer presented the current timetable and a radically longer day as the only possibilities, despite several moderate proposals from teachers. That account nevertheless contained an important reservation: the persuasive contrast depended on excluding realistic alternatives from consideration. The suggested response was to restore the intermediate options and evaluate them using the same criteria.

The article can criticise a longer day without pretending that every alternative is equally long. By excluding moderate proposals, it makes the present arrangement appear to be the only protection against disruption. Restoring those proposals changes the argumentative task: the writer must explain why the current timetable is preferable to each plausible option, using comparable criteria. That may require evidence about travel, staff workload and pupils concentration. The revision is substantial because it alters the choice readers are asked to make. Merely inserting a sentence that admits other views would be insufficient if the conclusion still relied on the original false contrast. The options must be represented accurately throughout the argument.

The conclusion remains specific to the conditions described. Another interpretation should account for the same details, identify any additional assumptions, and explain what evidence would change the judgement.

writing.prompt: Write an advisory commentary about the teaching case, using Source A only. Evaluate the initial proposal, explain the most important qualification, recommend a proportionate response, and identify what could change your judgement. Do not copy the model. Use an appropriate register for the people responsible at a draft proposal for a weekend bus route.
writing.sample:
The immediate objective should be to narrow the demand claim and add information about operating costs, frequency and variation across weekends. At a draft proposal for a weekend bus route, the initial suggestion was to revise an argument that jumped from one example to a universal conclusion. The relevant background is that the draft cited one crowded Saturday bus and declared that every weekend service would pay for itself, although no cost calculation appeared. Nevertheless, stronger adjectives would not repair the missing link between observed demand and financial viability. A defensible response must preserve the distinction this creates rather than resolve the difficulty by ignoring part of the account.

The crowded journey is a reason to investigate demand, not a financial forecast. To reach the latter, the proposal needs an estimate of how often similar demand occurs, what the service would cost and how fares or subsidy would meet that cost. A holiday trip might be unusual, so the next observations should include ordinary weekends. The revised paragraph can retain the vivid example as an introduction while changing the conclusion to a case for testing. This is a more important improvement than replacing everyday words with impressive alternatives. Readers should be able to see the missing link and judge the information supplied to bridge it. A polished leap remains a leap even when its vocabulary sounds authoritative.

I would record the recommendation together with its conditions and the information that could make it necessary to reconsider. The strongest objection should be answered in its actual form, not replaced by a more convenient one. If later evidence changes the position, the revision should be explained openly. The point is to make a proportionate decision that remains accountable to the details, rather than adopt a more impressive conclusion whose certainty the case cannot support.

speaking.sample: I would separate the original idea from the qualification that changes its meaning. The proposal was to revise an argument that jumped from one example to a universal conclusion. The relevant detail is that the draft cited one crowded Saturday bus and declared that every weekend service would pay for itself, although no cost calculation appeared. However, stronger adjectives would not repair the missing link between observed demand and financial viability. For that reason, I would narrow the demand claim and add information about operating costs, frequency and variation across weekends. This does not dismiss every contribution; it makes the decision more precise. If challenged, I would distinguish the stated details from my interpretation. I would also explain what information could change my mind, rather than defend the same conclusion regardless of the evidence.

assessmentListening.text: I want to explain a decision we reached during a proposal for a town shuttle. It would be easy to report only the most memorable phrase and miss why the group changed its approach. The relevant background was that the writer predicted universal demand from one crowded holiday trip. However, ordinary weekday demand and operating costs had not been measured. We therefore needed to repair the unsupported generalisation before polishing the language. That distinction mattered more than making the final summary sound confident. After discussing the alternatives, the group decided to collect representative demand data and prepare a cost comparison. The decision was not a claim that the initial observation had no value. It was a way to preserve what remained useful without carrying forward an implication the available detail could not justify. If someone later summarises our discussion, I would want both the reason for the concern and the agreed action to remain visible. Otherwise, a listener might reasonably understand a much stronger conclusion than we intended.

sourceA.title: 教学案例：a report on a volunteer transport service
sourceA.text:
At a report on a volunteer transport service, participants considered whether to recommend changes to booking procedures. The background was specific: drivers reported repeated route changes and passengers described uncertainty about pickup times, while the booking log contained no record of when changes were communicated. However, without that timing information the report could identify a coordination problem but not assign responsibility fairly. The proposed response was to introduce a time stamped confirmation process and review missed pickups after a defined trial.

Passengers and drivers both describe an experience of uncertainty, but their accounts do not yet establish when a change was made or communicated. The report should resist assigning responsibility to whichever group tells the most compelling story. A simple log could record the original booking, each revision, its confirmation and the eventual pickup. That would support later investigation while immediately improving coordination. The recommendation should name who maintains the log, how volunteers can access the current version and when results will be reviewed. It should also avoid creating unnecessary work that makes the procedure unlikely to survive. A modest system used reliably is more valuable than an elaborate recommendation that nobody has the time or authority to implement. The records reveal a coordination problem without identifying who caused it. The recommendation should name an owner, a deadline and a review criterion. Time stamped confirmations would make later route changes traceable. We should not assign blame where the necessary sequence is undocumented. The proposed trial addresses an observable process rather than a presumed attitude. An actionable finding connects the evidence with a decision someone can implement.

sourceB.title: 独立测验：a report on energy use in a small arts centre
sourceB.text:
A separate fictional case offers another opportunity to distinguish an observation from its interpretation. The people involved share enough common ground to continue working, but their initial description risks implying more than they have established. The difference becomes visible when the suggested action is compared with the available detail.

At a report on energy use in a small arts centre, the discussion concerned whether to prioritise savings without overstating an incomplete audit. There was a reason the idea initially appeared attractive: meter readings suggested heavy overnight consumption, but the building contained refrigeration equipment that had to remain on. That account nevertheless contained an important reservation: calling all night use waste would confuse necessary operation with avoidable consumption. The suggested response was to measure individual circuits before changing schedules and identify who can authorise each adjustment.

Overnight electricity use is a promising place to investigate, not a category that can automatically be eliminated. Refrigeration protects supplies that would otherwise spoil, and switching it off could produce costs greater than the electricity saved. The audit needs to distinguish essential loads from equipment that can safely follow a schedule. Measuring individual circuits would make that distinction more reliable. The report should then connect each proposed change to a responsible person, a safety check and an expected saving. A recommendation to be more efficient would sound agreeable while leaving nobody with an implementable task. Precision here concerns the decision as much as the number of units reported on a meter.

The conclusion remains specific to the conditions described. Another interpretation should account for the same details, identify any additional assumptions, and explain what evidence would change the judgement.

writing.prompt: Write an advisory commentary about the teaching case, using Source A only. Evaluate the initial proposal, explain the most important qualification, recommend a proportionate response, and identify what could change your judgement. Do not copy the model. Use an appropriate register for the people responsible at a report on a volunteer transport service.
writing.sample:
The immediate objective should be to introduce a time stamped confirmation process and review missed pickups after a defined trial. At a report on a volunteer transport service, the initial suggestion was to recommend changes to booking procedures. The relevant background is that drivers reported repeated route changes and passengers described uncertainty about pickup times, while the booking log contained no record of when changes were communicated. Nevertheless, without that timing information the report could identify a coordination problem but not assign responsibility fairly. A defensible response must preserve the distinction this creates rather than resolve the difficulty by ignoring part of the account.

Passengers and drivers both describe an experience of uncertainty, but their accounts do not yet establish when a change was made or communicated. The report should resist assigning responsibility to whichever group tells the most compelling story. A simple log could record the original booking, each revision, its confirmation and the eventual pickup. That would support later investigation while immediately improving coordination. The recommendation should name who maintains the log, how volunteers can access the current version and when results will be reviewed. It should also avoid creating unnecessary work that makes the procedure unlikely to survive. A modest system used reliably is more valuable than an elaborate recommendation that nobody has the time or authority to implement.

I would record the recommendation together with its conditions and the information that could make it necessary to reconsider. The strongest objection should be answered in its actual form, not replaced by a more convenient one. If later evidence changes the position, the revision should be explained openly. The point is to make a proportionate decision that remains accountable to the details, rather than adopt a more impressive conclusion whose certainty the case cannot support.

The relevant detail is that drivers reported repeated route changes and passengers described uncertainty about pickup times, while the booking log contained no record of when changes were communicated. However, without that timing information the report could identify a coordination problem but not assign responsibility fairly. For that reason, I would introduce a time stamped confirmation process and review missed pickups after a defined trial. This does not dismiss every contribution; it makes the decision more precise. If challenged, I would distinguish the stated details from my interpretation. I would also explain what information could change my mind, rather than defend the same conclusion regardless of the evidence.

assessmentListening.text: I want to explain a decision we reached during a report on a community pantry. It would be easy to report only the most memorable phrase and miss why the group changed its approach. The relevant background was that volunteers described frequent stock shortages but recorded no delivery times. However, the evidence showed a problem without identifying its precise cause. We therefore needed to avoid assigning blame before the sequence can be reconstructed. That distinction mattered more than making the final summary sound confident. After discussing the alternatives, the group decided to introduce a delivery log with named responsibilities and a review date. The decision was not a claim that the initial observation had no value. It was a way to preserve what remained useful without carrying forward an implication the available detail could not justify. If someone later summarises our discussion, I would want both the reason for the concern and the agreed action to remain visible. Otherwise, a listener might reasonably understand a much stronger conclusion than we intended.

sourceA.title: 教学案例：an editor working on a personal essay about migration
sourceA.text:
At an editor working on a personal essay about migration, participants considered whether to reduce ambiguity without smoothing away the narrators rhythm. The background was specific: short repeated sentences conveyed the speakers anxiety, while a pronoun in the third paragraph made it unclear which family member had left. However, treating every repetition as a fault would remove an intentional effect, whereas leaving the pronoun unresolved would preserve accidental confusion. The proposed response was to clarify the reference and discuss rhythm with the author before rewriting the repeated sentences.

The narrators short repeated sentences have an identifiable function: they make anxiety audible in the prose. Changing them merely because variety is usually recommended would impose an abstract rule at the expense of the essay. The pronoun problem is different. It prevents readers from knowing which family member acted and does not contribute a comparable effect. I would clarify that reference, then discuss any broader rhythm changes with the author. The editorial note should explain the distinction so that the writer can accept or reject a change intelligently. Preserving voice does not require leaving every difficulty untouched. It requires understanding which difficulties are doing intentional work and which are obstructing the intended experience. The repeated short sentences create a rhythm that serves the narrators anxiety. The ambiguous pronoun produces confusion rather than productive uncertainty. I would clarify the reference while preserving the deliberate repetition. An editor should be able to explain what each substantial change achieves. The smoother version is not automatically the more faithful one. Could this repetition be intentional rather than an oversight? We should ask the author before replacing the distinctive sentence pattern.

sourceB.title: 独立测验：an editor revising a natural history column
sourceB.text:
In this newly invented case, readers should attend to the relationship between a stated aim and the evidence used to defend it. The account does not invite a judgement about personalities. Instead, it supplies a limited situation in which a careful summary can preserve something that a confident headline loses.

At an editor revising a natural history column, the discussion concerned whether to distinguish decorative excess from useful imagery. There was a reason the idea initially appeared attractive: a comparison between moth wings and folded maps helped explain a pattern, but three additional metaphors competed with it in the same sentence. That account nevertheless contained an important reservation: removing every image would sacrifice an effective explanation along with the distracting ones. The suggested response was to retain the image that does explanatory work and simplify the surrounding sentence.

The first image gives readers a way to visualise a pattern they may not have seen. The later images compete for attention without adding a comparable explanation. An editor who removes them selectively can improve the column while preserving its accessible style. An editor who replaces the whole passage with technical description may solve one problem by creating another for the intended audience. The author should be able to see why one comparison remains and another goes. That explanation also helps future drafts. The relevant standard is not a ban on figurative language but a judgement about what each image contributes, whether it misleads, and how much work the surrounding sentence asks of readers.

The conclusion remains specific to the conditions described. Another interpretation should account for the same details, identify any additional assumptions, and explain what evidence would change the judgement.

sourceA.title: 教学案例：a learner research project on access to a neighbourhood park
sourceA.text:
At a learner research project on access to a neighbourhood park, participants considered whether to investigate how different entrances affect practical access. The background was specific: the researcher mapped steps, opening hours and bus stops, interviewed consenting users, and recorded the time of each observation. However, a small voluntary interview sample could reveal barriers without representing every resident or establishing how common each barrier was. The proposed response was to separate direct observation from testimony and explain the limits before proposing improvements.

The investigation should begin with a question the learner can answer responsibly: which observable entrance features make access easier or harder under specified conditions? Mapping steps and opening hours provides direct information, while interviews add experiences the map cannot show. Those forms of evidence should be labelled separately. A handful of volunteers may identify a serious barrier without establishing its prevalence across the neighbourhood. The learner should record consent, avoid unnecessary personal details and preserve conflicting accounts rather than select only convenient quotations. A recommendation can then address a documented obstacle while acknowledging what remains unknown. The quality of the project lies in the traceable link between question, method and conclusion, not the breadth of an unsupported final claim. The question must be narrow enough for the available evidence to answer. An interview can reveal a barrier without showing how widespread it is. I recorded the time and conditions of every direct observation. Participants should understand how their comments will be used before agreeing. The report separates what I observed from what residents told me. Convenient access to interviewees does not make the sample representative.

sourceB.title: 独立测验：a learner investigation of food packaging in a school canteen
sourceB.text:
This independent fictional case introduces a different setting. Its purpose is to test transfer, so the conclusion must be recovered from the new details rather than carried over from an earlier example. The participants have a practical decision to make, and an attractive first impression is not enough.

At a learner investigation of food packaging in a school canteen, the discussion concerned whether to study which changes might reduce unnecessary packaging. There was a reason the idea initially appeared attractive: the learner counted wrappers on five days and asked staff about hygiene requirements, but examinations changed attendance during two observations. That account nevertheless contained an important reservation: the counts offered useful examples but could not simply be multiplied into a reliable annual total. The suggested response was to repeat observations under ordinary attendance and distinguish essential packaging from replaceable items.

Multiplying a small count by the number of school days produces a precise looking annual figure. It does not make the sampled days typical. Examination attendance offers a specific reason to question the calculation rather than a vague warning that all data are unreliable. A better investigation would record ordinary and unusual days separately, note changes in meal participation and ask which wrappers serve necessary functions. It could then compare achievable alternatives on the same basis. The learner should seek permission before photographing people or recording comments and should avoid including identifying details unnecessarily. A transparent small project can support a modest recommendation without pretending to be a complete audit of the school year.

The conclusion remains specific to the conditions described. Another interpretation should account for the same details, identify any additional assumptions, and explain what evidence would change the judgement.

writing.prompt: Write an advisory commentary about the teaching case, using Source A only. Evaluate the initial proposal, explain the most important qualification, recommend a proportionate response, and identify what could change your judgement. Do not copy the model. Use an appropriate register for the people responsible at a learner research project on access to a neighbourhood park.
writing.sample:
The immediate objective should be to separate direct observation from testimony and explain the limits before proposing improvements. At a learner research project on access to a neighbourhood park, the initial suggestion was to investigate how different entrances affect practical access. The relevant background is that the researcher mapped steps, opening hours and bus stops, interviewed consenting users, and recorded the time of each observation. Nevertheless, a small voluntary interview sample could reveal barriers without representing every resident or establishing how common each barrier was. A defensible response must preserve the distinction this creates rather than resolve the difficulty by ignoring part of the account.

The investigation should begin with a question the learner can answer responsibly: which observable entrance features make access easier or harder under specified conditions? Mapping steps and opening hours provides direct information, while interviews add experiences the map cannot show. Those forms of evidence should be labelled separately. A handful of volunteers may identify a serious barrier without establishing its prevalence across the neighbourhood. The learner should record consent, avoid unnecessary personal details and preserve conflicting accounts rather than select only convenient quotations. A recommendation can then address a documented obstacle while acknowledging what remains unknown. The quality of the project lies in the traceable link between question, method and conclusion, not the breadth of an unsupported final claim.

I would record the recommendation together with its conditions and the information that could make it necessary to reconsider. The strongest objection should be answered in its actual form, not replaced by a more convenient one. If later evidence changes the position, the revision should be explained openly. The point is to make a proportionate decision that remains accountable to the details, rather than adopt a more impressive conclusion whose certainty the case cannot support.

assessmentListening.text: I want to explain a decision we reached during a student investigation of street lighting. It would be easy to report only the most memorable phrase and miss why the group changed its approach. The relevant background was that the student photographed four routes and interviewed willing passers by. However, the voluntary interviews did not represent every resident in the district. We therefore needed to report observed barriers without estimating unsupported population percentages. That distinction mattered more than making the final summary sound confident. After discussing the alternatives, the group decided to repeat observations at different times and document the sampling limits. The decision was not a claim that the initial observation had no value. It was a way to preserve what remained useful without carrying forward an implication the available detail could not justify. If someone later summarises our discussion, I would want both the reason for the concern and the agreed action to remain visible. Otherwise, a listener might reasonably understand a much stronger conclusion than we intended.

sourceA.title: 教学案例：a presentation proposing a shared tool library
sourceA.text:
At a presentation proposing a shared tool library, participants considered whether to answer questions about demand and maintenance. The background was specific: the presenter had survey responses from interested residents and a repair budget based on quotations, but no evidence about how often tools would return late. However, a confident presentation could make an untested operating assumption look like an established result. The proposed response was to defend the observed interest while proposing a small pilot to test return times and repair needs.

The presenter should not defend return times as though survey enthusiasm had measured them. Interest, venue costs, repair quotations and actual borrowing behaviour are different forms of information. The first three can justify trying a small service, while a pilot is needed for the fourth. Answering the question directly would make that distinction visible: the plan assumes timely returns, and that assumption has not been tested. The pilot should record delays and maintenance needs before the group invests in a larger collection. This response protects the documented parts of the proposal without treating the whole presentation as invulnerable. An audience can have more confidence in a plan that knows how to learn than in one whose author can only repeat assurances. The survey supports interest in the library, not a forecast of reliable returns. That question exposes an assumption I have not yet tested. I can defend the demand evidence while revising the operating plan. Let me answer the specific challenge before returning to the wider proposal. The repair quotation is documented, whereas the return rate remains uncertain. A small pilot would test the assumption more credibly than another opinion survey.

sourceB.title: 独立测验：a presentation about converting a car park into a garden
sourceB.text:
The next original fictional account presents a decision that looks straightforward until the relevant qualification is considered. There is no hidden correct opinion about the institution. The reading task is to establish what the account supports, what it leaves open, and what the proposed response actually changes.

At a presentation about converting a car park into a garden, the discussion concerned whether to respond to a question exposing an omitted accessibility issue. There was a reason the idea initially appeared attractive: the design included paths and raised beds, but the presenter had not checked the distance from accessible parking after the proposed conversion. That account nevertheless contained an important reservation: defending every detail would protect the presenters pride at the expense of the projects stated purpose. The suggested response was to acknowledge the omission, revise the access plan and explain which parts of the evidence remain useful.

The access question does not erase the benefits of the garden. It reveals a design requirement that the present plan has not satisfied. The presenter should therefore distinguish the environmental and community arguments from the assumption about how everyone reaches the site. A revised drawing can test whether accessible parking, paths and entrance distances work together. The response should not promise a solution before checking it, but can name the review needed and who should contribute. This preserves momentum without treating a questioner as an adversary. A defensible presentation is one whose claims can survive correction, not one whose author refuses every change to protect the appearance of certainty.

The conclusion remains specific to the conditions described. Another interpretation should account for the same details, identify any additional assumptions, and explain what evidence would change the judgement.

writing.prompt: Write an advisory commentary about the teaching case, using Source A only. Evaluate the initial proposal, explain the most important qualification, recommend a proportionate response, and identify what could change your judgement. Do not copy the model. Use an appropriate register for the people responsible at a presentation proposing a shared tool library.
writing.sample:
The immediate objective should be to defend the observed interest while proposing a small pilot to test return times and repair needs. At a presentation proposing a shared tool library, the initial suggestion was to answer questions about demand and maintenance. The relevant background is that the presenter had survey responses from interested residents and a repair budget based on quotations, but no evidence about how often tools would return late. Nevertheless, a confident presentation could make an untested operating assumption look like an established result. A defensible response must preserve the distinction this creates rather than resolve the difficulty by ignoring part of the account.

The presenter should not defend return times as though survey enthusiasm had measured them. Interest, venue costs, repair quotations and actual borrowing behaviour are different forms of information. The first three can justify trying a small service, while a pilot is needed for the fourth. Answering the question directly would make that distinction visible: the plan assumes timely returns, and that assumption has not been tested. The pilot should record delays and maintenance needs before the group invests in a larger collection. This response protects the documented parts of the proposal without treating the whole presentation as invulnerable. An audience can have more confidence in a plan that knows how to learn than in one whose author can only repeat assurances.

I would record the recommendation together with its conditions and the information that could make it necessary to reconsider. The strongest objection should be answered in its actual form, not replaced by a more convenient one. If later evidence changes the position, the revision should be explained openly. The point is to make a proportionate decision that remains accountable to the details, rather than adopt a more impressive conclusion whose certainty the case cannot support.

Restate the opposing view in its strongest reasonable form, then explain the remaining disagreement.
speaking.sample: I would separate the original idea from the qualification that changes its meaning. The proposal was to answer questions about demand and maintenance. The relevant detail is that the presenter had survey responses from interested residents and a repair budget based on quotations, but no evidence about how often tools would return late. However, a confident presentation could make an untested operating assumption look like an established result. For that reason, I would defend the observed interest while proposing a small pilot to test return times and repair needs. This does not dismiss every contribution; it makes the decision more precise. If challenged, I would distinguish the stated details from my interpretation. I would also explain what information could change my mind, rather than defend the same conclusion regardless of the evidence.

assessmentListening.text: I want to explain a decision we reached during a presentation about a neighbourhood repair event. It would be easy to report only the most memorable phrase and miss why the group changed its approach. The relevant background was that the presenter had reliable venue costs but no estimate of repair time. However, a questioner asked whether long queues would make the event impractical. We therefore needed to acknowledge the untested assumption without discarding the documented costs. That distinction mattered more than making the final summary sound confident. After discussing the alternatives, the group decided to run a small pilot and record waiting times before enlarging the event. The decision was not a claim that the initial observation had no value. It was a way to preserve what remained useful without carrying forward an implication the available detail could not justify. If someone later summarises our discussion, I would want both the reason for the concern and the agreed action to remain visible. Otherwise, a listener might reasonably understand a much stronger conclusion than we intended.
assessmentListening.delivery: Original fictional script. TTS or printed text does not substitute for independent assessment with unfamiliar human speech.
