sourceA.title: 教学案例：a learner preparing a language portfolio
sourceA.text:
At a learner preparing a language portfolio, participants considered whether to show progress without hiding the amount of assistance received. The background was specific: the portfolio included an initial report, reviewer comments and a revised version, with a record of dictionaries, translation tools and human support used. However, a polished final text alone could not show what the learner could produce independently under unfamiliar conditions. The proposed response was to retain the revision history and add a fresh timed task completed with clearly stated conditions.

A portfolio can demonstrate learning precisely because it reveals how a text changed. Removing the initial draft would conceal the decisions and assistance that produced the final version. I would include selected reviewer comments, the learners response to them and an account of any substantial rewriting by others. A fresh independent task should sit alongside the polished work, with its time limit and permitted tools stated. The two products answer different questions and should not be collapsed into one flattering score. Reflection is strongest when it identifies a transferable method the learner can apply again, not merely gratitude for corrections. Reviewers can then distinguish a developed revision skill from an unsupported claim of equal performance in every unfamiliar situation. The final essay shows the quality achieved with feedback, not necessarily unaided performance. I have included the first draft so that the revision process remains visible. The assistance record distinguishes dictionary use from substantial human rewriting. A fresh timed task provides evidence that the polished portfolio cannot supply. The reflection should identify a change in method rather than merely express satisfaction.

sourceB.title: 独立测验：a mentor reviewing a speaking portfolio
sourceB.text:
A separate fictional case offers another opportunity to distinguish an observation from its interpretation. The people involved share enough common ground to continue working, but their initial description risks implying more than they have established. The difference becomes visible when the suggested action is compared with the available detail.

At a mentor reviewing a speaking portfolio, the discussion concerned whether to distinguish rehearsed fluency from spontaneous interaction. There was a reason the idea initially appeared attractive: one recording showed an elegant prepared talk, while another captured an unplanned discussion with interruptions and requests for clarification. That account nevertheless contained an important reservation: the prepared talk demonstrated organisation but could not establish how the speaker handled unexpected contributions. The suggested response was to include both kinds of performance and describe the different abilities each makes visible.

Prepared performance and spontaneous interaction involve overlapping but different demands. A rehearsed talk allows the speaker to choose vocabulary, organise the sequence and practise difficult sounds in advance. An unscripted exchange requires attention to another persons contribution and sometimes a reformulation that was never planned. Neither recording should be discarded. Together they provide a richer picture, provided the preparation conditions are visible. The mentor should also note whether the listener repeatedly rescued the speaker or whether clarification was successfully initiated and resolved. A single smooth recording may be encouraging, but it cannot justify a broad claim about performance across unfamiliar situations. The portfolio should reveal that boundary rather than hide it.

The conclusion remains specific to the conditions described. Another interpretation should account for the same details, identify any additional assumptions, and explain what evidence would change the judgement.

sourceA.title: 教学案例：a fictional final course review
sourceA.text:
At a fictional final course review, participants considered whether to separate completion from demonstrated advanced competence. The background was specific: a learner completed every exercise but performed unevenly on an unfamiliar reading, a live discussion and an independently assessed essay several weeks later. However, a single percentage could conceal a strong reading result alongside unresolved speaking difficulties. The proposed response was to report the four skills separately, preserve assessor comments and plan targeted practice before reassessment.

The completion record deserves recognition, but the unfamiliar tasks provide the more relevant evidence about transfer. If reading is strong and spontaneous speaking remains uncertain, averaging them into one reassuring figure would obscure the next learning need. Each skill should be reported with conditions, assessor comments and the limits of the judgement. Disagreement between reviewers should lead to examination of the performance and criteria, not an unexplained compromise. The learner can then practise the weak area and return to a new task after an interval. This approach may produce a narrower conclusion than the learner hoped for, but it gives a credible direction for improvement. A course badge should record what has actually been established rather than borrow authority from an ambitious target label. Completing every exercise is evidence of persistence rather than proof of C2 proficiency. The unfamiliar task revealed a weakness hidden by repeated course items. We should report the four skills separately before considering any overall judgement. The delayed assessment tests retention and transfer rather than immediate recall alone. Two reviewers disagreed, so the result requires discussion rather than automatic averaging. The badge currently represents course completion, with proficiency still to be verified.

sourceB.title: 独立测验：an external review of an advanced language programme
sourceB.text:
In this newly invented case, readers should attend to the relationship between a stated aim and the evidence used to defend it. The account does not invite a judgement about personalities. Instead, it supplies a limited situation in which a careful summary can preserve something that a confident headline loses.

At an external review of an advanced language programme, the discussion concerned whether to evaluate whether its final badge represented transferable ability. There was a reason the idea initially appeared attractive: the review found high scores on repeated course items but no comparable results on new tasks assessed after a delay by independent reviewers. That account nevertheless contained an important reservation: the programme had evidence of practice success rather than proof that its advertised proficiency had been reached. The suggested response was to commission independent tasks, document conditions and describe the badge as course completion until validation is available.

Repeated items can show that learners remember practised material. They cannot reveal how much the same learners will understand when vocabulary, speaker and task change. The review therefore needs assessments protected from rehearsal, with conditions recorded and productive work evaluated independently. Different skills may show different results, so one average should not conceal a persistent weakness. Disagreement between assessors should trigger examination of evidence and criteria rather than an unexplained arithmetic compromise. Until such validation exists, a completion badge remains useful as a record of participation and effort. It becomes misleading only when the programme presents it as a proficiency judgement the available evidence has not established.

The conclusion remains specific to the conditions described. Another interpretation should account for the same details, identify any additional assumptions, and explain what evidence would change the judgement.

writing.prompt: Write an advisory commentary about the teaching case, using Source A only. Evaluate the initial proposal, explain the most important qualification, recommend a proportionate response, and identify what could change your judgement. Do not copy the model. Use an appropriate register for the people responsible at a fictional final course review.
writing.sample:
The immediate objective should be to report the four skills separately, preserve assessor comments and plan targeted practice before reassessment. At a fictional final course review, the initial suggestion was to separate completion from demonstrated advanced competence. The relevant background is that a learner completed every exercise but performed unevenly on an unfamiliar reading, a live discussion and an independently assessed essay several weeks later. Nevertheless, a single percentage could conceal a strong reading result alongside unresolved speaking difficulties. A defensible response must preserve the distinction this creates rather than resolve the difficulty by ignoring part of the account.

The completion record deserves recognition, but the unfamiliar tasks provide the more relevant evidence about transfer. If reading is strong and spontaneous speaking remains uncertain, averaging them into one reassuring figure would obscure the next learning need. Each skill should be reported with conditions, assessor comments and the limits of the judgement. Disagreement between reviewers should lead to examination of the performance and criteria, not an unexplained compromise. The learner can then practise the weak area and return to a new task after an interval. This approach may produce a narrower conclusion than the learner hoped for, but it gives a credible direction for improvement. A course badge should record what has actually been established rather than borrow authority from an ambitious target label.

I would record the recommendation together with its conditions and the information that could make it necessary to reconsider. The strongest objection should be answered in its actual form, not replaced by a more convenient one. If later evidence changes the position, the revision should be explained openly. The point is to make a proportionate decision that remains accountable to the details, rather than adopt a more impressive conclusion whose certainty the case cannot support.

speaking.prompt: Without reading a script, explain your response to the teaching case at a fictional final course review. Speak for two to three minutes, distinguish evidence from inference, and respond to a partner who disagrees.
followups: Which detail would most strongly justify changing your recommendation to report the four skills separately, preserve assessor comments and plan targeted practice before reassessment?
Restate the opposing view in its strongest reasonable form, then explain the remaining disagreement.
speaking.sample: I would separate the original idea from the qualification that changes its meaning. The proposal was to separate completion from demonstrated advanced competence. The relevant detail is that a learner completed every exercise but performed unevenly on an unfamiliar reading, a live discussion and an independently assessed essay several weeks later. However, a single percentage could conceal a strong reading result alongside unresolved speaking difficulties. For that reason, I would report the four skills separately, preserve assessor comments and plan targeted practice before reassessment. This does not dismiss every contribution; it makes the decision more precise. If challenged, I would distinguish the stated details from my interpretation. I would also explain what information could change my mind, rather than defend the same conclusion regardless of the evidence.

assessmentListening.text: I want to explain a decision we reached during an advanced course review. It would be easy to report only the most memorable phrase and miss why the group changed its approach. The relevant background was that learners scored highly on repeated quizzes but unevenly on delayed new tasks. However, the final badge had been advertised as proof of a proficiency level. We therefore needed to distinguish course success from independently demonstrated transferable ability. That distinction mattered more than making the final summary sound confident. After discussing the alternatives, the group decided to revise the badge wording and obtain external assessments using unfamiliar material. The decision was not a claim that the initial observation had no value. It was a way to preserve what remained useful without carrying forward an implication the available detail could not justify. If someone later summarises our discussion, I would want both the reason for the concern and the agreed action to remain visible. Otherwise, a listener might reasonably understand a much stronger conclusion than we intended.
assessmentListening.delivery: Original fictional script. TTS or printed text does not substitute for independent assessment with unfamiliar human speech.

units.title: 码头的新朋友
units.story: 渡船靠岸了。向导 Mia 带你走进小镇。先认识彼此，再领取第一张旅行地图。
units.end: Mia 记住了你的名字。你也有了在小镇的第一位朋友。

units.title: 寻找我的小屋
units.story: 房东 Ben 在林间街道等你。拿上钥匙和背包，问清路线，就能找到今晚的住处。
units.end: 你找到了公园旁的小屋，推开窗就是树叶的声音。

units.title: 广场上的下午
units.story: 午后，你走进 Nora 的咖啡馆。一次礼貌的请求，一句感谢，让陌生人慢慢熟悉起来。
units.end: Nora 邀请你加入小镇读书会。明天，你有了新的约定。

units.title: 属于我的小镇
units.story: 读书会前，你在长椅上发现一本书。找到主人，再向大家介绍自己，成为小镇的新居民。
units.end: 欢迎成为小镇居民。带着你的名字、故事和好奇心，准备下一段旅程。

units.title: 清晨的钟声
units.story: 和 Mia 交换作息，找到适合自己的学习节奏。
units.end: 你在小屋厨房完成了这段交流，收集到晨光邮票。下一段故事会带来新的表达任务。

units.title: 一周的节奏
units.story: 查看开放时间，比较习惯，安排一周。
units.end: 你在镇立图书馆完成了这段交流，收集到日程邮票。下一段故事会带来新的表达任务。

units.title: 共享的一天
units.story: 约好午餐，分配家务，区分习惯和正在发生的事。
units.end: 你在社区厨房完成了这段交流，收集到合作邮票。下一段故事会带来新的表达任务。

units.title: 留一点时间给自己
units.story: 调整约定，留出休息和学习时间。
units.end: 你在林间小屋完成了这段交流，收集到日常通行证。下一段故事会带来新的表达任务。

units.title: 市集采购单
units.story: 核对数量、价格和付款方式，完成采购。
units.end: 你在周末市集完成了这段交流，收集到市集邮票。下一段故事会带来新的表达任务。

units.title: 咖啡馆午餐
units.story: 阅读菜单，说明需要，核对账单。
units.end: 你在广场咖啡馆完成了这段交流，收集到点餐邮票。下一段故事会带来新的表达任务。

units.title: 穿过城市
units.story: 问清路线、距离和站台，再出发。
units.end: 你在中央车站完成了这段交流，收集到路线邮票。下一段故事会带来新的表达任务。

units.title: 办好一件小事
units.story: 预约服务，阅读规则，比较可选方案。
units.end: 你在城市服务中心完成了这段交流，收集到城市通行证。下一段故事会带来新的表达任务。

units.title: 昨天的旅程

units.end: 你在小镇展馆完成了这段交流，收集到回忆邮票。下一段故事会带来新的表达任务。

units.title: 遗失的背包
units.story: 描述当时情境与物品，拼起完整经过。
units.end: 你在失物招领处完成了这段交流，收集到线索邮票。下一段故事会带来新的表达任务。

units.title: 第一次的故事

units.end: 你在社区故事会完成了这段交流，收集到经历邮票。下一段故事会带来新的表达任务。

unitLiteracy.passage: Mia is from the town. Her new friend Alex is from China. They meet at the harbour and walk to the library together.
unitLiteracy.question: Alex 来自哪里？
unitLiteracy.answer: China
options: China
The town
Japan
unitLiteracy.writingPrompt: 写几句英文介绍角色 Alex，并问候新朋友。
unitLiteracy.sample: Hello! My name is Alex. I am from China. Nice to meet you.

unitLiteracy.passage: Ben has a key and a map. Alex has a bag. The house is near the park. Mia can help Alex find the house.
unitLiteracy.question: 谁有包？
unitLiteracy.answer: Alex
options: Alex
Ben
The driver
unitLiteracy.writingPrompt: 写一条消息说明你有包、需要帮助，并询问公园位置。
unitLiteracy.sample: I have a bag. Can you help me? Where is the park?

unitLiteracy.passage: Nora works at the cafe. Alex asks for water. Nora finds a bag under the table. Alex thanks her and talks about reading.
unitLiteracy.question: Nora 在哪里工作？
unitLiteracy.answer: At the cafe
options: At the cafe
At the station
At the school
unitLiteracy.writingPrompt: 用短句写一段咖啡馆交流，包括要水和感谢。
unitLiteracy.sample: I would like some water, please. Thank you very much for your help. I like reading.

unitLiteracy.passage: The reading club meets tomorrow. Ben cannot find his book, but Alex sees it on a bench. Alex asks Ben if the book is his.
unitLiteracy.question: 读书会何时见面？
unitLiteracy.answer: Tomorrow
options: Tomorrow
Yesterday
Next month
unitLiteracy.writingPrompt: 写一条简短告别消息，提到今天开心、明天再见。
unitLiteracy.sample: I am happy today. Thank you for a lovely afternoon. See you tomorrow.

unitLiteracy.passage: Mia gets up at seven. She has breakfast at home and goes to work by bus. Her brother starts work earlier, so he leaves before breakfast.
unitLiteracy.question: Mia 怎样上班？
unitLiteracy.answer: By bus
options: By bus
By bike
On foot
unitLiteracy.writingPrompt: 写一小段介绍角色的起床、早餐和交通方式。
unitLiteracy.sample: I get up at seven. I usually have breakfast at home, and then I go to work by bus.

unitLiteracy.passage: The library opens at nine. Nora visits twice a week. She usually reads in the afternoon, but she does not go on Sundays because the library is closed.
unitLiteracy.question: Nora 每周去几次？
unitLiteracy.answer: Twice
options: Twice
Once
Every day
unitLiteracy.writingPrompt: 写几句说明你读书的时间和每周去图书馆的频率。
unitLiteracy.sample: I sometimes read in the afternoon. I visit the library twice a week, but I do not go on Sundays.

unitLiteracy.passage: Ben is free at lunchtime. He and Mia agree to meet outside the library. In the evening, Ben is cooking while Mia washes the dishes after dinner.
unitLiteracy.question: 午餐前约在哪里见？
unitLiteracy.answer: Outside the library
options: Outside the library
Inside the kitchen
At the station
unitLiteracy.writingPrompt: 写一条约见消息，说清时间、地点和晚上的安排。
unitLiteracy.sample: Are you free at lunchtime? Let us meet outside the library. I am cooking dinner this evening, so I cannot meet later.

unitLiteracy.passage: Alex studies English for twenty minutes each day. Before bed, Alex turns off the phone and reads. Tomorrow, the meeting moves from three to four.
unitLiteracy.question: 会议改到几点？
unitLiteracy.answer: Four
options: Four
Three
Twenty
unitLiteracy.writingPrompt: 写一条消息解释你每天的学习时间，并提出改约见时间。
unitLiteracy.sample: I spend twenty minutes learning English each day. Can we meet at four instead of three tomorrow? I need some time to study first.

unitLiteracy.passage: At the market, Nora buys two bottles of water and a sandwich. The sandwich costs three pounds. She pays by card and keeps the receipt.
unitLiteracy.question: Nora 买几瓶水？
unitLiteracy.answer: Two
options: Two
Three
Five
unitLiteracy.writingPrompt: 写采购便条，说明需要两瓶水，并问三明治价格。
unitLiteracy.sample: I need two bottles of water. How much is this sandwich? I would like to pay by card and keep the receipt.

unitLiteracy.passage: Ben orders vegetable soup and a drink without sugar. The cafe offers food to take away, but Ben decides to eat there. He checks the bill before paying.
unitLiteracy.question: Ben 决定在哪里吃？
unitLiteracy.answer: At the cafe
options: At the cafe
At home
On the bus
unitLiteracy.writingPrompt: 写一段点餐请求，包含汤、不加糖的饮料和堂食。
unitLiteracy.sample: I would like the vegetable soup and a drink without sugar, please. I would like to eat here. Could I see the bill afterwards?

unitLiteracy.passage: To reach the museum, walk to the next crossing and turn left. Bus six stops outside the station. The museum is ten minutes away on foot from there.
unitLiteracy.question: 在下一个路口应怎样走？
unitLiteracy.answer: Turn left
options: Turn left
Turn right
Go back
unitLiteracy.writingPrompt: 写给朋友的路线提示，提到路口左转和步行十分钟。
unitLiteracy.sample: Turn left at the next crossing. The museum is about ten minutes away on foot. You can ask at the station if you need help.

unitLiteracy.passage: The service centre accepts appointments by phone. The library next door lends books for three weeks. Its computer area is open on public holidays, but appointments at the service centre are not available then.
unitLiteracy.question: 哪项服务公共假日仍开放？
unitLiteracy.answer: The computer area
options: The computer area
Service centre appointments
Telephone repairs
unitLiteracy.writingPrompt: 写一条询问信息，问预约方法和图书可借多久。
unitLiteracy.sample: I would like to make an appointment. Could you tell me how to book it? I would also like to know how long I can keep a library book.

unitLiteracy.passage: Yesterday, Mia visited a museum with Ben. They had lunch by the river. On the way home, Mia missed the bus, so they walked and talked about the exhibition.
unitLiteracy.question: 他们为什么步行？
unitLiteracy.answer: Mia missed the bus
options: Mia missed the bus
The weather was bad
The museum was closed
unitLiteracy.writingPrompt: 写几句按顺序讲述参观、午餐和回家方式。
unitLiteracy.sample: Yesterday, we visited the museum. Then we had lunch by the river. I missed the bus, so we walked home and talked about the exhibition.

unitLiteracy.passage: Alex was waiting at the stop when it started to rain. After getting on the bus, Alex noticed the blue bag was missing. A passenger later gave it to the driver.
unitLiteracy.question: 谁把包交给司机？
unitLiteracy.answer: A passenger
options: A passenger
Alex
The museum guide
unitLiteracy.writingPrompt: 写一小段丢包经过，包括当时的情境和最终线索。
unitLiteracy.sample: I was waiting at the stop when it started to rain. Later, I realised I had left my blue bag on the bus. A passenger gave it to the driver.

unitLiteracy.passage: Nora grew up near the sea and used to ride to school. When she first cooked for friends, she forgot the salt. She laughs about it now because the friends still enjoyed the meal.
unitLiteracy.question: Nora 第一次为朋友做饭时忘了什么？
unitLiteracy.answer: Salt
options: Salt
The plates
The time
unitLiteracy.writingPrompt: 写一段关于第一次尝试的短故事，并说明你学到了什么。
unitLiteracy.sample: The first time I cooked for friends, I forgot to add salt. They still enjoyed the meal. The experience taught me to check the details before serving food.

unitLiteracy.passage: Although the trip began badly, Ben enjoyed it. A neighbour helped with the bags. Ben felt nervous at first but became more confident after asking people for help. Everyone arrived safely in the end.
unitLiteracy.question: Ben 的感受怎样变化？
unitLiteracy.answer: From nervous to more confident
options: From nervous to more confident
From happy to angry
From confident to frightened
unitLiteracy.writingPrompt: 写一个有转折和结尾的经历段落。
unitLiteracy.sample: Although the journey was difficult, we enjoyed the trip. A neighbour helped with our bags. I felt nervous at first, but asking for help made me more confident. In the end, we arrived safely.

unitLiteracy.passage: Mia is going to the coast next month. She has reserved a window seat on Friday morning. She prefers the train because it is comfortable, and will pack a jacket in case it gets cold.
unitLiteracy.question: 为什么要带外套？
unitLiteracy.answer: In case it gets cold
options: In case it gets cold
Because the train is delayed
To carry food
unitLiteracy.writingPrompt: 写一段行前计划，包含目的地、交通和行李理由。
unitLiteracy.sample: I am going to visit the coast next month. I prefer the train because it is comfortable. I will reserve a window seat and pack a light jacket in case it gets cold.

unitLiteracy.passage: The guest has booked two nights. Breakfast is included, but a quieter room must be requested. Check-out is at eleven. Reception can keep luggage until the afternoon.
unitLiteracy.question: 退房后前台可以帮助什么？
unitLiteracy.answer: Keep luggage
options: Keep luggage
Provide a free train ticket
Extend every stay
unitLiteracy.writingPrompt: 写给旅店的简短询问信，提到房间需求和寄存行李。
unitLiteracy.sample: Hello, I have a reservation for two nights. Could we have a room away from the lift? May I leave my luggage at reception after checking out? Please let me know the arrangements.

unitLiteracy.passage: The train is delayed by an hour. The group considers a direct coach, which costs less but takes longer. If the weather is good, they still hope to go hiking after arriving.
unitLiteracy.question: 长途汽车的取舍是什么？
unitLiteracy.answer: Cheaper but slower
options: Cheaper but slower
Faster but more expensive
Free but cancelled
unitLiteracy.writingPrompt: 写几句比较两个交通方案，并给出一个条件下的计划。
unitLiteracy.sample: The coach costs less, but it takes longer than the direct train. I would prefer the train if it leaves soon. If the weather is good, we will go hiking after we arrive.

unitLiteracy.passage: Nora wants to keep the total cost under two hundred pounds. She hopes to try local food and visit a quiet beach. The group will stay two nights and return on Sunday.
unitLiteracy.question: 他们什么时候返回？
unitLiteracy.answer: Sunday
options: Sunday
Friday
Monday
unitLiteracy.writingPrompt: 写一段简短旅行计划，说明预算、期待和返回时间。
unitLiteracy.sample: We would like to keep the total cost under two hundred pounds. I am looking forward to trying the local food. We will stay for two nights and return on Sunday.

unitLiteracy.passage: At the service point, a visitor describes a headache and asks to speak to a doctor. The assistant checks the appointment time. The visitor repeats the details to make sure they have understood correctly.
unitLiteracy.question: 访客为何重复安排？
unitLiteracy.answer: To confirm understanding
options: To confirm understanding
To cancel every appointment
To give medical advice
unitLiteracy.writingPrompt: 写一条求助信息，说明不适并请求专业人员帮助。
unitLiteracy.sample: I have had a headache since this morning. Could I speak to a doctor, please? I would like to check the appointment time so that I understand the arrangements correctly.

unitLiteracy.passage: A guest reports that the heater is not working. The cold makes it difficult to sleep. The guest asks for a visit today and requests another room if the heater cannot be repaired.
unitLiteracy.question: 无法修好时，客人希望什么？
unitLiteracy.answer: A different room
options: A different room
A longer holiday
A new ticket
unitLiteracy.writingPrompt: 写一段清楚的故障说明、影响和请求。
unitLiteracy.sample: The heater in my room is not working, and the cold is making it difficult to sleep. Could someone check it today? If it cannot be repaired, I would like to change rooms.

unitLiteracy.passage: A customer returns a jacket that does not fit. She has the receipt and the original packaging. After discussing a replacement and a refund, she chooses a replacement in a smaller size.
unitLiteracy.question: 顾客最终选择什么？
unitLiteracy.answer: A smaller replacement
options: A smaller replacement
A full refund
A repair
unitLiteracy.writingPrompt: 写一条退换请求，说明购买情况、问题和希望的处理方式。
unitLiteracy.sample: I bought this jacket yesterday, but it does not fit. I still have the receipt and the original packaging. Could I exchange it for a smaller size? That solution would work for me.

unitLiteracy.passage: The caller thinks there has been a misunderstanding about an extra charge. The assistant explains the fee, writes down the details and agrees to send confirmation by email.
unitLiteracy.question: 最后同意怎样发送确认？
unitLiteracy.answer: By email
options: By email
By taxi
By post only
unitLiteracy.writingPrompt: 写几句请求澄清一项收费，并要求书面确认。
unitLiteracy.sample: I think there has been a misunderstanding about the extra charge. Could you explain what it means? I would appreciate it if you could send the details and a confirmation by email.

unitLiteracy.passage: Nora invites friends to dinner. Ben would love to come, but he already has plans. He suggests another day. Mia accepts and offers to bring fruit to help with the meal.
unitLiteracy.question: 谁提出带水果？
unitLiteracy.answer: Mia
options: Mia
Ben
The organiser
unitLiteracy.writingPrompt: 写一条接受或婉拒邀请的消息，并说明下一步安排。
unitLiteracy.sample: Thank you for inviting me to dinner. I would love to join you, but I already have plans. Could we meet another day instead? I would be happy to bring some fruit next time.

unitLiteracy.passage: At the gallery, Mia meets a friend who helped her move. They talk about photography. Instead of changing the subject immediately, Mia asks what her friend enjoyed most and invites her to explain more.
unitLiteracy.question: Mia 怎样延续话题？
unitLiteracy.answer: By asking follow-up questions
options: By asking follow-up questions
By leaving immediately
By ignoring the answer
unitLiteracy.writingPrompt: 写一条交流消息，介绍共同兴趣并提出一个追问。
unitLiteracy.sample: I have been interested in photography for years. It was lovely to talk about the gallery with you. What did you enjoy most about the exhibition? Could you tell me more about your favourite picture?

unitLiteracy.passage: Some club members prefer a large event, while Ben would rather meet in a smaller group. He explains that smaller groups give everyone more time to contribute. He also recognises that larger events can introduce people to new friends.
unitLiteracy.question: Ben 偏好小团体的理由是什么？
unitLiteracy.answer: More time for everyone to contribute
options: More time for everyone to contribute
No one needs to talk
It always costs nothing
unitLiteracy.writingPrompt: 写一个有理由、也承认另一面好处的偏好段落。
unitLiteracy.sample: I would rather start with a small group because everyone would have more time to contribute. However, I understand that a large event could help us meet more people. Perhaps we could try both at different times.

unitLiteracy.passage: Leo congratulates a friend on a new job. Later, another friend describes a difficult day. Leo listens and offers help rather than changing the topic. Before leaving, they agree to keep in touch.
unitLiteracy.question: 朋友难过时 Leo 怎样回应？
unitLiteracy.answer: Listens and offers help
options: Listens and offers help
Changes the topic
Offers congratulations only
unitLiteracy.writingPrompt: 写几句回应朋友的喜忧，并表达愿意保持联系。
unitLiteracy.sample: Congratulations on your new job! I would love to hear more about it. I am also sorry that you have had a difficult day. Is there anything I can do to help? Let us keep in touch.

unitLiteracy.passage: Leo describes two years of English study and an event he helped organise for new students. He explains a strength, then gives an example of a challenge: managing time while keeping everyone informed.
unitLiteracy.question: 他用什么支持能力介绍？
unitLiteracy.answer: A specific event experience
options: A specific event experience
Only a list of adjectives
An unrelated holiday story
unitLiteracy.writingPrompt: 写一段简短自我介绍，用一个经历支持你的长处。
unitLiteracy.sample: I have studied English for two years. I am good at explaining ideas clearly, and I helped organise an event for new students. Managing the time was challenging, but I learned to keep the team informed and ask for help when necessary.

unitLiteracy.passage: The team must submit a report by Friday. Mia collects information while Leo prepares slides. They have finished the main research, but the introduction needs work. They ask the coordinator whether a short extension is possible.
unitLiteracy.question: 哪部分仍需要完善？
unitLiteracy.answer: The introduction
options: The introduction
The finished slides only
The event invitation
unitLiteracy.writingPrompt: 写一封进度邮件，说明已完成、待处理内容和请求。
unitLiteracy.sample: Hello, we have completed the main research, but the introduction still needs work. I can collect the remaining information while you prepare the slides. Would it be possible to extend the deadline by two days so that we can check the final report carefully?

unitLiteracy.passage: The display compares two service options. The cheaper option requires more travel, while the other saves time. The team says the survey suggests a preference, but they still need to consider older users and the cost of changes before making a recommendation.
unitLiteracy.question: 为什么不能只看调查偏好？
unitLiteracy.answer: Other needs and costs must also be considered
options: Other needs and costs must also be considered
Preferences never matter
The decision has already been made
unitLiteracy.writingPrompt: 写一段比较两个方案的建议，并说明还需考虑的因素。
unitLiteracy.sample: The second option is more convenient because it takes less time, although it costs more. The survey suggests that many people prefer it. However, we should also consider the needs of older users and the cost of the changes before making a final recommendation.

unitLiteracy.passage: Nora writes an enquiry email explaining why she wants to join a programme. She asks for further information and a reply by Thursday. She ends by summarising her goal and thanking the reader, rather than introducing unrelated questions at the end.
unitLiteracy.question: 这封邮件结尾应做什么？
unitLiteracy.answer: Summarise and thank the reader
options: Summarise and thank the reader
Introduce unrelated topics
Repeat every sentence
unitLiteracy.writingPrompt: 写一封简短询问信，包含目的、理由、具体请求和礼貌结尾。
unitLiteracy.sample: Hello, I am writing to ask for further information about the programme. I would like to join because I want to communicate more confidently and learn from other participants. Could you send me the schedule and entry requirements? I would appreciate a reply by Thursday. Thank you for your help.

unitLiteracy.passage: Water at the research station passes through a mesh that removes large particles. It then enters a treatment tank. After treatment, technicians test a sample before allowing the water into storage. A failed sample is treated again. The station records the amount reused, but this record alone does not show whether the process is cheaper than buying water.
unitLiteracy.question: 不合格水样如何处理？
unitLiteracy.answer: Treat it again
options: Treat it again
Store it immediately
Stop all records
unitLiteracy.writingPrompt: 说明水处理顺序，并指出记录重复利用量不能证明什么。
unitLiteracy.sample: Water passes through a mesh and enters a treatment tank. Technicians then test a sample before storage. If it fails the test, it is treated again. The amount reused is recorded, but this does not establish whether the system saves money. We would need information about treatment and purchasing costs.

unitLiteracy.passage: A cycling survey reached people through an online neighbourhood group. Most respondents wanted safer junctions. Only a few respondents lived outside the city centre. The report recommends a wider survey before deciding which routes to improve. The preferences of this sample should not be treated as the views of all residents.
unitLiteracy.question: 为何建议扩大调查？
unitLiteracy.answer: The sample has limited coverage
options: The sample has limited coverage
Nobody wants safer junctions
All residents already answered
unitLiteracy.writingPrompt: 概括发现、抽样局限及下一步。
unitLiteracy.sample: Most respondents wanted safer junctions, but the survey reached a limited online group. Few participants lived outside the centre. A wider survey would give people from other areas a chance to respond. The current results describe this sample and should not be presented as the preferences of every resident.

unitLiteracy.passage: A repair cafe lends tools and teaches residents how to mend household items. The writer welcomes the idea because access to tools can matter more than owning them. However, the article asks who will maintain the equipment. It does not state whether the cafe will charge a membership fee.
unitLiteracy.question: 关于会员费文章说明了什么？
unitLiteracy.answer: It does not say
options: It does not say
Membership is free
Everyone must pay
unitLiteracy.writingPrompt: 概括作者的支持、保留意见和缺失信息。
unitLiteracy.sample: The writer supports the repair cafe because residents can use tools without buying them. However, someone must maintain the equipment. The article does not tell us whether membership fees will be charged. We should distinguish this missing information from an explicit statement that the service is free.

unitLiteracy.passage: A town tested a booking system at one small clinic for three weeks. Waiting times fell, but extra staff were present throughout the trial. The report cannot separate the effect of the system from the effect of staffing. It recommends further testing under ordinary conditions before expanding to every clinic.
unitLiteracy.question: 什么因素妨碍归因？
unitLiteracy.answer: Extra staff were present
options: Extra staff were present
No patients attended
All clinics were tested
unitLiteracy.writingPrompt: 写一段面向公众的谨慎说明，包含发现、限制和下一步。
unitLiteracy.sample: Waiting times fell during the trial, which is encouraging. However, extra staff were present, so the improvement cannot be attributed to the booking system alone. The trial was also short and involved one clinic. Further testing under normal staffing conditions is needed before deciding whether the system should be expanded.

unitLiteracy.passage: The council proposes cheaper bus fares. Supporters say this would improve access to work. Critics point out that a cheap service is of little use when buses are unreliable. A joint proposal combines a limited fare reduction with a trial timetable. The council will compare usage and punctuality before extending the scheme.
unitLiteracy.question: 共同提案包括什么？
unitLiteracy.answer: Lower fares and a trial timetable
options: Lower fares and a trial timetable
Only new roads
Cancel all bus services
unitLiteracy.writingPrompt: 提出明确观点，解释一项理由并回应可靠性问题。
unitLiteracy.sample: I support a limited fare reduction because affordable transport can improve access to work. However, lower prices alone will not help if buses are unreliable. The council should also test the timetable and monitor punctuality. This would provide evidence about both affordability and service quality before a wider commitment is made.

unitLiteracy.passage: Two schools are considering evening classes. One proposal uses existing rooms, while another requires a new building. Existing rooms cost less initially but may be unavailable during examinations. A shared calendar could reduce this problem. The committee has not yet compared running costs over a full year.
unitLiteracy.question: 还缺什么比较？
unitLiteracy.answer: Annual running costs
options: Annual running costs
The colour of the rooms
The names of all pupils
unitLiteracy.writingPrompt: 比较两方案，提出有条件建议并指出缺失证据。
unitLiteracy.sample: Using existing rooms appears less expensive initially, although examination schedules could limit access. A shared calendar may reduce conflicts, so I would test this option before building new facilities. However, the committee should compare annual running costs and room availability. The cheaper starting cost does not necessarily establish which option is better over time.

unitLiteracy.passage: A company reports that flexible hours improved satisfaction. The survey was voluntary, and fewer than half the staff replied. Managers also changed during the same period. The findings are useful for identifying questions, but they do not prove that flexible hours caused every improvement. Anonymous interviews may help explain the results.
unitLiteracy.question: 哪种结论过度？
unitLiteracy.answer: Flexible hours caused every improvement
options: Flexible hours caused every improvement
Some staff replied
Interviews may add information
unitLiteracy.writingPrompt: 解释证据为什么不足以证明因果，并建议补充研究。
unitLiteracy.sample: The survey suggests a possible benefit, but participation was voluntary and fewer than half the staff responded. Management also changed, so several explanations remain possible. Anonymous interviews could explore why people felt differently. A broader follow-up would help determine whether the responses represent staff generally, rather than only the people who chose to reply.

unitLiteracy.passage: A city plans car restrictions near schools. The aim is safer streets, but some disabled residents rely on vehicle access. A revised plan includes permits and a trial period. The writer supports the aim while arguing that exceptions must be practical and easy to request. The plan will be reviewed after a term.
unitLiteracy.question: 作者的立场是什么？
unitLiteracy.answer: Support with practical exceptions
options: Support with practical exceptions
Reject all safer streets
Remove every permit
unitLiteracy.writingPrompt: 写有条件结论，平衡安全与无障碍出行。
unitLiteracy.sample: I support safer streets near schools, provided that residents who need vehicle access can obtain practical exceptions. A permit system should be clear and accessible, rather than creating another barrier. A trial with feedback from disabled residents would help identify problems before permanent restrictions are introduced. Safety and access both need explicit attention in the review.

unitLiteracy.passage: The original workshop time was Tuesday at nine, but a later notice changes it to Thursday at ten. Participants must bring identification. Materials are supplied at no extra charge, but lunch is not included. Registration closes on Monday. The notice says to write no more than two words for each short answer.
unitLiteracy.question: 最终活动是哪天？
unitLiteracy.answer: Thursday
options: Thursday
Tuesday
Monday
unitLiteracy.writingPrompt: 解释最终安排、免费内容及不包含项目。
unitLiteracy.sample: The final arrangement is Thursday at ten, replacing the earlier Tuesday plan. Participants need identification, and registration closes on Monday. Materials are provided without an additional fee, but lunch is not included. When answering questions, I should use the corrected details and follow the stated word limit rather than copying every word from the notice.

unitLiteracy.passage: In a classroom chart, cycling represented twenty percent of journeys in 2018 and thirty percent in 2023. Walking stayed at forty percent. The remaining journeys used other modes. The chart describes shares, not the total number of journeys. No information about weather, fares or reasons for travel is provided.
unitLiteracy.question: 骑车比例增加多少个百分点？
unitLiteracy.answer: Ten
options: Ten
Fifty
Thirty
unitLiteracy.writingPrompt: 写图表概述，报告变化和稳定项，不编造原因。
unitLiteracy.sample: Overall, the share of cycling increased, while walking remained stable. Cycling rose from twenty percent in 2018 to thirty percent in 2023, a change of ten percentage points. Walking accounted for forty percent in both years. The chart does not show the total number of journeys or explain why the proportions changed.

unitLiteracy.passage: An essay question asks whether employers should offer training and who should pay for it. A response discussing only the benefits of learning would leave part of the question unanswered. A useful plan states a position, explains employer and employee interests, and considers how costs might be shared. Examples should develop the argument rather than replace it.
unitLiteracy.question: 只讨论学习好处会漏掉什么？
unitLiteracy.answer: Who should pay
options: Who should pay
The spelling of employers
The date of the course
unitLiteracy.writingPrompt: 用一段论证回答雇主培训及费用分担，包含解释和例子。
unitLiteracy.sample: Employers should provide training that is necessary for a job because competent staff benefit the organisation and its customers. For example, a new booking system may require practical instruction for everyone who uses it. The employer should normally cover such costs. Optional qualifications with wider personal benefits could involve shared funding, depending on the circumstances.

unitLiteracy.passage: A practice interview begins with familiar questions, moves to a longer personal account and ends with a broader discussion. A transcript can reveal missing words or repeated content, but it cannot reliably capture every pause, stress pattern or intelligibility problem. Reviewers need to listen to the original audio when assessing pronunciation and fluency.
unitLiteracy.question: 评价发音需要什么？
unitLiteracy.answer: The original audio
options: The original audio
Only a word count
Only correct spelling
unitLiteracy.writingPrompt: 说明三部分练习，并解释为什么转写不能替代听评。
unitLiteracy.sample: The practice interview moves from familiar questions to a longer account and then to a broader discussion. I should respond naturally and develop relevant ideas rather than repeat a fixed script. A transcript can help review content, but pronunciation and fluency require listening to the original audio. Correct recognition alone is not a quality score.

unitLiteracy.passage: A learner completed a baseline before studying and a different form after six weeks. The second task had a similar format, but its difficulty has not been calibrated. A higher result is encouraging, although form difficulty and practice may contribute. A delayed task and independent review would add evidence about retention and expression quality.
unitLiteracy.question: 为什么不能把增分都归因于课程？
unitLiteracy.answer: Difficulty and practice may contribute
options: Difficulty and practice may contribute
No baseline exists
Both scores are identical
unitLiteracy.writingPrompt: 解释前后测的价值与限制，提出延迟测方案。
unitLiteracy.sample: The learner has useful before-and-after evidence because the baseline came before the course. However, the forms have not been calibrated, so their scores are not perfectly comparable. Practice and task difficulty may also contribute. A new delayed task and independent review of expression would provide stronger evidence, without proving that the course alone caused the change.

unitLiteracy.passage: A reading error log shows that the learner often chooses statements that sound reasonable but are not supported by the text. The next plan includes finding the relevant sentence and explaining why each alternative is unsupported. It avoids repeating only familiar correct answers. A new passage will be used to check transfer.
unitLiteracy.question: 下一轮重点是什么？
unitLiteracy.answer: Checking textual support
options: Checking textual support
Memorising answer letters
Repeating only easy answers
unitLiteracy.writingPrompt: 根据错误类型制定两项练习与一次陌生复测。
unitLiteracy.sample: The plan should focus on evidence in the text. First, the learner can locate the relevant sentence and explain how it supports the answer. Second, the learner can describe why the alternatives are unsupported or contradicted. A new passage should then check transfer. Repeating the same answer letters would not provide comparable evidence of understanding.

unitLiteracy.passage: Two reviewers independently assess one writing sample. They agree about organisation but differ substantially on task response. Each gives a quotation and an explanation. The sample is sent for discussion rather than silently averaging the disagreement. The reviewers use local training criteria; the record is not an official IELTS result.
unitLiteracy.question: 分歧大时应怎样做？
unitLiteracy.answer: Further review with evidence
options: Further review with evidence
Hide the disagreement
Claim an official score
unitLiteracy.writingPrompt: 说明双人独立复核、证据及分歧处理规则。
unitLiteracy.sample: Two reviewers should assess the sample independently and record evidence for each judgement. If they disagree substantially, the sample needs further review. A numerical average would hide an unresolved difference about task response. The record can guide revision, but local training criteria should not be presented as an official IELTS score or a validated prediction.

unitLiteracy.passage: The island council considers a six-week evening transport trial. Success criteria include punctuality, attendance and access for residents with different needs. A review will compare outcomes with the baseline and record costs. Even positive results would justify only a cautious next step because a short local trial may not represent every season or neighbourhood.
unitLiteracy.question: 正面结果能支持什么？
unitLiteracy.answer: A cautious next step
options: A cautious next step
Success in every setting
No further review
unitLiteracy.writingPrompt: 写出最终建议，涵盖行动、衡量标准、限制与下一步。
unitLiteracy.sample: I recommend a limited evening transport trial with clear criteria for punctuality, attendance and access. The review should compare outcomes with a baseline and record costs. Residents with different needs should be included. Positive results would support a cautious next step, but a six-week local trial cannot establish that the service will work equally well in every season or neighbourhood.

unitLiteracy.passage: Nora is practising how to handle an unfamiliar situation involving air travel. Her first response is: "My connecting flight has been cancelled. Could you check the next available connection?" She then adds: "I need to arrive before tomorrow evening because my tour starts then." The other person asks: "What time do you need to reach your destination?" Nora needs to answer the question rather than simply repeat her prepared statement. In a separate situation, another traveller says: "My suitcase did not arrive on the belt. Here is the baggage receipt." The proposed next step is: "Could you give me a reference number and explain how delivery will be arranged?" These two situations require different details even when some useful expressions overlap. A clear response identifies what is known, asks about what remains uncertain and confirms the next action. It should not invent an agreement that the other person has not made. Before ending the conversation, Nora checks whether she has explained her needs and understood any conditions. She records one point that still needs clarification, then tries a new version of the task without reading the original response.
unitLiteracy.question: 文中明确指出，Nora应如何回答对方追问？
unitLiteracy.answer: Answer the question rather than repeat a prepared statement
options: Answer the question rather than repeat a prepared statement
Repeat the prepared statement regardless of the question
Invent an agreement before checking conditions
unitLiteracy.writingPrompt: 结合两种情境，概括双方需求和不确定信息，写一个不同细节的回应，并说明如何确认下一步。
unitLiteracy.sample: The first situation requires a clear explanation of the problem and a practical next step. My connecting flight has been cancelled. Could you check the next available connection? I need to arrive before tomorrow evening because my tour starts then. However, the speaker still needs to answer the follow-up question. In the second situation, the details have changed. My suitcase did not arrive on the belt. Here is the baggage receipt. Could you give me a reference number and explain how delivery will be arranged? I would confirm the relevant conditions before assuming that a solution has been agreed. If I did not understand part of the reply, I would ask for clarification and repeat the important details in my own words. This would help both speakers identify any remaining misunderstanding. I would separate the information explicitly provided from assumptions that merely seem plausible. Where a condition is missing, I would ask a specific question instead of presenting a guess as a fact. The reply should give the other person enough context to respond without requiring them to reconstruct the whole situation. A useful revision would remove vague references, connect each example to the main point and check whether the conclusion follows from the details. Someone might argue that this makes the exchange too long. In response, I would keep the main request concise and offer additional explanation only when it is needed. Clear communication depends on relevance as well as accuracy. Finally, I would confirm the agreed action, who is responsible and when a further response is expected. If no agreement has been reached, that uncertainty should remain visible rather than being hidden behind polite language.

unitLiteracy.passage:
When a broken lamp appeared in our community hall, several volunteers offered to take responsibility for it. Nobody promised to make a profit. The purpose of our repair café was to reduce waste and give neighbours an opportunity to exchange practical skills. Before the first session, we carried out a survey. Most residents wanted help with small electrical items, but a few asked for advice on torn clothes.
Our biggest mistake was to set an unrealistic deadline. We advertised that every repair would be finished within an hour. An experienced engineer pointed out that checking an item safely might take longer than fixing it. We changed the notice and asked visitors to describe their problem in advance. This simple step made a considerable difference to the atmosphere.
By the third Saturday, people were bringing stories as well as objects. One woman explained that her radio had belonged to her father. Although its market value was low, replacing it would not have met her needs. We could not guarantee success, but we paid close attention to her explanation. When the radio finally worked, the whole room applauded. I realised that providing a service sometimes means understanding what matters to someone before deciding what action to take.
unitLiteracy.question: Why did the café change its notice?

unitLiteracy.writingPrompt: Write an article explaining how a community service can meet different people’s needs. Include an example and one limitation.
unitLiteracy.sample:
A useful community service begins with listening. It is tempting to buy impressive equipment first, but an expensive solution may fail if nobody understands the problem. A short survey and several conversations can give organisers a much clearer picture of local needs.
For example, a repair café might discover that visitors care about familiar objects because of their personal history. Volunteers should therefore ask what an item means to its owner as well as what is broken. Clear limits are equally important. Promising to repair everything immediately creates pressure and can lead to unsafe decisions. A realistic booking system allows time for proper checks.
There is one important limitation: volunteers cannot replace qualified professionals in every situation. Dangerous electrical work should be referred to an expert. Explaining this boundary honestly helps maintain trust. In my view, the most successful service combines practical help with careful communication, rather than measuring success only by the number of objects repaired.

unitLiteracy.passage:
When a broken lamp appeared in our community hall, several volunteers offered to take responsibility for it. Nobody promised to make a profit. The purpose of our repair café was to reduce waste and give neighbours an opportunity to exchange practical skills. Before the first session, we carried out a survey. Most residents wanted help with small electrical items, but a few asked for advice on torn clothes.
Our biggest mistake was to set an unrealistic deadline. We advertised that every repair would be finished within an hour. An experienced engineer pointed out that checking an item safely might take longer than fixing it. We changed the notice and asked visitors to describe their problem in advance. This simple step made a considerable difference to the atmosphere.
By the third Saturday, people were bringing stories as well as objects. One woman explained that her radio had belonged to her father. Although its market value was low, replacing it would not have met her needs. We could not guarantee success, but we paid close attention to her explanation. When the radio finally worked, the whole room applauded. I realised that providing a service sometimes means understanding what matters to someone before deciding what action to take.
unitLiteracy.question: What mattered most about the radio?
unitLiteracy.answer: Its connection with the owner’s father.
options: Its connection with the owner’s father.
Its high selling price.
Its modern design.

unitLiteracy.passage:
The roof above our college library used to be an empty concrete surface. Turning it into a garden sounded attractive, but the first proposal was rejected because its financial calculations were incomplete. A student team then worked with an engineer to check the building’s capacity and the accessibility of the stairs. Their revised proposal was less ambitious but much more practical.
Instead of planting large trees, they selected lightweight containers and vegetables that could survive windy conditions. Participation was voluntary, and beginners were given simple instructions. At first, some plants grew unevenly because different groups watered them without checking the soil. The solution was not stricter punishment but a clear weekly record showing what had already been done.
The garden eventually became a quiet place for reading and conversation. Its educational value was unexpected. Students who rarely spoke during lessons confidently explained how compost developed. However, the organisers resisted describing the project as completely sustainable. Delivering soil and replacing damaged containers still used resources. Their end of year report listed both achievements and limitations. This honesty made future funding more likely because supporters could see that the team understood the difference between an attractive idea and a carefully managed activity.
unitLiteracy.question: Why was the first garden proposal rejected?
unitLiteracy.answer: Its financial calculations were incomplete.
options: Its financial calculations were incomplete.
The library was closing permanently.
Students refused to participate.
unitLiteracy.writingPrompt: Write a report recommending how to organise a college rooftop garden. Discuss practical preparation and volunteer participation.
unitLiteracy.sample:
This report recommends a small rooftop garden that students can maintain safely and consistently. The proposal should begin with an engineering check rather than a list of attractive plants. The building must support the equipment, and access should be suitable for the intended volunteers.
Once these conditions are confirmed, the college should start with lightweight containers and a limited range of vegetables. A modest project would be easier to manage than an ambitious design that depends on constant expert attention. Clear instructions and a shared watering record would help beginners contribute without accidentally repeating one another’s work.
Participation should remain voluntary, with short training sessions available to new members. Students could also record plant growth and explain their observations to other classes.
Finally, the project should publish maintenance costs and difficulties alongside achievements. The garden may offer valuable learning and a pleasant meeting place, but a realistic report should not describe it as completely sustainable without examining the resources it uses.

unitLiteracy.passage:
Our geography group had planned to spend a weekend measuring streams in the hills. Although the weather forecast mentioned showers, nobody expected the road to close. Had our tutor not checked the transport website on Friday evening, we would have reached the station with no way to continue. Instead, we stayed in town and redesigned the project.
Some students felt that a local canal could not provide worthwhile evidence. Our tutor asked us to identify the question we actually wanted to answer. We were investigating how recent rainfall affected water flow, not proving that distant places were more interesting. The canal, which was monitored by a public agency, offered a reliable record for comparison. By the end of Saturday, we had collected more usable observations than our original schedule would have allowed.
The revised project still had weaknesses. Since water levels were controlled by gates, we could not attribute every change to rain. We explained this limitation in the report instead of hiding it in a footnote. What impressed our tutor most was not the amount of data but the care with which we interpreted it. The cancelled journey had forced us to distinguish an appealing location from a suitable research method.
unitLiteracy.question: Why did the group avoid a wasted journey?
unitLiteracy.answer: The tutor checked the transport website.
options: The tutor checked the transport website.
The station phoned every student.
Rain had stopped before Friday.
unitLiteracy.writingPrompt: Write an essay: Is changing a plan a sign of failure? Discuss preparation and flexibility.
unitLiteracy.sample:
Changing a plan is often treated as evidence that somebody prepared badly. Although poor preparation can cause difficulties, I believe that a sensible change may actually show good judgement.
Careful planning is valuable because it makes responsibilities and limits clear. A group travelling to collect information should check transport, equipment and safety requirements. Without this preparation, even a simple activity can waste time. However, no plan can predict every change in circumstances. Weather, illness or an unexpected closure may make the original arrangement unsuitable.
In these situations, the important question is whether the purpose can still be achieved. If students can investigate the same research question locally, a shorter journey may be the better choice. They should explain any limitations rather than pretend that the revised method is perfect.
In conclusion, a plan should guide decisions rather than prevent them. Success depends on combining preparation with the willingness to reconsider a method when the evidence changes.

unitLiteracy.passage:
A neighbourhood library began lending drills, sewing machines and gardening equipment alongside books. Its supporters argued that people should not need to buy an expensive tool for a single afternoon’s work. The scheme could reduce household costs and unnecessary production, provided that shared equipment was maintained properly.
Before joining, members attended a short safety session. Staff recorded the condition of each item and kept a small supply of replacement parts. The most popular tool was a carpet cleaner, which several families had previously hired from a commercial shop. A booking calendar prevented arguments about availability, although weekends still filled quickly.
The organisers discovered that environmental benefits were harder to calculate than expected. If a member drove across town to borrow something inexpensive, the journey might cancel part of the saving. Durable tools that replaced several purchases offered a clearer benefit. The library therefore prioritised reliable equipment and encouraged collection during other planned trips.
Six months later, the project had not transformed the local economy, but it had changed conversations about ownership. Members began asking whether access mattered more than possession. The team published repair costs as well as borrowing figures, allowing residents to judge both the practical value and the resources needed to keep the service running.
unitLiteracy.question: What was the main purpose of the tool library?
unitLiteracy.answer: To provide access without requiring individual purchases.
options: To provide access without requiring individual purchases.
To sell new tools at a profit.
To replace every local shop.
unitLiteracy.writingPrompt: Write an essay on whether sharing products is always better than owning them. Discuss cost and environmental impact.
unitLiteracy.sample:
Sharing products can help people save money and use fewer resources. However, whether it is better than ownership depends on the product and the way the service operates.
The financial argument is strongest for equipment that is expensive but rarely needed. A household may use a powerful drill only once a year, so paying a small borrowing fee makes sense. Sharing can also reduce the number of products manufactured. This benefit is greater when the equipment is durable and easy to repair.
There are disadvantages, however. Members may need the same item at the same time, particularly during holidays. Travelling a long distance to collect a small object can also reduce the environmental saving. Moreover, somebody must pay for storage and maintenance.
I therefore support sharing schemes with realistic booking systems and transparent costs. Ownership remains reasonable for frequently used personal items. The best approach is to compare actual needs rather than assume that either sharing or buying is always the responsible choice.

unitLiteracy.sample:
Sharing products can help people save money and use fewer resources. However, whether it is better than ownership depends on the product and the way the service operates.
The financial argument is strongest for equipment that is expensive but rarely needed. A household may use a powerful drill only once a year, so paying a small borrowing fee makes sense. Sharing can also reduce the number of products manufactured. This benefit is greater when the equipment is durable and easy to repair.
There are disadvantages, however. Members may need the same item at the same time, particularly during holidays. Travelling a long distance to collect a small object can also reduce the environmental saving. Moreover, somebody must pay for storage and maintenance.
I therefore support sharing schemes with realistic booking systems and transparent costs. Ownership remains reasonable for frequently used personal items. The best approach is to compare actual needs rather than assume that either sharing or buying is always the responsible choice.

Its supporters argued that people should not need to buy an expensive tool for a single afternoon’s work. The scheme could reduce household costs and unnecessary production, provided that shared equipment was maintained properly.
Before joining, members attended a short safety session. Staff recorded the condition of each item and kept a small supply of replacement parts. The most popular tool was a carpet cleaner, which several families had previously hired from a commercial shop. A booking calendar prevented arguments about availability, although weekends still filled quickly.

The team published repair costs as well as borrowing figures, allowing residents to judge both the practical value and the resources needed to keep the service running.

unitLiteracy.passage: The former railway station stood empty for years before a local group proposed a shared workspace. Rather than assume that everyone needed a private office, the organisers interviewed potential users about their routines. Freelance designers wanted quiet desks, whereas people running small shops mainly needed a place for occasional meetings. These contrasting needs persuaded the group to divide the building into several areas with different booking rules. The ticket office became a silent room, while the waiting hall was suitable for conversations and shared equipment. Despite limited funding, the group invested in good lighting because poor conditions would discourage people from returning. Membership fees covered ordinary running costs, but major repairs still required support from the council and local businesses. At first, several members complained that the booking website allowed some people to reserve too many afternoons. The organisers responded by introducing a weekly limit rather than blaming members for using the existing system. Within three months, bookings were distributed more evenly, although the most convenient times remained particularly popular with commuters. The project’s success depended less on fashionable furniture than on matching practical arrangements to the way members actually worked. Its report recommended regular consultation, recognising that a flexible service must continue adapting as the community and its working habits change.
unitLiteracy.question: Why were interviews carried out?
unitLiteracy.answer: Users had different working routines.
options: Users had different working routines.
The station was still operating trains.
Furniture had already been ordered.
unitLiteracy.writingPrompt: Write an article explaining what makes a shared workplace useful. Discuss facilities and fair access.
unitLiteracy.sample:
A shared workplace should offer more than an attractive photograph for its website. Its real value comes from helping people do their work comfortably and reliably.
Facilities matter, but different tasks require different conditions. Somebody editing a long report may need silence, while a small business owner may want a room for a lively meeting. Separating these activities is usually more effective than asking everyone to tolerate the same level of noise. Reliable lighting and internet access are also sensible priorities before expensive decoration.
Fair access is equally important. If a few members can book every convenient afternoon, others may stop paying for the service. Clear reservation limits and a visible cancellation policy help prevent this problem.
Finally, organisers should consult users regularly. Working habits can change, and a successful arrangement this year may become unsuitable later. A useful workplace is therefore one that combines dependable basic facilities with a willingness to adjust its rules when genuine difficulties appear.

unitLiteracy.passage: Our town’s first walking guide was written by a historian whose knowledge was impressive but whose sentences were extremely long. Although the information was accurate, visitors often stopped reading before they reached the description of the next building. The tourism office invited residents and language learners to help produce a version that would be easier to follow. Each volunteer was asked to explain one location in fewer than a hundred words without removing its main historical significance. This limit forced writers to decide which details were essential and which could be provided separately for interested readers. One contributor replaced an unfamiliar architectural term with a brief description of what visitors could actually see above the door. Another checked whether references such as this and it clearly pointed to the correct building rather than the previous one. The team read the draft aloud because a missing word or awkward connection was often easier to notice by listening. They also walked the route with first time visitors, who revealed that two directions depended on a shop sign that had disappeared. The final guide used permanent landmarks and included enough context for readers to understand why each stop had been selected. It was not simply shorter than the original; its organisation made the relationship between places and explanations much clearer for newcomers. The experience taught the volunteers that successful editing requires attention to grammar, meaning and the reader’s situation at the same time.
unitLiteracy.question: Why did readers stop using the original guide?
unitLiteracy.answer: Its sentences were too long.
options: Its sentences were too long.
Its historical facts were all false.
It had no buildings in it.
unitLiteracy.writingPrompt: Write a report recommending improvements to a visitor guide. Consider language and directions.
unitLiteracy.sample:
The current walking guide contains useful historical information, but visitors may find it difficult to follow. Two changes would make it more practical without removing its educational value.
First, the language should be revised. Several sentences contain too many ideas, and technical terms appear without explanation. Shorter sentences would help, but the aim should be clarity rather than a strict word limit. Essential unfamiliar terms could remain if a brief explanation followed them.
Second, the directions should rely on permanent landmarks. A reference to a temporary shop sign may become inaccurate within a few months. Street names and the visible features of buildings would be safer choices. Each instruction should also make clear whether visitors need to turn before or after a particular point.
I recommend testing the revised guide with people who do not know the town. Asking them to walk the route would reveal problems that experienced residents might overlook. Their experience should inform the final version.

unitLiteracy.passage: When the night train returned to our region, newspaper headlines described it as a complete solution to uncomfortable travel. My first journey suggested a more complicated picture, although I was pleased to reach the city without losing a working day. The compartment was quiet enough for reading, but the movement made deep sleep difficult for passengers unfamiliar with overnight trains. A fellow traveller explained that saving a hotel bill mattered more to her than arriving completely rested for a holiday. For a businessman preparing to give a presentation, however, the same trade off might be much less attractive or practical. Ticket prices were lower when booked early, so comparisons with flights needed to use equivalent dates and booking conditions. The operator advertised reduced environmental impact, but its short publicity leaflet did not explain how the figures had been calculated. This absence did not prove the claim false; it meant that a careful reader needed additional information before accepting it. At the destination, a convenient tram connection helped passengers avoid a costly taxi ride from an airport far outside town. That advantage depended on where travellers actually needed to go, rather than on the station’s central location in itself. I would choose the train again for a relaxed visit, while considering other options before an important morning meeting. The service expands our choices, yet its usefulness cannot be judged accurately without considering the priorities and circumstances of different passengers.
unitLiteracy.question: What does the writer think of the train?
unitLiteracy.answer: Its value depends on the traveller’s priorities.
options: Its value depends on the traveller’s priorities.
It is unsuitable for every passenger.
It always guarantees deep sleep.
unitLiteracy.writingPrompt: Write an essay: Should travel choices be judged mainly by price? Discuss two other considerations.
unitLiteracy.sample:
Price is an important part of a travel decision, especially for people with a limited budget. Nevertheless, comparing tickets alone can give a misleading picture of which option is best.
Time should also be considered. A cheap flight may require a long journey to an airport and an early arrival for security checks. A more expensive train could bring a passenger much closer to the final destination. The relevant comparison is therefore the whole journey rather than the advertised travelling time.
Comfort matters differently according to the purpose of the trip. Somebody going on holiday may enjoy an overnight train despite sleeping less well. A person preparing for an important meeting might reasonably prefer a different arrangement.
In my view, travellers should begin with their actual priorities and compare options under similar booking conditions. The cheapest ticket can be a good choice, but it is not automatically the most economical or suitable journey overall.

unitLiteracy.passage: At the first meeting about restoring a woodland path, volunteers disagreed about whether visitors needed more information or fewer signs. The discussion initially seemed to concern appearance, but it soon revealed different ideas about who would use the route. Regular walkers already recognised the turns, whereas families visiting for the first time wanted reassurance that they were not lost. This difference explained why an apparently unnecessary marker could still be valuable to somebody with less local knowledge. Rather than choose one group’s preference, the team walked the path with visitors who had never seen it before. At a fallen tree, everyone paused because the original route continued behind branches that concealed the next turning point. The team cleared those branches first, which solved a navigation problem without adding another object to the landscape. Further along, however, two equally visible paths led in different directions, so a small arrow remained necessary at that junction. Its wording referred to the destination rather than merely saying continue, allowing walkers to connect the instruction with their map. After the changes, visitors made fewer wrong turns, although heavy rain later created a separate problem with the muddy surface. The final maintenance plan therefore separated tasks concerned with understanding the route from tasks concerned with moving along it safely. This distinction helped volunteers agree on priorities, because solving a communication problem would not automatically repair a damaged physical path.

unitLiteracy.answer: The contrast between familiar and first time walkers.

A difference in tree species.
The cost of two maps.
unitLiteracy.writingPrompt: Write an article explaining how to make a walking route easier for newcomers to follow.
unitLiteracy.sample:
People who know a walking route well often underestimate how confusing it can be for newcomers. Improving a route should therefore begin with observation rather than simply adding more signs.
First, invite someone unfamiliar with the area to follow the path. Notice where they hesitate and ask what information they expected to find. A hidden turning may become clear after a few branches are removed. In that case, an additional sign would create unnecessary clutter.
At a genuine choice between two paths, however, a clear marker is useful. It should name a destination that also appears on the map. An instruction such as continue may not help someone who cannot identify the intended direction.
Finally, organisers must distinguish clear navigation from physical safety. Excellent signs will not repair a muddy surface or a broken bridge. A good maintenance plan addresses both needs separately and checks the route again after changes in weather or vegetation.

unitLiteracy.passage: I agreed to help record our neighbourhood podcast because I thought speaking into a microphone would be the easy part. To be honest, I was far less comfortable when I heard my first recording and noticed how quickly I interrupted people. My colleague said the energy was promising, which sounded encouraging until she added that the guests hardly finished a sentence. She was not asking me to sound less interested; she wanted me to leave enough space for a worthwhile answer. At the next interview, I prepared fewer questions and listened for points that could lead naturally to a follow up. There were uncomfortable pauses, although the guest later told me that those moments had helped her collect her thoughts. I would not describe the result as polished, but the conversation was certainly more revealing than our first attempt together. One listener suggested background music, and I can see the attraction, especially when an episode begins with a long introduction. Still, music underneath every answer might make careful listening harder for some people, so we are testing it only between sections. What surprised me most was how much editing depended on understanding the speaker’s intention rather than removing every hesitation automatically. A small pause can signal uncertainty, and cutting it out may make a cautious statement sound stronger than the speaker intended. I am pleased we tried the project, but I now think of interviewing as a listening skill before considering it a performance.
unitLiteracy.question: How does the speaker view the first recording?
unitLiteracy.answer: It revealed an interviewing weakness.
options: It revealed an interviewing weakness.
It was technically impossible to hear.
It proved guests had nothing to say.
unitLiteracy.writingPrompt: Write a review of a community podcast. Mention a strength, a weakness and a practical recommendation.
unitLiteracy.sample:
Our neighbourhood podcast offers a welcome opportunity to hear local people discuss experiences that rarely appear in the news. Its strongest feature is the range of guests, from shop owners to volunteers restoring public gardens.
The most recent episode was particularly interesting because the interviewer allowed the guest to explain why the work mattered personally. These details made the conversation more memorable than a simple list of achievements. Occasional pauses also sounded natural rather than unprofessional.
However, the introduction was too long, and background music sometimes made quieter answers difficult to hear. This could discourage listeners who use small speakers or have difficulty separating speech from other sounds.
I recommend shortening the opening and keeping music between sections instead of underneath the interview. A written summary with the guest’s main points would improve access as well. Overall, the programme is worth developing, provided that the team continues to put understandable conversation ahead of decorative effects.
